News.title: Granada earthquake - live: Powerful 5-magnitude tremor hits Spain as tourists flee
News.content:
A state of emergency has been declared after the earthquake rocked southern Spain with warnings issued about powerful aftershocks

A powerful 5-magnitude earthquake has hit part of Spain popular with tourists, leaving a trail of destruction as panicking holidaymakers ran from their hotels.

The southern city of Granada, known for its stunning Alhambra Palace, was rocked by the tremor at around 1am local time (midnight in the UK). Homes and cars have been wrecked with images showing rubble in streets and officials warning aftershocks could bring more destruction.

Antonio Sanz Cabello, vice-president of the Andalusian government, said in a post on X that authorities had declared an emergency.

"If you're in Granada, you've felt the earthquake, you're okay, and your home shows no damage, stay calm and avoid entering and exiting buildings unnecessarily," he said. "On the street, stay away from facades, cornices, balconies, walls, and other elements that could fall."

Today's earthquake follows another tremor in Granada in July which measured 3.7 on the Richter scale.

News.title: Nigel Farage warned public 'deserve answers' over finances despite by-election win
News.content:
Nigel Farage warned public 'deserve answers' over finances despite by-election win

EXCLUSIVE:The Labour chair accused the Reform UK leader of delivering weeks of 'political theatre' rather than explain his £5 million ' gift' from Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

View 2 Images Nigel Farage was warned the by-election doesn't change questions about his finances (Image: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock)

The public deserves answers over Nigel Farage’s finances and winning a by-election against a man dressed as a bin doesn’t ‘let him off the hook’, Bridget Phillipson has claimed.

‌



The Labour chair accused the Reform UK leader of delivering weeks of “political theatre”, rather than explain the “scandal” of his £5 million “gift” from Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

‌



Since the farcical vote, which saw Mr Farage face off with Count Binface, the Reform chief has not been seen in public, and even failed to show up for the result of the £250,000 contest he triggered.

‌



Now Ms Phillipson has warned him nothing has changed, and that Labour won't stop fighting for the truth.

View 2 Images Bridget Phillipson vowed Labour would not let Nigel Farage 'off the hook' (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Shutterstock)

‌



Writing for The Mirror, she said: “Nigel Farage wants this week’s by-election to draw a line under the questions surrounding his and Reform UK's finances.

“Spoiler alert: it does not. While he may have won a totally unnecessary by-election, the scandal he’s embroiled in will not magically disappear. Labour will not let him off the hook, because the public deserve to know where the money came from, what it was for, and why it wasn’t declared.

“Was it for security? Was it a reward for Brexit? Was it in exchange for something else? It should be a simple question for Farage to answer – yet his story keeps changing.”

‌



Just after Mr Farage's hollow victory, it emerged that the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards probe into Mr Farage's £5million gift has resumed.

Ms Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, said Mr Farage could have explained himself, but instead put the people of Clacton through a by-election for no reason.

In a firm warning to the former city banker, she said: “Unfortunately for Farage, despite his desperate attempts at distraction, the questions are not going away.

‌



“And Labour will not let him off the hook, because the public deserve to know where the money came from, what it was for, and why it wasn’t declared. Time is running out for Nigel Farage and Reform to come clean.”

Mr Farage has said the gift was not political and insisted he has done nothing wrong. The Reform leader also claimed did not attend the official count for the by-election because he had been advised by police to stay away due to a “credible threat” against him.

Ms Phillipson mocked Mr Farage over spending his summer “fighting with a bin”, and vowed Labour would keep working to bring back hope.

Article continues below

She added: “We know there is more to do. But while Farage and Reform continue to be mired with sleaze, scandal and questionable finances – Labour is fighting every day to build a fairer country, bring back hope and get Britain believing again."

News.title: Emergency phone alert chaos as fire services make plea after being inundated with calls about neighbours' BBQs
News.content:
Emergency phone alert chaos as fire services make plea after being inundated with calls about neighbours' BBQs

Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned last week that Britain is turning into a 'tinderbox' as the severe weather sparks a near-constant parade of wildfires in England and Wales

View 4 Images Wildfires have been raging across the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Fire services across the country have urged people not to call 999 to report people having barbecues after services were inundated with messages from nosey neighbours.

Millions of people living in England and Wales received a message via the Government's mobile alert system on Friday warning them "not to light anything that could spark a fire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks". The alert also asked people to call 999 with any reports of a fire.

But in the wake of the vital advice, people have been calling the emergency number to report neighbours having barbecues, leading fire services to issue an important clarification.

Moment family run for their lives as doorcam captures home engulfed by wildfire READ MORE :

Fire service says what you must NOT do if you spot people barbecuing in heatwave ban READ MORE :

View 4 Images Millions of people received an emergency alert on Friday (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Surrey Fire & Rescue Service was among those experiencing a “high volume” of 999 calls after the warning was rolled out. The service said in a statement on X, formerly Twitter, that people should only contact emergency services if there is a qualified emergency or a fire "producing significant smoke".

A spokesperson for the service said: “Please only call 999 if there is an emergency or a fire producing significant smoke.

“We understand residents may be concerned, but we are unable to respond to reports of neighbours having BBQs, bonfires or campfires in their gardens unless there is an emergency.” The service said it supported the Government’s message and advised against bonfires, fireworks, campfires or disposable barbecues in the dry conditions.

View 4 Images (Image: Getty Images)

Gloucestershire Fire and Rescue Service was also forced to issue a clarification after saying it appreciated the "vigilance" from the general public.

In a statement on Facebook it asked people to call 999 only if there is “a genuine emergency or an immediate risk to life, property or the environment”. That message was echoed by South Wales Fire and Rescue Service, who asked for 999 calls only to report “a new emergency”.

Nineteen homes were destroyed on Thursday in a wildfire in the West Midlands which spread across more than 500 acres in Stourbridge, with the military called to assist emergency services in south Wales.

View 4 Images (Image: Jam Press/Robert Taylor)

Several fires were being tackled across the area on Friday, with around 100 personnel deployed, and a further 100 arriving that evening. They were on hand to distribute water and provide logistical support during a record year for fires.

England and Wales have seen 1,017, with 11 major incidents declared by fire services in just one 24 hour period starting on Thursday.

Phones sounded off across the country on Friday after the Prime Minister warned that "tinderbox" Britain was ready to catch fire and warned the public of a difficult weekend ahead. He said while meeting firefighters in Stourbridge: "I've never seen scenes like this in Britain, where you just see a whole house gutted, smoldering.

Article continues below

"We have to face up to the changing climate (...) there's no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy."

News.title: One million students urged to get free Meningitis B jabs after deadly outbreak
News.content:
One million students urged to get free Meningitis B jabs after deadly outbreak

Since the scheme was launched on July 20, fewer than 100,000 youngsters have had the two-part Meningitis B vaccination

View 3 Images A million youngsters in England are eligible for the free vaccine (Image: Jam Press/NHS)

Students have been issued an urgent warning to get free Meningitis B jabs as soon as possible.

‌



Health experts say young people need to act now so they will be protected against the killer disease when university terms start next month.

‌



A million youngsters in England are eligible for a two-dose vaccination available at local pharmacies as part of a new NHS campaign.

‌



The one-off programme was launched after three students died earlier this year in separate clusters in Kent and Berkshire. A further cluster was recorded in Weymouth, Dorset.

But since the scheme was launched on July 20, fewer than 100,000 youngsters have had the two-part vaccination.

View 3 Images Students receive the Meningitis B vaccine at the University of Kent sports hall on March 19, 2026 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Pharmacist Wendy Lee of Well Pharmacy said: “Starting university means youngsters are meeting lots of new people and often living in close-contact settings such as halls of residence, where infections can spread more easily.

“MenB can become serious very quickly, and vaccination is a simple way to give students and parents peace of mind before they head off to university.

“A big thing to remember is this is not a single vaccination. The course requires two doses given at least four weeks apart.

‌



“So, we encourage students and parents to book now so they are protected rather than waiting until university is about to start.”

The jabs are available to young people who were in Year 13 during the 2025/26 academic year, first-time university students under 25 who will be living in halls or other residential accommodation, and international students under 25 starting at university this year.

Meningitis B is a serious bacterial infection that can cause life-threatening meningitis and septicaemia within hours of infection. One in 10 cases are fatal.

‌



During the cluster in Kent in March, two young people died, including 18 – year-old A-level student Juliette Kenny.

A second victim, a 21-year-old student at the University of Kent, was not publicly named at the family’s request.

View 3 Images The one-off programme was launched after three students died earlier this year in separate clusters in Kent and Berkshire. (Image: Getty Images)

‌



In May 2026, 17-year-old Lewis Waters died from the infection during a separate cluster in the Reading area of Berkshire.

The Kent outbreak, described as unprecedented by then-Health Secretary Wes Streeting, was linked to an event at a nightclub in Canterbury.

Meningitis can develop rapidly and early symptoms can sometimes be mistaken for flu or other illnesses.

‌



Symptoms may include a temperature, headache, vomiting, muscle pain, cold hands and feet, confusion, drowsiness, a stiff neck, dislike of bright lights and a rash that does not fade under pressure.

Anyone concerned about symptoms should seek urgent medical help.

Pharmacists can provide advice on the signs and symptoms of meningitis, when to seek urgent medical care and whether patients are eligible for the free NHS Meningitis B vaccination.

Article continues below

The jab is available at participating pharmacies, including those run by Well, in England. Students and parents can check eligibility and find their nearest pharmacy through the NHS website.

For those who are not eligible for the NHS programme, vaccination is also available privately at many pharmacies.

News.title: Andy Burnham urged to 'step up' on child poverty as families battle summer holidays
News.content:
Andy Burnham urged to 'step up' on child poverty as families battle summer holidays

EXCLUSIVE: Leading charities and children's experts have sounded the alarm over child poverty levels across the UK - as they present their demands to new PM Andy Burnham

View 3 Images Andy Burnham has been urged to 'step up' and help families struggling with the school holidays (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham has been urged to “step up” and help families struggling with the school holidays as parents battle another summer plagued by the cost-of-living crisis.

‌



The new Prime Minister's first days in power saw a rapid-fire list of cost-of-living announcements, including a £2 bus cap, a 20% business rates cut for pubs and a VAT cut to electricity bills from October.

‌



But experts warn extra holiday support is urgently needed for families, who are being forced to go without essentials like food and basic toiletries as extra summer costs hit their pockets.

‌



Children’s Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza said it is a “disgrace” that more than four million kids are living in poverty across the UK. Dame Rachel, who is currently travelling the country speaking to youngsters, told The Mirror: “It is a disgrace that so many children continue to live in dire poverty – without a warm, safe home, suitable clothing, enough fresh food.

Parents urged to check if children can get free school meals after rule change READ MORE :

View 3 Images Children’s Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza said child poverty levels are a 'disgrace' (Image: PA)

"I met a boy who had to curl up at night because his family couldn’t afford a big enough bed. I’ve spoken to children who are too ashamed to have friends over because of mould; another told me a rat bit her face. A girl said she was terrified to walk home from school at dusk because of poor street lighting. Poverty undermines every part of a child’s life – from education to health to their future opportunities.”

‌



Dame Rachel is calling for free bus travel for school-age children - something that is currently in place for under 15s but just for the month of August - and for automatic enrolment for free school meals to ensure no eligible child misses out.

A mum-of-three, who works 32.5 hours a week as a teaching assistant, told The Mirror the summer holidays are a time so many parents “dread” because of the extra financial pressures. The single mum, who did not want to be named and is from Lancashire, said she relies on Universal Credit as her low wage of £1,400 is not enough to cover her rent, bills, childcare costs and other expenses.

She said: “I don't even just see it with just myself. I see it with the parents, the children I work with. They struggle. They dread the holidays because of the cost of extra things.” She said her money worries “massively” impact her mental health, adding: “I get low because of it. I wish I could give my kids a better life, so we weren’t literally living hand to mouth like we do.”

‌



View 3 Images Families are struggling to pay their bills and feed their children, with more than four million kids living in poverty across the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Ahead of this autumn’s Budget, the Prime Minister faces calls from leading charities to lift the benefit cap and look at reforming Universal Credit to help those most in need. The benefit cap is a limit on the total amount of financial support working-age households can receive from most state benefits.

Critics - such as Barnardo's - say the cap “limits the support available to some of the families who are struggling the most”. Other experts, including the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, are demanding reform of Universal Credit with the introduction of an independent process to ensure all families can afford the essentials.

‌



There were also calls for eligibility to be expanded for holiday support, such as existing programmes like the holiday activities and food (HAF) programme, which provides healthy meals, enriching activities, and free childcare places to children from low-income families.

Barnardo's chief executive Lynn Perry told the Mirror: "When schools close, many families face the loss of free school meals, additional childcare costs, the challenge of keeping children active during the long break and it can be the hardest time of the year.”

She welcomed the Government having scrapped the two-child benefit limit, but added: “There is much more to do and we need to bring down the numbers living in poverty overall – including lifting the benefit cap which limits the support available to some of the families who are struggling the most.

‌



"The Government should also set out plans to tackle holiday hunger, including extending eligibility for holiday food and activity support.”

Ruth Talbot, founder of Single Parent Rights, criticised that the benefit cap is the same for a single parent with children as it is for a couple, at £1,835 per month. She said: “Almost 60% of single parents (58%) who are benefit capped have a child aged 0-4, yet we know how hard it is to work with small children.

“The idea that a single mother with a baby is expected to earn the same as a couple combined to avoid being benefit capped is as cruel as it is self-defeating.” She added: “The government needs to step up and help families, especially single parents who are juggling life on one income.”

‌



Peter Matejic, chief analyst at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: "Families with children are more likely to be going without essentials like food, adequate clothing and basic toiletries compared to other families on low incomes. During term time, schools might be able to plug some of those gaps. We need to reform Universal Credit and introduce an independent process to ensure all families can afford the essentials, including in the school holidays.”

Kate Anstey, head of education policy at the Child Poverty Action Group, said: “The PM has said tackling the cost of living is a priority. That has to mean more support for children in low-income families because their well-being and their life chances are on the line.”

More than two million children benefit from free school meals during term time, which means extra pressure on family shopping lists over the holidays.

‌



Plus, parents who need their children looked after while they’re at work are expected to fork out an average of £1,145 per child to cover the six-week summer childcare this year, CORAM Family and Childcare Trust analysis showed last month.

Responding, a Government spokesperson said: “We’re determined to turn the tide on poverty after years of rising hardship. Our recent statistics show that effort is beginning to make a difference - household incomes have risen 5% in real terms, food bank usage has fallen, and food insecurity is down.

“Our Child Poverty Strategy will lift 550,000 children out of poverty in 2030 – the biggest expected reduction in a single parliament.

Article continues below

"We’ve also cut VAT on electricity to give families breathing space, increased the National Minimum Wage and are delivering the first ever sustained above-inflation increase to Universal Credit.

“Alongside this, the government's £200m-a-year Holiday Activities and Food programme provides meals, activities and childcare to children from low-income families.”

News.title: Met Office maps show 28 UK areas face downpours on Tuesday as charts turn blue
News.content:
Met Office maps show 28 UK areas face downpours on Tuesday as charts turn blue

Weather maps show the UK will see much-needed heavy rain on Tuesday coming from a low pressure system over the Atlantic

View 4 Images Rain is expected in multiple parts of the UK (Image: Amer Ghazzal/REX/Shutterstock)

Multiple parts of the UK face heavy downpours on Tuesday with Met Office maps showing a band of rain moving south down the country.

‌



A low pressure system sitting to the northwest of the British Isles will bring the heavy rain to the Highlands of Scotland at first before the bad weather moves through northern England at around 1am.

‌



The rain then moves into Wales later in the morning, according to the maps, and down the western side of the country in a band which stretches across the UK to Lincolnshire in the east. There could be up to 30mm of rain falling an hour when the rain is at its heaviest in Cumbria early on Tuesday morning.

‌



View 4 Images Rain sweeping across the UK at 1am on Tuesday (Image: WXCHARTS)

The wet weather is forecast as the UK cools after it was scorched by a fifth heatwave of the year. It had its hottest day of the year on Thursday with temperatures hitting 38.1C at Kew Gardens in London.

But the rain is unfortunately unlikely to come as far south as many of the areas that have been worst affected by wildfires and drought, the Met Office maps show. and won't be enough to make up for the dry spell.

‌



Forecaster Honor Criswick said: " There is some rain in the forecast but a lot of that continues to be focused towards the northwest, low pressure drifting in towards the south of Iceland.

"Eventually frontal systems do start to push their way south and eastwards but they are rather weak features so we will see some spots of rain across some of the south but small amounts and certainly not enough to make too much of a difference compared to the dry summer we’ve had so far."

A Met office forecast for the start of next week tells of the rain and temperatures which are closer to normal for the time of year.

‌



It reads: "Rain moving across Scotland and Northern Ireland through Monday, perhaps reaching southern areas overnight. This clearing to sunny spells and scattered showers Tuesday and Wednesday. Temperatures largely near average."

View 4 Images A rain map for Tuesday at 4am (Image: WXCHARTS)

Looking further ahead, the outlook appears unsettled for the end of August with more rain on the horizon. A forecast from the national weather agency for August 20-29 reads: "The first few days of this period are likely to be rather changeable, with many parts of the UK seeing showers or perhaps some longer spells of rain.

‌



"Thereafter, high pressure becomes increasingly probable over the north and west, with low pressure to the south of the UK. This will lead to further spells of showers and longer spells of rain, but the north may see more in the way of drier conditions.

"Within this broad pattern, there is potential for Atlantic lows to spread across the UK at times, which would bring more widespread rain and perhaps strong winds. Temperatures are more likely to be above normal than below overall, though the possibility of widespread or exceptional heat is perhaps a little lower than in recent weeks."

View 4 Images At 7am the rain clouds bringing heaviest showers are further south (Image: WXCHARTS)

News.title: Body found in search for Brit teen George Smyth who vanished after call for help while hiking
News.content:
Body found in search for Brit teen George Smyth who vanished after call for help while hiking

Bristol university student George Smyth, 18, went missing while on a solo hiking trip in Valea Gigănesti, in Romania

View 2 Images A body has been found in the search for George Smyth (Image: Jam Press/Newport Salop RUFC)

A body has been found in the search for a Brit teenager who vanished while on a hiking trip after making a desperate call in which he said he was exhausted and suffering from hypothermia.

‌



Bristol university geology student George Smyth, 18, went missing while on a solo hiking trip in Valea Gigănesti, Romania, in November.

‌



At the time, his mother told local outlet Observator News: "He left his college in the UK on Sunday, without telling us, to go hiking alone. His phone last had a signal in an isolated area in the mountains. He made a heart-wrenching call to 112 on Sunday evening.

‌



"His backpack was found at the same location from where he called for help. We flew to Romania immediately and are trying to support the search teams as best we can."

The teenager was understood to have been walking to the village of Bran, home to Bran Castle, which is popularly known as Dracula's Castle. Rescuers believe he reached the Tiganesti valley - over 6,562 feet above sea level - where he made the emergency call

View 2 Images Rescue teams in Romania spent months searching for George (Image: Jam Press/Salvamont Brasov)

‌



Avon and Somerset Police said today: "A body has been found as part of the search for missing 18-year-old George, who went missing while hiking in Romania.

"We have been notified by local authorities in Romania that a body had been found in the Bucegi Mountain region of the European country."

‌



They added: "While formal identification has not yet taken place, it is believed to be George Smyth, a geology university student from Bristol, who went missing in November 2025."

The Brit teen’s family have been notified and are being supported, police added. George's loved ones said: "We are all devastated by George’s death. He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends.

"We want to thank Salvamont Mountain Rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George; despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions.

Article continues below

"They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time."

They also thanked Avon and Somerset Police and University of Bristol. The family added: "Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye."

News.title: Earliest and latest times Royal Mail can knock on doors and 'pause' deliveries
News.content:
Earliest and latest times Royal Mail can knock on doors and 'pause' deliveries

Knowing when your post will arrive helps you plan your day

View 3 Images Royal Mail has strict times when staff should never knock on the door (Image: © Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

People can spend hours waiting for the postie to turn up with an important letter or parcel. Sometimes people are given time slots or tracking numbers, but for most things in the Royal Mail system, it is anyone's guess when it will arrive.

‌



Royal Mail claims on its website that most UK deliveries arrive at your door within a general timeframe. Letters and smaller parcels are typically delivered from Monday to Saturday, generally during the course of the working day.

‌



Delivery speed also relies on which service you paid for. Royal Mail says First Class is delivered by the next working day (including Saturdays), while Second Class typically takes two to three working days .

‌



Posties can make drop-offs as early as 7am or as late as 4.30pm, giving Brits a rough nine-hour window to expect a knock on the door or their post through the letterbox. The exact timing depends on your local route and how busy things are.

Parcels can also show up later than people expect, with deliveries sometimes stretching into the early evening - especially when demand spikes or disruption hits. Royal Mail’s guidance suggests some packages may arrive as late as around 6pm, and it adds that remote areas, peak periods like Christmas, or severe weather can all push drop-offs back.

View 3 Images Royal Mail should never make a delivery before 7am

‌



If Royal Mail delivers your post before 7am, you could call customer support to report the early delivery, if you so wish. You could ask them to speak to your local delivery office, which typically gives the postperson a reminder about the standard Royal Mail start time for deliveries.

When do Royal Mail pause deliveries?

There are several times when your post and parcels will just not arrive. Sunday is the most common day for the post to get complicated.

Because it isn’t part of Royal Mail’s everyday 'standard' pattern. That said, the company indicates some services - such as Tracked 24 - may include Sunday parcel deliveries in certain locations.

‌



View 3 Images Royal Mail will not bring post or parcels on these specific days

Bank holidays are another point at which the postal system generally comes to a halt as Royal Mail says it doesn’t deliver or collect on UK bank holidays. That applies across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, with service returning on the next working day.

For example, the next upcoming bank holiday for England and Wales falls on Monday, August 31. In this case, the post due to arrive on this day would come on Tuesday, September 1 - along with anything that was not delivered on Sunday, August 30.

Article continues below

Do Royal Mail ever deliver twice in one day?

If you’re hoping for a second visit the same day, the answer is usually no. Royal Mail generally delivers once per day per address, though there can be rare exceptions, such as when an item requires a signature or when volumes force extra rounds.

News.title: Jason Arday death 'tragedy on so many levels' says PM
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, described him as "very down" after resigning from Cambridge.

"He was very upset. He felt that there was no way out. He effectively wasn't leaving the house. He had lost a lot of weight," Andrews said.

"There should be a wakeup call to just how bad black academics actually have it in academia."

Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy also told the programme "the idea that an academic would be dragged through this amount of media scrutiny is unheard of".

Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said that people who "made many hard comments must now consider the impact of their words", describing it as a "deeply concerning and very sad case".

Prior to his appointment at Cambridge, Arday had worked as a professor at the University of Glasgow.

Shadow communities secretary Sir James Cleverly said he was angered by the "tragic" death and said "a number of people at a number of academic institutions have serious questions to answer".

When asked by the BBC on Saturday if the University of Cambridge needs to answer questions over its duty of care, Cleverly said the university should "ask themselves how he got into this position, how he ended up being in the eye of the storm, what could and should have happened to prevent this long before it got to this tragic situation".

Arday had denied plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and said the recent controversy had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

Questions were also raised about parts of his life story, including that he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised Â£5.5m for charity.

He later said the run was actually completed over a 12-day period to allow for rest days - and that the huge sum was raised with the help of others.

Arday's appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time.

Announcing his resignation last week, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny of him had become "too great".

He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.

"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

Earlier this week, Cambridge announced an independent investigation around the circumstances of Arday's appointment.

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

In a statement on Saturday, a spokesperson for the university said it was "saddened to hear of the tragic loss of Professor Jason Arday".

News.title: Analysis: Arday's death will send shockwaves through a divided academia
News.content:
There was another reason this row had such a high profile. Arday was a celebrity academic known as much for the remarkable life story he told, of an autistic child who didn't speak until 11, or learn to read and write until 18.

Other aspects of his personal narrative came under scrutiny, and he had to clarify that Â£5m raised for charity had been as part of a group effort, and that a 600 mile running challenge had taken twice as long as originally claimed.

Some who had signed a public letter of support quietly removed their names.

By the time he resigned his Cambridge position last week Arday said the "relentless accusations" had taken a "profound toll" on him and his family.

He suggested they had been racially motivated.

There are many unanswered questions which a coroner will no doubt be expected to consider about his circumstances and state of mind in the days before his death.

In the immediate aftermath of his death, his family said Arday had been subjected to a "campaign of misinformation" that was too much for this "gentle man".

Others think that he attracted so much scrutiny because he was a black man in a prominent position.

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us."

There has been deep unease among some academics of colour who feel the ferocity of the debate was due to Arday being a young black academic.

Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, told Newsnight in the wake of his death: "This is not just something that has happened in the past two weeks, we've seen the stories, this goes back three and a half years.

"The very day he got the position at Cambridge he had a Freedom of Information request asking about his credentials. He had all the right-wing people in America and the UK writing in to see if he was credible.

"Some people didn't believe a black man should be in that position at Cambridge.

"It's been a three-and-a-half-year toll which has come its head now."

What is certain is that Arday had sought to defend his reputation, using a high-profile firm of lawyers to send a letter to a journalist from Times Higher Education who first questioned his work.

The University of Cambridge initially robustly defended Arday then announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure amid growing disquiet.

In 2023, as an elite university which had been criticised for a lack of diversity, Cambridge had been keen to make some high-profile non-white appointments. It had already made a huge effort to ensure admission of students was more diverse.

Whoever was appointed into such a high profile post would have faced scrutiny and Arday had a slighter research track record than some others in the field.

Dr Jo Grady, general secretary of the University and College Union, described Jason Arday's death as "devastating".

"There are so many questions that need to be answered. The level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to, has been sickening. It must be investigated."

For the University of Cambridge now there will be the difficult task of holding together an academic community divided and shocked by the controversy and now the death of Jason Arday.

It had announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure at the university and a review of how senior staff are chosen.

Now all of that has been overtaken by his sudden and shocking death.

News.title: Fire services stretched as residents still not home
News.content:
Eleven major fires in the past 48 hours and 43 new wildfires since Friday have left services under "incredible pressure", a fire boss has said.

Phil Garrigan from the National Fire Chief's Council (NFCC) said major incidents had been declared across the UK, including in Stourbridge, Sandwell, Pershore and Stoke-on-Trent in the West Midlands, as well as in Hampshire and South Wales.

Many residents forced to flee their homes following the fires are still in the dark about when they can return.

In Stourbridge, where 38 houses have been destroyed or damaged, frustrated residents said they were not getting any answers, although it was hope they may go home later on Saturday.

West Midlands Assistant Chief Fire Officer Simon Barry told residents the fire there was under control and they were just dampening down hot spots.

He said as far as the service was concerned, homes were no longer at risk and he hoped some residents whose homes had been unaffected would be able to move back on Saturday evening.

In a recorded online briefing, Dudley Council chief executive Balvinder Hera stressed residents should not return home until explicitly told they could do so.

She said decisions to reopen roads were being taken on a street-by-street basis, with the council working closely with emergency services.

Police were keen to hear from people with information or video footage that could assist inquiries and had asked the public not to speculate on the fire's cause, she said.

An online fund, external has been set up by the council to allow people to donate to those affected.

News.title: Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets as coffin taken to Swansea home
News.content:
Legendary singer Bonnie Tyler has made a final journey to her Mumbles home, with thousands of emotional fans lining the streets to pay their respects.

The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a hospital in Portugal.

At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.

Despite Tyler's career taking her all over the world, she has been described by those living in the coastal suburb of Mumbles as a "Swansea girl through and through", and someone who "never forgot where she came from".

People were invited to "pay their respects" by lining roads, as her coffin was driven through.

News.title: Met Police apologises for data breach involving alleged Al Fayed victims
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has apologised after it inadvertently disclosed email addresses of around 140 people who say they were sexually abused by the late Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

Scotland Yard confirmed to the BBC it copied in all those who had signed up to receive a monthly email update for victims instead of blind copying them.

The update revealed a further three suspects in their 70s and 80s had been interviewed under caution, bringing the total number interviewed to seven.

The force said it had referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). It is considering providing further support to the victims along with additional safeguards.

A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC a monthly update sent to victims on 11 August regarding Operation Cornpoppy had contained details of progress in the investigation.

Operation Cornpoppy is the Metropolitan Police investigation into people who may have facilitated or enabled sexual offending by Al Fayed.

The spokesperson said: "Due to human error, recipients' email addresses were visible to others on the distribution list. The issue was identified quickly and immediate action was taken.

"We understand the impact this may have on victims and sincerely apologise. Everyone affected was contacted directly on the day of the incident.

"The incident is being investigated as a matter of priority, and we are reviewing our processes to help prevent a similar breach from happening again."

The force said the breach affected victims who had opted in to receive updates from the investigation team, but recipients had been split into smaller groups, meaning email addresses were only visible within those groups rather than across the entire cohort.

The BBC understands around 140 people have signed up to the updates.

The force has previously said 154 victims have reported allegations connected to Al Fayed and that supporting survivors remains at the heart of the investigation.

It said the incident had been formally recorded within the investigation records and they would continue to monitor the circumstances and impact of the breach, including reviewing alternative methods of updating victims that would reduce the risk of human error.

The force added that victim-survivors remained its priority and said it was committed to providing updates to those involved in the investigation.

News.title: Sellers puzzled by bulk orders suspect secondhand books being destroyed to train AI
News.content:
Something mysterious has been happening in the world of secondhand books.

Over the last few months independent booksellers have been observing a strange pattern of purchases which have seen scores of their novels being shipped to far-off warehouses.

In a typical week, Stuart Manley, from Barter Books, in Northumberland, would sell two or three thousand books. But one recent single bulk order from a Canadian company equalled what he would expect to move in seven days.

He says he has "never seen the like of this after 30 years in the second-hand book trade".

Mr Manley is not alone. Booksellers from around the world have been reporting similarly unusual mega orders.

They aren't sure what the final destination for their books is.

But the suspicion is that they are not being bought for avid overseas readers but instead something else with a voracious appetite for new information: AI.

News.title: When my dog died, my grief was overwhelming and complicated
News.content:
Gemma Champ, a writer from north London, rescued her cat Frankie as a kitten 17 years ago, when she lived in Abu Dhabi. Frankie died at home in January, and at first she felt "ridiculous for making such a fuss".

"I sent out a WhatsApp to all who'd known and loved him - and it turned out everyone had amazing memories of him. He wasn't just a cat. One friend said it was like 'a legendary beast from the great plains has left us.'

"We can see from social media that there's a whole community of people out there who have gone through the same experience and the same pain, so you don't feel like you're just being a drama queen - I think that's definitely how it would have been seen years ago."

After Greg James' dog died, the presenter said he wouldn't be on his show the next day. But getting employers to agree to this isn't always easy.

In 2019, Emma McNulty's 14-year-old terrier Millie died suddenly. Feeling sick with grief, McNulty, from Glasgow, said she was too upset to go into work. Unable to find someone to cover her shift, she said her part-time job in a sandwich shop was terminated. She then launched an online petition asking for employers to recognise pet bereavement.

No country mandates that employers offer paid time off after the death of a pet. Kara Stott, head of in-house legal and general counsel at law firm Peninsula, said more UK employers were starting to show flexibility with workers whose pets had died, even if a change to the law does not appear imminent.

But introducing formal pet bereavement policies has its challenges, Stott tells the BBC.

"Points to consider include how do you define a pet - does the policy just cover cats and dogs or would hamsters, rabbits, goldfish, horses, snakes, or other animals be included?"

Gemma, who is freelance, took a few days off work after Frankie's death, with the support of her "incredibly kind" client. "I doubt I could have done that if I'd been employed," she says, "and I think I'd have been weeping in the toilets at the office."

The reaction from friends and family to Frankie's passing confirmed that her sense of grief was real, she says, and she appreciated that people took it seriously.

"I do think, or hope, that people are learning not to dismiss this very profound and long-lasting relationship so easily."

News.title: Many Canadians are boycotting the US - here's where they're travelling instead
News.content:
Prior to US President Donald Trump's re-election, Kent Truscott and his family, from London, Ontario, had taken multiple trips south of the border, including to California and most recently New York in 2023.

But since late 2024, "my family and I have completely decided to boycott the United States", he told BBC.

That meant cancelling a trip last spring to Texas to watch the SpaceX Starship launch with his brother. The two had planned to fly down from Toronto, rent a car and stay a week to watch the launch, likely spending "thousands of dollars".

Truscott and his wife decided to spend that money in Canada instead â the Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, to be exact.

Their decision is a response to US tariffs and the president's comments about annexing their country. More than a year after Trump's return to the White House, many Canadians like Truscott are still holding firm on their boycott on travel to the US.

News.title: Woman allegedly tasered, raped and beaten by ex-partner, court hears
News.content:
A woman was allegedly tasered, raped and beaten in her home by her ex-partner, a court has heard.

In a special court sitting at Lisburn Magistrates' Court, a man aged in his 40s was charged with two counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, threats to kill, non-fatal strangulation, entering as a trespasser to commit rape and assaults including causing actual bodily harm.

He cannot be identified to protect the identity of the woman.

The court heard the man had turned up at the woman's house on two previous occasions, once with a baseball bat, but it was "marked as a domestic".

Warning: This article contains details of sexual assault that some readers may find distressing.

A detective constable told the court on 14 August staff at the Ulster Hospital contacted police to report the woman had presented with significant injuries which she disclosed had been caused by her ex-partner who was also at the hospital.

Officers attended and the woman said she was asleep in bed when she woke to find the defendant was in the room having broken in and was holding a taser.

He physically assaulted the victim and attacked her with the taser.

She described him threatening to kill her and covering her mouth with his hand before raping her twice.

When he agreed to take her to hospital he stopped on a road and discarded the taser, which has also been recovered by police.

The woman sustained a broken nose and bruising to her face and neck.

The defendant was arrested at the hospital and provided a pre-prepared statement accepting that he let himself into the house but denying the offences insisting everything was consensual.

However, he could not account for the injuries.

News.title: Military sent in to help emergency services fight wildfires across Wales
News.content:
On Friday, Stephen Kinnock, Secretary of State for Wales, said military personnel had been deployed for logistical support and to help "ease the pressure on the ground".

Despite cooler temperatures on Saturday, crews across Wales are continuing to battle fires.

Mid & West Wales Fire and Rescue Service (MWWFRS) said crews had spent more than 90 hours on "operational incidents" in Llanwrtyd Wells, Merthyr Tydfil and Ebbw Vale.

"It has been tough, however, we have been overwhelmed by the support we have received during this time," the service said, thanking local businesses "that have kept us fuelled with food and drinks".

Residents had been evacuated from their homes after a fire near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, with a councillor describing the situation as "scary", as the fire made its way towards the village.

On Saturday, MWWFRS said firefighters remained at the scene and were continuing to "make progress in responding" to the fire, describing it as a "challenging and dynamic incident".

It asked people to stay away from the area, particularly around Rhandirmwyn, saying "roads need to remain clear for emergency vehicles".

"Visiting the area can increase traffic, create additional risks and impact emergency response efforts," it said, urging people to "respect all road closures".

A fire was also seen above Cwm, Ebbw Vale on Friday evening.

Sallie Jones, a spokesperson for Cwm Task Force, said the community has been working together.

"If it was a different wind direction, it could have been total devastation," she said.

"The whole village was fearful, with people calling up last night asking us if they were safe to sleep there.

"That's what we're here for, reassurance and being there as a community."

News.title: Public urged to avoid 'surrounded' New Forest fire site
News.content:
The public has been urged to avoid an area where crews are working to dampen down a wildfire.

The blaze in the New Forest began when a van caught fire on the A31 last Sunday. The road will remain closed until at least Thursday, National Highways has said.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said it has received reports of members of the public accessing the site where its crews are working.

It comes after an earlier update from the fire service on Saturday, saying the fire was now "fully surrounded" after firefighters worked through the night. HIWFRS added: "We will still be on scene for a number of days as we damp down and extinguish hotspots."

The service added: "Accessing an active fire ground puts people at risk, impacts our firefighting operations, risks damage to the critical equipment we have on site, and could therefore cause further delays to this lengthy incident."

News.title: Heathrow Airport roads reopen after mains burst
News.content:
All roads to Heathrow Airport have reopened after earlier disruption caused by flooding from a burst water main on a ring road.

The flooding along Inner Ring Road West prevented access to the central terminal area (CTA), which includes Terminals 2 and 3, a number of other buildings and the road network.

Heathrow Airport has confirmed the airport is now operating as normal and has apologised for the inconvenience after the road closures were made just before 06:00 BST.

Passengers are still being advised to use public transport where possible due to heavy congestion on the roads.

The travel disruption left some passengers struggling to get to their planes on time.

George Smyrniadis, 79, missed his flight to Frankfurt where he was headed for a school reunion on Saturday afternoon.

Smyrniadis, who got in touch via BBC's Your Voice, said: "I was upset. It's the first reunion I've missed since 1987.

"I was so downhearted I just wanted to get home.

"The whole airport seemed completely chaotic, but I got the impression the airlines just carried on as though nothing was wrong - and if you missed your flight you just missed it."

Smyrniadis said his trip from Portsmouth went well until he left the M4, at which point he was sat in traffic for 90 minutes travelling a distance which usually takes him about 10 minutes.

"By the time I got to security it was too late - it was already 09:30BST so they wouldn't let me go through any further."

News.title: Bride dazzles in thrifty wedding with £2 charity shop dress
News.content:
A couple tied the knot in a thrifty-themed wedding with the bride dazzling in a Â£2 charity shop wedding dress.

Gina and Jacob Dodds, from Hoole in Chester, said "I do" in a ceremony held at the city's Storyhouse arts and cultural centre on Wednesday.

Both Gina's dress and engagement ring were bought from the Hope House Children's Hospice outlet while guests were also invited to wear outfits sourced from charity shops - raising money for a range of good causes.

"If we were going to have a wedding then we wanted it to be about more than just us - we wanted it to be about helping other people," she said.

News.title: Body found in search for UK student missing on Romania hike
News.content:
Tributes are being paid to an 18-year-old who went missing on a hiking trip to the Romanian mountains.

George Smyth, a University of Bristol student from Shropshire, had been missing since 23 November in the Bucegi mountains, despite daily searches, BraÈov Mountain Rescue said.

Avon and Somerset Police confirmed they had been notified by Romanian local authorities that a body had been found in the region. While formal identification has not yet taken place, the body is believed to be his.

"We are all devastated by George's death. He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends," his family said.

They added: "We want to thank Salvamont Mountain Rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George; despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions. They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.

"We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset Police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family.

"Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye. We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss."

News.title: Baby puffins make uninhabited island their new home
News.content:
Footage of a puffling - a baby puffin - bred on the Copeland Islands off the County Down coast has been captured for the first time.

The seabirds, synonymous with Rathlin Island off County Antrim, are not indigenous to the uninhabited Lighthouse Island, so no population existed there until an introduction scheme was launched around 2013.

There are now around 30 breeding pairs of puffins, which is being seen as a real success story.

They arrive to the island each April, and this year - in fact, just last month - trail cameras near their burrows in the ground filmed a young puffling out of its burrow, and an adult puffin bringing fish back to feed its young.

Attempts to attract puffins to Lighthouse Island included setting up fake "decoy" puffins, and a solar powered speaker system broadcasting its call.

News.title: Six people arrested after man abducted in Edinburgh
News.content:
Six people have been arrested in East Lothian after a man was abducted in Edinburgh.

Police Scotland said it received a report that a man had been abducted in the Canonmills area of the capital at about 22:30 on Thursday.

A 22-year-old man was later traced in Longniddry on Friday and taken to hospital as a precaution.

Five men - aged 21, 21, 22, 23 and 45 - and a 40-year-old woman have been arrested and police say inquiries are ongoing.

A section of the A198, which runs through the village of Longniddry, has been shut by police and a diversion is in place.

Officers believe this was a targeted incident and there is no risk to the wider public.

Det Insp Robbie Wallace said: "We understand an incident of this nature will be concerning but please be assured our inquiries are ongoing.

"Police will remain in the Longniddry area while this investigation continues and anyone with any concerns, or information, can approach these officers."

One report on social media said armed officers had been seen removing someone from a car.

Lothian Buses posted that some services were unable to serve the village and its routes had been diverted due to the road closure.

Longniddry is a coastal village about 15 miles (24km) from Canonmills.

News.title: Bulls v New Zealand LIVE: All Blacks face final warm-up before Springboks series
News.content:
The All Blacks play one final warm-up before taking on South Africa ( Getty )

New Zealand conclude their preparations for the massive Test series against South Africa as they take on the Bulls at altitude in Pretoria.

Dave Rennie’s side are two-from-two so far on tour after following a scratchy showing against the Stormers with an altogether more comprehensive win over the Sharks. This, though, could well be their toughest encounter yet, with plenty of experience in the ranks for the Bulls – perennial United Rugby Championship challengers.

A shift to the Highveld and Loftus Versfeld will provide another challenge for Rennie and his squad to deal with as the All Blacks boss looks to narrow down his selection for the Springboks. Richie Mo’unga has arrived on tour to bolster the playmaking options but is not yet involved – who will put their hand up for Test involvement with the first clash in Johannesburg just a week away?

Follow all of the latest from the clash in Pretoria with our live blog below:

News.content:

Charlotte Touzalin was a young teenager when she began experiencing unexplained weight gain, irregular menstrual cycles, and unwanted facial hair—the same baffling health issues that had plagued her mother for decades without a medical explanation.

"I’d go home and I’d cry," said Touzalin, now an 18-year-old college student living in Colorado. "I didn’t understand why all this weight was coming back or why my friends didn’t have to shave their faces and I had to."

Touzalin and her mother, Anne Schultz, were eventually diagnosed with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, a hormonal condition that affects 1 in 8 women worldwide. However, unlike her mother, Touzalin is entering young adulthood with renewed hope after participating in a clinical trial evaluating blockbuster GLP-1 medications as a treatment.

An expanding body of research indicates that these anti-obesity drugs may also work for the disorder known as PMOS—not only by encouraging weight loss, but also by improving insulin resistance, hormone balance, and ovulation. These factors are central to the condition, which was renamed from polycystic ovary syndrome earlier this year to move the focus away from ovaries and cysts.

open image in gallery Charlotte Touzalin with her mother, Anne Schult ( AP Photo/Brittany Peterson )

"We need to do a better job taking care of it," said Dr. Melanie Cree, who has led three studies testing GLP-1 drugs for PMOS, including the trial Touzalin joined. "We are finding them incredibly effective and really exciting for improving symptoms in women with this condition."

PMOS is a mysterious and maddening disease

Navigating PMOS can be a frustrating and mysterious journey for patients. Diagnosis frequently takes years because symptoms vary significantly, overlap with other medical conditions, and are sometimes dismissed by doctors.

Although the hereditary condition often correlates with excess weight, it does not affect all women the same way. Currently, there is no single known cause or curative therapy, leaving patients to manage symptoms through lifestyle modifications and oral contraceptive pills to regulate periods.

Two primary hormones drive the condition: insulin, which enables blood sugar to enter cells, and testosterone, which contributes to bone density, muscle mass, and sexual drive.

Most women living with PMOS experience insulin resistance regardless of body size, according to Cree, who serves as the PMOS clinic director at Children’s Hospital Colorado. When insulin levels remain high, the excess hormone can go directly to the ovaries, triggering them to produce excess testosterone. This imbalance frequently leads to severe acne, missed periods, and unwanted facial hair.

open image in gallery GLP-1 medication used in the polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome trial ( AP Photo/Brittany Peterson )

Schultz, 43, was completely unaware of the condition when her own irregular periods and abdominal bloating first started around age 18. Along with enduring the same difficulties as her daughter, she faced ovarian complications and multiple miscarriages, which occur more frequently in women with PMOS.

After receiving various mismatched diagnoses, Schultz finally learned she had PMOS around the same time her daughter endured a similarly drawn-out medical runaround.

Schultz recalled discussing Touzalin’s symptoms with a pediatrician who was evaluating her daughter primarily for binge eating and ADHD.

Schultz remembered telling the doctor: "There's gotta be something else going on here."

Touzalin noted that she felt "heard for the first time" when a nurse practitioner began connecting the pieces a few years ago. Cree formally diagnosed her last year.

"It was like a godsend," Schultz said through tears. "We finally had an answer and some kind of a path for her."

In Cree's trial, Touzalin administered weekly semaglutide injections over a 10-month period. Her abnormal hair growth slowed, her periods normalized, and for the first time, she felt full after eating and stopped gaining weight continuously.

"I became a happier version of myself," she said. "I felt like a normal person."

As research on GLP-1s for PMOS continues, insurers put up barriers

Touzalin’s results reflected broader trial outcomes. Early clinical data published in June in the journal Fertility and Sterility revealed that eight out of 11 participants completing the trial lost at least 10 percent of their body weight. The median weight loss was about 42 pounds, accompanied by a 52 percent median drop in testosterone. Six women experienced more frequent periods, with four returning to monthly cycles.

Across all three of Cree’s clinical investigations, women taking GLP-1 medications lost more weight than control groups, while showing marked drops in testosterone, blood sugar, and insulin levels. While Touzalin’s trial evaluated weekly semaglutide shots, Cree’s other studies examined oral semaglutide pills and exenatide injections.

International research has demonstrated similarly positive outcomes. Although study sizes remain small, some experts believe GLP-1 drugs show promising potential for addressing metabolic dysfunction in PMOS. Others argue that current evidence remains uncertain, noting that further trials are currently underway.

As research continues, a growing number of doctors are prescribing GLP-1 drugs off-label for PMOS and observing improvements in their patients. However, obtaining insurance coverage remains a widespread obstacle because the medications are not approved to treat the condition.

"I use these medicines a great deal," said Dr. Rana Malek, an endocrinologist with the University of Maryland Medical System.

open image in gallery Charlotte Touzalin holds a photo of herself, provided by Bre Blake Photography, showing her before participating in a PMOS study, in Elizabeth, Colo., on Friday, July 10, 2026 ( AP Photo/Brittany Peterson, Bre Blake Photography )

Among patients suffering from insulin resistance, Malek noted that she typically uses the drugs to assist with weight loss.

Medical professionals stress that individual results vary. GLP-1 medications do not work for everyone and can cause side effects such as nausea and constipation. Furthermore, patients often regain weight if they discontinue treatment.

Still, the drugs offer substantial relief for many PMOS patients, making it frustrating when insurance denials block access, Malek noted. Beyond the lack of approval for PMOS, several insurers refuse coverage for weight loss treatments altogether.

Touzalin recently encountered this barrier firsthand. Upon concluding her participation in the study, she no longer received free medication and had to stop taking GLP-1s in June.

Schultz remains determined to get her daughter back on the medication. She is fighting her insurance provider while pursuing a backup plan to obtain the drug through a manufacturer assistance program. Although Schultz would like to try GLP-1s for her own PMOS symptoms, she noted that her daughter comes first.

Touzalin hopes for a future where any PMOS patient can access the medication when needed.

"It’s something that could help a lot of other people," she said.

Eighteen children were among the nearly 70 people killed when an overloaded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe this week, police said Saturday after rescuers recovered more bodies.

The ferry capsized in strong waves Tuesday and police said 22 more bodies were recovered since then, bringing the death toll to 68.

The aging ferry was traveling from Kariba town to rural and fishing communities in the country's northwest, where roads are damaged and public transportation is scarce. Authorities have not said how many people were aboard or how many remain missing.

Estimates have put the number of passengers as high as 153, while authorities say the ferry’s capacity is 90. Zimbabwe’s disaster management agency has said 77 people were rescued.

Authorities initially said the number of children aboard was unknown because those below ticketing age were not included in passenger estimates. A police list released later showed that 16 of the child victims were aged 10 or younger, with the youngest just 1.

Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, created by damming the mighty Zambezi River in the late 1950s and early 1960s. It stretches more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) and is up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places.

Zimbabwe and Zambia share the lake, with their border running through its middle.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has upgraded its recent egg recall over salmonella fears to the most serious level.

The recall, which applies to 19 million eggs, has been moved to Class I, meaning “a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death.”

Nearly 100 people have fallen ill, with 26 hospitalized. There have not yet been any confirmed deaths.

The recall applies to eggs sold under the Country Morning, Cal-Maine Sunups, Brookshire’s, Simple Truth, and Kroger brand names. They will have sell-by or best-by dates between July 20, 2026 and August 17, 2026.

Salmonella symptoms typically emerge between 12 to 72 hours after eating contaminated food. They include diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps, and usually last four to seven days. The FDA warns that children younger than five, the elderly, and people with weakened immune systems are likely to have more severe infections.

19 million eggs have been recalled over salmonella concerns, with the FDA recently upgrading it to the most serious recall ( Reuters )

According to the FDA, the recalled eggs were shipped to stores in Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana.

They were sold via Kroger stores in Texas and Louisiana; Brookshire Grocery stores in Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Louisiana, and other smaller retailers in those states as well as Mississippi and New Mexico.

If any eggs included in the recall have already been purchased, they should be thrown away or returned to the point of purchase for a refund. The FDA recommends that if eggs are being stored without their original packaging and may have been part of the recall, they should also be thrown away.

The egg recall comes as the U.S. continues to battle a major outbreak of cyclosporiasis, a parasitic illness that causes explosive diarrhea. Federal data released this week show 4,173 confirmed cases across 41 states, with another 7,400 reports awaiting confirmation by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Michigan has recorded the highest number of reported cases, with state officials linking thousands of illnesses to contaminated lettuce. The parasite can cause severe diarrhea, vomiting, fever, body aches, dehydration and extreme fatigue.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Tuesday the outbreaks were “under control,” despite the rising number of reported cases.

“We have done extensive forensics, epidemiological forensics and we have identified the source of the outbreak. We, and the companies that are involved, have implemented a recall,” Kennedy told reporters.

News.title: Man United v AC Milan LIVE: Ruben Amorim defeats former side after defensive collapse in final pre-season friendly
News.content:
Manchester United face a reunion with former manager Ruben Amorim as they take on AC Milan in their final pre-season friendly before the start of the new Premier League season.

Amorim was sacked at the start of the year after a wretched spell at Old Trafford having arrived with considerable fanfare. The Portuguese coach is settling into Milan after being appointed by the Serie A club, though is already facing familiar issues as he looks to embed his favoured three-at-the-back formation.

Michael Carrick has done strong work since replacing Amorim as Manchester United manager, and will hope his squad can build more confidence and cohesion before the campaign proper begins. Carrick is eager to do more business in the transfer market but his selection here may be instructive with just a week to go until United’s opening game against Hull.

The family of former University of Cambridge professor Jason Arday has issued a statement following his death.

Prof Arday, who resigned following a plagiarism row, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to an address in Battersea, just after 3pm on Friday to a report that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.

The Metropolitan Police said his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

In a statement issued by his publisher Simon & Schuster UK, Prof Arday’s family said they are “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.

Prof Arday, a professor of sociology of education who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, quit following a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.

Jason Arday resigned following a plagiarism row ( PA )

An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Prof Arday of wrongdoing.

The University of Cambridge said it would run an independent review of “all relevant processes” alongside an investigation into how Prof Arday was appointed by its Faculty of Education.

Last week, the university confirmed it would continue its investigation into the circumstances around Prof Arday’s “appointment and tenure” after he quit, adding that findings will feed into a review of the process for appointing senior roles.

Over the weekend, he cancelled events promoting his forthcoming memoir.

Publisher Simon & Schuster previously said that the book, Great And Unfortunate Things, would be published in the UK on August 27.

The family’s statement in full

In a statement issued by his publisher Simon & Schuster UK, Prof Arday’s family said:

“Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.

“The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.

“We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son.

“We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long.”

News.title: Bedbug infestations are on the rise and they could be more dangerous to humans than previously thought
News.content:
