Sometimes called the vampires of the insect world, bedbugs spend daylight hours hidden in crevices before emerging at night to feed on human blood.

While generations of children have grown up with a nursery rhyme warning them to sleep tight and avoid their bite, recent trends offer little reassurance: infestations are rising, reaching their seasonal peak during the warmer months.

Adding to concerns, some scientists think the pests could potentially transmit the antibiotic-resistant superbug MRSA.

For centuries, the parasites have tormented households and prompted public alarm. In 2018, New York City authorities removed at least six municipal buses from service following reports of bedbugs crawling on seats. A similar disruption occurred in Paris in 2023, where sightings in cinemas, trains, and buses generated widespread concern ahead of the 2024 Olympic Games.

open image in gallery In 2023, University of South Dakota researchers published the results of an experiment — using blood capsules with an artificial skin — that demonstrated bedbugs could acquire MRSA during one feeding and spread it during a later one ( AP Photo/Allen G. Breed )

"They certainly are out there," said Christopher Hayes, a North Carolina State University assistant professor who has been bitten by bedbugs more than 50 times in the course of research.

"And if you're unaware, if you're not on top of your game, it's easy to bring them into your home."

Bedbugs really do come out at night

Roughly the size of an apple seed, the reddish-brown insects are estimated by some researchers to date back to the era of the dinosaurs. However, they are best known for their persistent ability to cohabit with and feed upon human hosts.

Capable of squeezing into narrow gaps in furniture, they also hide in clothing, linens and mattresses. Though difficult to spot directly, their presence is frequently betrayed by small, dark excrement stains.

While bedbugs remain a year-round threat, they historically flourish during the summer. They typically emerge under the cover of darkness, crawling onto exposed skin and utilizing a beaklike body part to pierce human tissue and siphon blood over several minutes.

Because the bite itself is painless, physical reactions vary significantly. Some individuals develop itchy, red welts within a day or two, while others show no physical response at all.

This absence of symptoms presents a distinct hazard, as individuals unaware of ongoing bites can quickly find themselves dealing with a severe infestation.

Bedbugs’ threat to humans

The health impacts of unmanaged infestations were highlighted in a 2020 French medical journal case report.

The paper documented a 70-year-old man living alone in a Paris suburb who collapsed on the street. Upon admission to a hospital emergency department, doctors diagnosed him with dementia alongside severe anemia resulting from prolonged blood loss.

Medical staff discovered bedbugs actively feeding on his neck, head, and shoulders. A subsequent inspection of his apartment revealed thousands of the insects inhabiting his mattress, walls, flooring, and curtains.

open image in gallery Further research is required to confirm whether bedbugs actually transmit MRSA to humans in real-world settings ( AP Photo/Allen G. Breed )

Historically, experts considered bedbugs incapable of transmitting infectious diseases between humans. Their internal anatomy and digestive processes were believed to prevent pathogens from passing on effectively, according to Chow-Yang Lee, an entomologist at the University of California at Riverside.

However, a 2023 study conducted by researchers at the University of South Dakota challenged this assumption. Utilizing artificial skin and blood capsules, the experiment demonstrated that bedbugs could contract MRSA during one feeding session and subsequently spread it during a later meal.

Further research is required to confirm whether bedbugs actually transmit MRSA to humans in real-world settings, noted study co-author Jose Pietri, now based at Purdue University. Nevertheless, "it changes the perspective of what bedbugs do, in terms of public health," Pietri said.

Bedbugs’ resistance to pesticides

Bedbug populations across developed nations experienced a sharp decline following World War II due to the widespread application of the chemical pesticide DDT. In 1972, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency banned DDT for most applications, citing evidence of environmental harm and potential human health risks.

By that time, bedbugs had already begun developing immunity to the chemical. According to Lee, growing insecticide resistance has driven a sustained resurgence of the pests in recent decades.

Determining the exact scale of the resurgence remains difficult. Pest control firms publish annual rankings of U.S. cities with the highest infestation rates—with Orkin currently placing Chicago at No. 1, while Terminix identifies Philadelphia as having the biggest problem. However, these lists rely on corporate customer call volumes rather than rigorous scientific surveys.

Many infestations occur within public or low-income housing developments, where property managers may not engage the commercial firms compiling those statistics, Lee noted in an email.

How to protect yourself from the pests and treat them

Pest management specialists emphasize that prevention is the most effective defense, urging individuals to avoid bringing the insects into their living spaces in the first place.

Travelers frequently transport bedbugs home from lodging establishments. Prior to unpacking in a hotel room, guests should inspect the premises by pulling back bedsheets and mattress covers to check for live insects or fecal spots.

Luggage should never be placed directly on beds or carpeted floors near sleeping areas; instead, bags can be stored in light-colored trash bags or placed inside the bathtub. Upon returning home, suitcases should be unpacked outdoors, and all laundry transferred directly to the washing machine and dryer.

Secondhand furniture and household items also serve as common vectors. Hayes advised visually inspecting all pre-owned goods and treating them prior to bringing them indoors. Experts recommend vacuuming, steaming, or applying heat to furniture, or isolating items in a garage or storage unit for several days.

For clothing, items should be laundered and run through a high-heat dryer cycle for an hour. Non-washable items like shoes can be placed in a freezer for a week "to make sure that everything in there that could be alive is taken care of," Hayes said.

For those dealing with an active infestation, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency provides self-treatment instructions, though the process is labor-intensive and requires systematically sealing harborage spaces and treating affected goods.

The guidance also warns against common missteps.

"You can't just blast random chemicals and expect it's going to work because there's a fairly high likelihood that they'll be resistant to some of the first-line insecticides," Pietri said.

Consequently, experts strongly recommend hiring licensed professional exterminators experienced in bedbug eradication, though services can cost hundreds or thousands of dollars.

Alternative control methods beyond chemical treatments exist. For instance, silica dust formulations work by absorbing the moisture from a bedbug's body, causing fatal dehydration.

Thermal treatments using sustained dry heat are also highly effective, destroying both eggs and adult insects. However, the process requires maintaining temperatures of at least 122 degrees Fahrenheit (50 degrees Celsius) and carries a risk of damaging personal property, meaning it must be carried out by professionals.

"I think the biggest piece of advice is just people shouldn't panic," Hayes said. "They just need to take action. If you think you have bedbugs, don't wait to deal with it."

News.title: Newcastle kit fiasco sums up haphazard pre-season
News.content:
Newcastle United 1 Bayer Leverkusen 2

Newcastle’s pre-season friendly against Bayer Leverkusen at St James’ Park took a bizarre turn when a kit clash prompted the hosts to change shirts midway through the first half.

The German team’s white away kit with blue trim proved hard to distinguish from Newcastle’s home strip, which has a white back and blue stripes across the shoulders.

During the first-half hydration break, Newcastle decided to change into their lilac third kit, which improved the viewing experience for fans who took to social media to question the original choice of kits.

Newcastle would go on to lose the game 2-1 in new manager Matthias Jaissle’s first game at St James’, a result which followed a 3-1 reverse against Everton on Wednesday evening.

Leverkusen, the 2023-24 Bundesliga champions now managed by Spaniard Carles Martínez Novell, scored after just 44 seconds through a powerful Ibrahim Maza strike.

News.title: Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn
News.content:
Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Mowbray: It feels like a defeat

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

News.title: How to have the perfect slow-paced holiday in Zakynthos
News.content:
Zakynthos, also known as Zante, is renowned for raucous nightlife, but there’s a far more authentic side to the Venetians “Fiore di Levante” (Flower of the East). For such a small island, scenery is extremely varied: the southern coastline – home to Laganas’ notorious nightlife strip – also encompasses the pristine beaches of Zakynthos Marine Park, where loggerhead sea turtles come to nest, while some of the island’s best-known attractions, including Navagio Beach on the cliff-lined northerly coast, can only be reached by boat.

Birthplace of the man who penned Greece’s national anthem, Zakynthos was also a magnet for literary greats: Byron lay in state here and philhellene Edgar Allan Poe wrote a sonnet to the island’s “verdant slopes”.

Last but not least, food is a powerful lure here: sit in a rustic sea view tavern sipping local Verdea white wine with a plate full of traditional kouneli stifado – a garlic and tomato-soaked rabbit stew – and you’ll be hooked.

News.title: Ebola doctors ‘step back’ from WHO in drug trial ethics row
News.content:
Two leading doctors have “stepped back” from long-held positions with the World Health Organization amid a row over the ethics of an Ebola drug trial underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The randomised control trial, called Ebo-Pep, is testing whether an experimental antiviral is an effective post-exposure treatment.

But experts believe the study’s design puts healthcare workers on the frontline of the epidemic at risk, because it means medics exposed to Ebola might receive a placebo treatment.

“We owe them [healthcare workers] a duty of care to do the best possible thing, and a 50 per cent chance of getting a placebo tablet is not that,” said Prof Tom Fletcher, director of the Global Health Trials Unit at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. The WHO’s health emergencies clinical unit has also deployed him to Ebola ‘Red Zones’ for more than a decade.

This week, Prof Fletcher and eight other experts based in the UK, US, Uganda, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Canada published their concerns in Nature Africa, calling for a “careful reconsideration” of the trial protocol.

They said they are not against Ebo-Pep or randomised trials, but warned there are “additional ethical obligations” when including healthcare workers in studies like this, given the case fatality rate currently stands at 40 per cent.

Prof Fletcher said: “Ebo-Pep is a really good trial, it’s the trial we’ve talked about doing for years. But we’re talking about [protecting] the ‘one-per-centers’, the people who willingly step into one of the most dangerous environments in the world.”

News.title: Wildfire watch: Inside London’s fire control centre on the hottest day of the year
News.content:
“It’s been relentless, an immense number of calls,” says Yvonne Woodhams, control room commander at the London Fire Brigade’s headquarters on the morning of what turned out to be the hottest day of the year so far.

Inside a nondescript building in South-west London, dozens of fire brigade dispatchers field calls from the public and direct the city’s 5,000 or so firefighters across 102 stations to where they are most needed.

In the middle of another heatwave and on a day when temperatures rose to just above 38 degrees, the control room was busy – the scale and frequency of wildfires in London’s parks and grasslands are now considered unprecedented.

Above the dispatchers there is a live map, with red dots representing each active fire, sprawling from Enfield in the north to Purley in the south.

Wildfires nearly always have a human origin like dropped cigarette butts, glass bottles that magnifies the sunlight, or the now-temporarily banned portable barbecues.

But it’s the tinderbox that London has become which is worrying firefighters.

Scorching hot, low-humidity weather, a bit of wind, and tinder-dry vegetation can cause the smallest spark to ignite an inferno. Conditions like this have been described as “fire weather” by the author John Vaillant.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

Treasury officials have predicted UK growth of just 0.3pc in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked for the rest of this year.

That is far lower than the 1.6pc predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March, based on assumptions made before the start of the war. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Iran war threatens to cripple growth, Treasury warns Burnham | Officials predict economic expansion of just 0.3pc in 2027 if Strait of Hormuz stays blocked

2) Britain facing £54bn bill for North Sea shutdown | Costs soar amid shortage of specialised ships needed to clear up abandoned oil rigs

3) Ban on zero-hours contracts to cost companies up to £3bn | Businesses face huge bill to offer workers guaranteed hours under Employment Rights Act

4) Nvidia’s AI push has echoes of Enron, says Big Short investor | Michael Burry claims chip giant is engaging in ‘circular’ financing

5) Shadow bank founder battles to stave off bankruptcy threat | Paresh Raja launches legal claim to prevent administrators from chasing him for repayment

What happened overnight

Asian shares were mostly higher, powered by gains for AI-related stocks including computer chips as regional markets tracked a rally on Wall Street.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 advanced 1.6pc to 68,601.21. In South Korea, the Kospi jumped 4pc, climbing to 6,844.65, as shares in Samsung Electronics surged 5.4pcc. Computer chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 7.1pc.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.3pc to 3,967.28, while the Shanghai Composite index added 0.5pc to 3,967.65.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.4pc to 9,155.80.

Data from the US on Wednesday showed consumer prices had risen in line with analysts’ expectations in July.

Wall Street stocks were boosted on Wednesday by gains made by tech companies CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer, both of which closed up by more than 19pc.

The Nasdaq Composite ended the session up 0.5pc, with the S&P 500 up nearly 0.3pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished the session marginally down.

Oil prices were little changed as investors weighed the deadlock in talks between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was broadly flat at nearly $89 a barrel.

Sports.title: Chelsea 3 Real Sociedad 1: Xabi Alonso’s lethal new front three shine on first outing as Enzo endures mixed reception
Sports.content:
THE ICE COLD era has begun at Stamford Bridge, with the Blues lethal new front three in action for the first time together.

Morgan Rogers went 1-0 up against Cole Palmer in the goalscoring charts for Chelsea since the Aston Villa man signed on for £117m, although he didn’t pull out the celebration fans are waiting to see from the pair of pals.



Fans showed up in their thousands to watch Rogers, among others, for the first time, and didn’t leave disappointed when he opened the scoring inside 11 minutes.

Rogers got by far the biggest cheer ahead of kick-off when the teams were read out, and about 15 minutes later came the birth of his first Chelsea chant, to the tune of “I just can’t get enough” by Depeche Mode.



His decision not to pull out the iconic celebration might have to do with the nature of the goal, or perhaps there is a romance in him waiting to link up with pal Palmer to do it for the first time at Stamford Bridge together.

It was a Pedro Neto cross from the right hand side onto the head of Joao Pedro that created the goal, with a header towards the far post being well kept-out by Alex Remiro, only for Rogers to be on hand to tap it in from close range.

Chances came and went for both sides, with the Blues seeming to be in the ascendency until disaster struck before half-time.

Deja-blue, you might say. Chelsea dominate and are undone by a spot of poor defending.

That came in the 44th minute, when Jon Mikel Aramburu struck an excellent finish into the bottom right corner with his left foot, after some confusing-looking defending from the Blues in their new three-at-the-back shape.

Chelsea of last season would have let the game slip from there.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

But not Xabi Alonso‘s side.

When Rogers looked like he might be able to steal Palmer’s limelight, Palmer reminded Stamford Bridge exactly what he is capable of.

The second half was hardly underway when Palmer seemed to spin a web around former Man City man Sergio Gomez on the right hand side, and tie him up in knots before laying the ball off to Reece James – it was his cross that found the head of the lethal Joao Pedro to make it 2-1.



With Palmer and Rogers behind him, Pedro might just become unstoppable – that finish was his seventh in as many pre-season matches, and Fulham will be more than wary of facing him in the Blues’ season opener next Monday night.

Before the game was up, he made it eight in seven.

Xabi Alonso rung in the changes with 20 minutes to go, with Rogers and Palmer both substituted, but opted to keep his dangerous number 20 up top.



Another decision that paid off, with Pedro racing through on goal down the right hand side after a great through ball by Malo Gusto, slotting the ball into the far corner to grab a brace and give his side a two-goal cushion.

One decision from Alonso that fans weren’t so sure of, was bringing on Enzo Fernandez.

The Argentine midfielder has been subject to plenty of transfer talk this summer about wanting to leave Stamford Bridge, as well as irritating some England fans by scoring against them in the World Cup semi-final.

He was initially booed by supporters when he came on, who seemed to quickly forgive him and chanted his name moments later – he continued to get a mixed reception throughout.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Chelsea sat comfortably with the lead though, as fan-favourite Estevao fired over the bar with the Blues in control.



Xabi Alonso’s side gave a good account of themselves for the final time before they face Fulham in their Premier League opener next Monday night, with a few defensive errors to work on – and a Fernandez situation to work out – before the season starts.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes fluffs another penalty just minutes after Man Utd stars tackle one another for calamitous goal
Sports.content:
BRUNO FERNANDES spurned a penalty for the second match in a row as AC Milan youngster Lorenzo Torriani read him like a book.

The Manchester United skipper fluffed his lines from 12 yards in a shootout win over Leeds on Wednesday, putting his effort wide of the right-hand post.



He changed things up after earning a shot at redemption against the Rossoneri when the referee pointed to the spot for a foul in Youri Tielemans.

But Torriani was agile enough to stop Fernandes’ low drive, which was heading for the left-hand corner.



Fernandes, 31, is normally a dab hand from the spot.

But United’s last two pre-season matches will have done little to boost his confidence.



His miss capped off an embarrassing end to the first half for the Red Devils in Wroclaw, Poland.

Just five minutes prior, team-mates Harry Maguire and Andrey Santos fell over each other trying to defend a Milan attack.

That left bags of space for Goncalo Ramos to run into, and he rolled the ball square for Samuel Chukwueze to make it 1-1.

United stars will have been desperate to get one over on Milan as they are managed by former Red Devils head coach Ruben Amorim.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

The Premier League giants did draw first blood when Fernandes’ corner was nodded home by Maguire inside two minutes.

And they retook the lead early in the second period when Patrick Dorgu punished a woeful mistake from Filippo Terracciano.

Sports.title: Chelsea ratings: Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro combine brilliantly as Marco Palestra’s defensive frailties exposed
Sports.content:
CHELSEA appear to be peaking at the right time as Xabi Alonso’s men picked up a 3-1 win over Real Sociedad in their final pre-season game.

The Blues welcomed the La Liga side to Stamford Bridge before they open the season with a west London derby away to Fulham on August 24.



Morgan Rogers opened the scoring for Chelsea after just 11 minutes to show the home fans what they can expect from their new £117million man.

Venezuelan Jon Aramburu equalised for the visitors on the stroke of half-time.



However, just after the restart, Joao Pedro put Chelsea back in front off a Reece James assist.

After a raft of changes for both sides, it was Pedro once again who scored in the 77th minute to seal a 3-1 win for Alonso and co.

SunSport provides the detailed player ratings from Chelsea’s last friendly of the summer.

ROBERT SANCHEZ – 6

Will be unhappy his defence allowed so many shots in the first half but only had to make one very good save, plus one more stop, before Sociedad grabbed a cracking equaliser.

Untroubled before going off just past the hour.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

WESLEY FOFANA – 6

Shaky early on when Sociedad found space on his side of the pitch and never looked totally in control even when he got to the pace of the game.

Clearly has more of a future at Chelsea than many suspected, though, and improved as the game went on, probably looking more at ease in the centre of the back three..



MAXENCE LACROIX – 5

Started well, showing his ability to pass out from the back but then seemed to lose concentration at times. Important challenge to deny Orri Oskarsson, although there were suspicions of a foul.

A solid enough debut, though, and fits the brief of Chelsea signing Premier League-ready players.

LEVI COLWILL – 6

Vocal and authoritative from the start, winning his duels and making good decisions on his passes. But found himself exposed by Palestra playing so high and wide in front of him.

Willing to get forward at times, too. Showed the quality and leadership which Chelsea missed so much last season when he was injured.

PEDRO NETO – 7

Again looked well-suited to right wing-back role. Did his defensive work more effectively than Palestra but it was his forward contribution which impressed most.

Stretched Sociedad with his pace and sent in some good crosses, including the one which led to the opening goal. Switched to inside left after first wave of Chelsea subs.

REECE JAMES – 6

Initially very comfortable in central midfield, spreading play ahead of opening goal and picking other good passes. But it was alarming how much space Sociedad were able to find in the Chelsea half.

Excellent cross led to Pedro restoring the lead before giving way to Fernandez.

MOISES CAICEDO – 6

Job was mainly to tidy up messes and keep the ball moving, which he did well enough. But probably would have been booked in a non-friendly game for first-half foul and he had a role in Chelsea losing control. Not his best outing but little to worry about either.



MARCO PALESTRA – 5

Offered plenty going forward early on with his movement and energy. But his less convincing contribution at the other end became more and more obvious, as he left Colwill outnumbered more than once before the equaliser.

COLE PALMER – 6

Showed flashes of his ability in the odd pass or dribble or dummy or shot.

But did not consistently affect the game, often having to drop deep in search of the ball. Kept trying to make things happen on a day he was outshone by the friend alongside him for an hour.

MORGAN ROGERS – 7

Johnny on the spot to score, then began combining well with Joao Pedro. Stuck to inside left channel, leaving Palestra to play wide.

Offered the kind of movement and runs in behind which Chelsea sometimes lacked last season.



JOAO PEDRO – 8

Fine header forced save which led to Rogers goal and soon tested Sociedad ‘keeper Remiro again.

Faded as Chelsea lost control of the first half, but headed in early in the second and drew another save. Confident finish to seal the game and looks set for another stellar season.

SUBS

MIKE PENDERS (for Sanchez, 62) – 6

Had almost nothing to do as Chelsea bossed the remainder of the game.

JOSH ACHEAMPONG (for Lacroix, 62) – 6

Played on the right of the back three as Fofana tucked into the middle.

Looked quick and athletic as ever, with more than one impressive surge forward.

ENZO FERNANDEZ (for James, 62) – 5

Uncomfortable atmosphere as some fans booed him and others sang his name. Shoehorned into a holding role, which is not his position, but did nothing wrong.

MALO GUSTO (for Rogers, 62) – 7

Not known for his defence-splitting passes but made immediate impact to set up Pedro for the goal which killed the game. Yet appears well down the pecking order now.



ROMEO LAVIA (for Caicedo, 76) – 5

Could have a role to play this season in Alonso’s preferred 3-4-2-1 formation, but mainly as a sub or in cup games. Showed his class and strength with a run and pass through for Pedro, but also guilty of giving the ball away.

JAMIE GITTENS (for Palmer, 76) – 5

Claimed a penalty after taking a tumble in the box. Signed last summer as a left winger, he was asked to play inside left this time. Must be fearing a frustrating season to come.

PEP CHAVARRIA (for Palestra, 76) – 5

Another to make his Chelsea debut, playing in the same high role Palestra had occupied. Did not have much opportunity to do anything wrong or right.

JORREL HATO (for Colwill, 76) – 5

Will wonder how much game time he is going to get this season after an impressive end to the last campaign. Will probably need others to get injured to regain a starting place.

ESTEVAO WILLIAN (for Neto, 76) – 6

Announcement of his name brought one of the biggest cheers of the afternoon. Looked lively without making a decisive contribution and fired over bar late on.

Sports.title: Newcastle’s entire starting XI forced to change kit 25 minutes into pre-season friendly vs Bayer Leverkusen
Sports.content:
IT HAS been a summer of change at Newcastle – and it was the same when it came to their kit during a showdown with Bayer Leverkusen.

The Magpies now have Matthias Jaissle in the dugout following Eddie Howe’s decision to quit.



And Bruno Guimaraes followed the likes of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali through the exit door when he completed a £75million move to Arsenal last week.

Newcastle’s preparations for the new campaign took another shock twist when they locked horns with Leverkusen in a pre-season friendly.



The Magpies were forced to change out of their iconic black and white stripes during a hydration break midway through the first half.

A kit clash had been causing havoc in the early stages of the meeting at St James’ Park.



Newcastle decided to bite the bullet after 25 minutes and their new violet third shirt was quickly dished out to the starting XI.

Nick Woltemade, Yoane Wissa and Sven Botman were among the stars who rushed to pull on the strip as Jaissle gave fresh instructions.

Lewis Hall, who wants to join Manchester United in a late summer deal, was also left red-faced.

And the unexpected alteration seemed to do the trick for Newcastle as they quickly drew level.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The Magpies had fallen behind inside the opening 60 seconds when Ibrahim Maza found a way past £25.7m summer arrival Lukas Hornicek.

But, not long after ditching their home shirt, Malick Thiaw grabbed an equaliser.

Leverkusen still ended up condemning their Premier League opponents to a 2-1 defeat thanks to Victor Boniface’s late winner.

Newcastle are set to round off their pre-season programme by hosting Strasbourg in another friendly tomorrow.



And the Tyneside giants will get their top-flight campaign underway against Liverpool on August 23.

Sports.title: Enzo Fernandez BOOED by Chelsea fans as divisive Argentine makes Stamford Bridge return after flirting with transfer
Sports.content:
CHELSEA fans were fiercely divided over Enzo Fernandez upon his return to action.

There were loud boos when Fernandez replaced Reece James in the 61st minute of Chelsea‘s final pre-season friendly against Real Sociedad.



But there were also plenty of fans cheering the midfielder’s name, with boos and chants continuing when the Fernandez was on the ball.

The Argentina international took the armband from James when he replaced the right-back.



Fernandez, 25, who scored against England in the World Cup semi-final, has been trying to force a move away from Stamford Bridge.

Manchester City, under former Chelsea manager Enzo Maresca, are admirers but were given a deadline of Friday at 5pm to meet the £120million asking price.



It remains to be seen whether City attempt to test Chelsea’s resolve, but the Blues now expect Fernandez to stay at the club for this season.

The club presented the player and his agent, Javier Pastore, conditions for a sale in May and have not received a bid all summer.

Fernandez openly criticised the club while on international duty with Argentina in March and flirted with Real Madrid, who eventually published a statement saying they would not be pursuing a deal.

Pastore, the former Paris Saint-Germain and Argentina midfielder, has also spoken publicly about pursuing a move away from Chelsea.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Fernandez returned to training with Chelsea this week having had an extended break following the World Cup, with new manager Xabi Alonso making it clear he wants him to stay at the club.

Shortly after his arrival, Alonso made the point of calling Fernandez to discuss his place in the squad.

Sports.title: Infamous ballboy kicked by Chelsea star Eden Hazard set to sell vodka company for £500MILLION
Sports.content:
THE ballboy who was kicked by Eden Hazard is set for a monster pay day – after edging towards flogging his business in a money-spinning deal.

Charlie Morgan, 30, hit the headlines when he was booted during Swansea City’s League Cup semi-final second leg against Chelsea in 2013.



And Hazard’s shock foe has gone on to make himself a multi-millionaire since setting up Au Vodka.

Morgan and co-founder Jackson Quinn are now on course for a huge windfall.



The pair have entered advanced talks to sell their alcoholic beverage empire in a deal worth an eye-watering £500MILLION.

American drinks giant Sazerac Company are on the verge of snapping up the business from Swansea fan Morgan and Quinn.

It is expected that the duo will bag payouts worth more than £100m each when the deal goes through.

But it is unknown whether Morgan, whose incident with Hazard led to the Chelsea legend being sent off, will still have a role within the company.

A minority stake in Au Vodka was sold to private equity firm Metric Capital in 2023.

And Morgan piled more cash into the business by relocating to a fully gold HQ last year.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Au Vodka has been endorsed by the likes of Floyd Mayweather, Ronaldinho and Jake Paul, who has a tattoo showing the company’s bottle.

Morgan was hilariously reunited with Hazard, 35, and they took a cheeky photo together two years ago.

The former Stamford Bridge favourite, who furiously kicked out when the Welshman held up play more than a decade earlier, uploaded the snap onto social media.

Hazard included a caption which read: “A nice thing about retirement is catching up with old friends. You have come a long way in 11 years my friend.”

Sports.title: Tottenham set to make up to £20million from Ashley Phillips transfer despite never playing a game for Spurs
Sports.content:
TOTTENHAM stand to make up to £20million from the sale of Ashley Phillips to Middlesbrough.

And the North Londoners could even earn more in the future due to a sell-on clause.



Spurs have sold centre-back Phillips, 21, to Championship outfit Boro for an initial £7m.

But there are £13m worth of add-ons also attached to the deal, and Tottenham also hold a 20 per cent sell-on clause on the player.



While they have matching rights too, meaning that if Boro look to sell the player in the future, Spurs will have the option to match any bid accepted from another club.

Phillips has quietly racked up a tonne of games in England‘s second tier during back-to-back loan spells with Stoke, following another temporary spell at Plymouth.



But with so many centre-backs at Roberto De Zerbi‘s disposal, Spurs have decided to cash in on the youngster, whom they signed from Blackburn for around £2m in 2023.

He follows fellow central defenders Cristian Romero and Radu Dragusin, who have left for Atletico Madrid and Fiorentina respectively, out the door.

De Zerbi has new signings Jan Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi vying for a slot alongside Micky van de Ven, who recently signed a new five-year deal.

The Italian boss also has Kevin Danso and Ben Davies as back-up.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Phillips is the latest player to leave in what has been a transformative summer in N17, with a multitude of players coming and going.

At Boro, Phillips will join Will Lankshear, who also left Spurs for Teesside in a £20m deal earlier this summer.

Sports.title: Mykhailo Mudryk reveals brutal reality of drugs ban as he had 20 months in wilderness and unable to train at Chelsea
Sports.content:
MYKHAILO MUDRYK says he trained like a mad man to stay permanently ready for his Chelsea return.

The Ukrainian, 25, was provisionally suspended in December 2024 after failing an anti-doping test.



He was unable to train at Cobham, let alone play for the Blues, which led to 20 gruelling months of solo sessions – including some on the 3G pitch at non-league Uxbridge FC.

Mudryk was cleared to return last month when an agreement was reached to reduce his four-year FA ban following an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport.



And now he has shed light on the effort it took to stay razor-sharp so that he could hit the ground running whenever the call came.

Mudryk told the Chelsea website: “I missed a lot of the process, the training sessions, games especially, to compete to win and to always be hungry for more.



“I’d say it was like a pre-season for 18 months. So I’ve been training, I’ve been training hard. I didn’t give up and I just tried to work as hard as I could.

“I was working six days a week with proper recovery, with a proper sleep schedule, food, everything. Everything was the same, just double sessions per day.

“It was to come back and to show myself again in the football world. That was my mission and I knew what I had to do for that. Only through hard work can you reach something.”

Mudryk, who set Chelsea back an initial £61million in 2023, returned to action in a friendly defeat to Juventus last week.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

But he missed a load of Stamford Bridge drama while he was away.

The former Shakhtar Donetsk speedster was sidelined for Enzo Maresca‘s exit, two Calum McFarlane interim spells, Liam Rosenior‘s entire stint in charge, and Xabi Alonso‘s appointment.

So he is relieved to now be back in the thick of the action.

Mudryk added: “It’s been a while, so to stand back at the same training ground, it’s a really happy moment for me.

“I feel good, I feel great. I’m grateful to be back on the pitch. It was such a nice feeling to see everyone again. It was a warm welcome.”



Mudryk is expected to leave Chelsea on loan this summer, and he would reportedly favour a Premier League move over signing for Strasbourg or suitors from Italy.

Sports.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal twist, Bradley Barcola to Liverpool update, Man Utd's new plan
Sports.content:
Romero goodbye message

Cristian Romero has released an emotional goodbye message to Tottenham on his Instagram account.

He said: "Today, I say goodbye to a place that, for five seasons, was much more than a club. It was my home, my challenge and the place where my family and I built such an important part of our lives. I leave with a heart full of memories and enormous pride for everything we lived and achieved together.

"When I arrived, I had a clear dream: to leave my name in this club’s history. I knew the only way was through hard work, sacrifice and achieving something that had seemed so difficult for so long: lifting a trophy again. And we did it.

"The journey wasn’t perfect, but I don’t want that to define my goodbye. I choose to remember the happy moments, the lessons, the people who stood by me and, above all, the love I received during these five years. Thank you to everyone at the club who shared this journey with me. Coaches, teammates, staff and every person working behind the scenes you are all part of my story and have a place in my heart.

"And to the fans: Thank you for loving me, respecting me and making me feel like one of you from day one. Thank you for every hug, every song, every flag, every applause and for always being there. I know I wasn’t perfect, but one thing gives me peace: I always gave everything. I defended this shirt with pride and with all my heart.

"THANK YOU FOR EVERYTHING. I’m leaving the club, but a part of my heart will always remain here. Once I was one of you. Today, I leave as one of you forever. With all my love and respect. Thank you for everything. And goodbye @spursofficial."

Sports.title: Bournemouth issue statement following 'disgusting' email to long-serving staff member
Sports.content:
Bournemouth issue statement following 'disgusting' email to long-serving staff member

Bournemouth emailed a number of staff members, including one who'd worked at the club for nearly 60 years, to confirm that they would no longer be required for the new Premier League season

View 2 Images Bournemouth came under fire for their handling of the decision (Image: Dan Mullan/Getty Images)

Bournemouth have issued a statement in response to backlash from their own supporters after sacking a long-serving employee. The Premier League side recently emailed several members of their matchday team to confirm that their services would no longer be required for the 2026-27 season.

‌



A relative of the employee, a man in his 70s, labelled the decision 'disgusting' in a message on X, tagging Bournemouth CEO Jim Frevola. The post read: "A relative of ours has been working on match days for @afcbournemouth for nearly 60 years.

‌



"Programme selling, car park duty and various other roles. 2 weeks before the season starts he received this from the club. A disgusting approach @jimfrevola club should be ashamed."

‌



Frevola replied to the post and insisted that the club would look into the situation. On Saturday, Bournemouth released a statement in response to the criticism.

‌



"AFC Bournemouth has seen the concerns raised regarding changes to some of our matchday staffing arrangements," it read. "We have reviewed the way these changes were communicated to some long-serving members of our matchday team and recognise that it did not reflect the standards we expect of ourselves as a club.

"People who have given many years of service to AFC Bournemouth deserve to be treated with appreciation and respect. We are contacting those affected directly to listen to their concerns and review their individual circumstances.

"As part of our preparations for the new season, we have made changes to a number of matchday roles and working requirements as we continue to strengthen the safety and security of the stadium, its perimeter and surrounding areas. These changes are important, but so too is the way we communicate with and treat the people who have served our club.

‌



View 2 Images Bournemouth will embark on a historic campaign (Image: LOF/BSR Agency/Getty Images)

"We should have handled this better, and we will do better. We are grateful to everyone who has contributed to AFC Bournemouth over the years, and particularly those who have served the club for decades."

It is understood that Bournemouth reached out to the aforementioned man before the statement was released. He last worked in the car park of the Vitality Stadium but has now been offered a role in a different area ahead of the new season.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers scores first Chelsea goal as fans make Enzo Fernandez feelings clear
Sports.content:
Morgan Rogers scores first Chelsea goal as fans make Enzo Fernandez feelings clear

Chelsea wrapped up their preparations for the new season with a comfortable win over La Liga side Real Sociedad on Saturday

View 2 Images Morgan Rogers impressed on his debut in Chelsea blue (Image: Getty Images)

Chelsea concluded pre-season with a 3-1 win over Real Sociedad on Saturday afternoon. The Blues got off to the perfect start with Morgan Rogers netting his first goal for Xabi Alonso's side 11 minutes into his debut.

‌



Joao Pedro's header landed in Rogers' path for a simple tap-in. But Alonso's men were run ragged for much of the first half - indebted to several smart saves from Robert Sanchez.

‌



Chelsea were eventually punished with a stunning volley from Jon Aramburu shortly before half-time to draw the visitors level. Alonso opted to send out an unchanged side in the second half, and his players responded. Joao Pedro rose highest from a brilliant Reece James cross to restore Chelsea's lead in the 47th minute.

‌



Enzo Fernandez deadline passes as Chelsea reject transfer amid Man City interest READ MORE :

Eva Carneiro slams Jose Mourinho and John Terry after Netflix dredge up Chelsea controversy READ MORE :

The Brazilian then got his brace to seal the win with a fine finish in the 77th minute. Here are Mirror Football's talking points from the game...

FOLLOW OUR CHELSEA FB PAGE! Latest Blues news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Rogers impact

Morgan Rogers has begun life at Chelsea in perfect fashion. The former Aston Villa star played his first match since England's third-placed playoff victory over France at the World Cup this summer.

‌



And off the back of an impressive campaign at Villa Park - the ex-Middlesbrough attacker impressed before being replaced early into the first-half.

Enzo booed

Enzo Fernandez certainly did not get the reception he would have hoped for when coming on in the second half. The 25-year-old was given an extended break after reaching the World Cup final with Argentina - a match which saw him sent off.

That red card came after he scored the equaliser in the semi-final against England and celebrated by cupping his ears in front of the supporters. Could it be his behaviour in that last four victory over the Three Lions which caused such fury?

‌



Or the transfer speculation linking him with first Real Madrid and then Manchester City? Whatever it was, the midfielder has some work to do if he wants to win back the support of the Blues faithful - though there were pockets of cheers included with the booing.

View 2 Images Enzo Fernandez received a frosty reception (Image: Getty Images)

Pedro still in form

After an impressive debut campaign at Stamford Bridge, there will have been concerns of a drop off, particularly after missing out on the World Cup squad with Brazil.

‌



But the forward played a key role in Rogers' goal before scoring himself at the start of the second half. He then wrapped up the win with a superb finish. A sharp pre-season for the striker.

Sanchez impresses

For all of Robert Sanchez's deserved criticism, the Spaniard put on a convincing display today with several key saves in the first half. It was the former Brighton keeper's best performance in a Chelsea jersey for some time.

But for his sharp stops in the opening 45 minutes, Alonso's team would have been behind at the break. Instead, the Spanish shot-stopper has given his manager some food for thought over his side's perceived goalkeeping issues.

Article continues below

Palmer off it

Cole Palmer has work to do if he is to be ready for Chelsea's Premier League opener at Fulham on August 24. The talented Englishman had the summer off after not being involved in Thomas Tuchel's World Cup squad, but still doesn't look up to speed.

Sports.content:
Alejandro Garnacho's ex loses home she lived in with Aston Villa star's son as update issued

Alejandro Garnacho joined Aston Villa on loan from Chelsea, which has had a knockdown impact on people close to him

View 3 Images Alejandro Garnacho's ex-partner has shared a heartbreaking update (Image: Jasmin Walter - UEFA/UEFA via Getty Images)

Alejandro Garnacho's ex-girlfriend has been forced to bid farewell to her home in England due to "decisions made by other people." Eva Garcia confirmed she was "leaving with a broken heart" and will exit the home alongside her son Enzo.

‌



The Aston Villa star's ex-partner shared a heartfelt post on social media about her departure, likely prompted by the couple's breakup in 2025. Following a four-year relationship - in which they had a child together - Garnacho and Garcia ended things.

‌



She wrote on Instagram: "I never imagined that one day I would have to say goodbye to the house where my son and I have rebuilt our lives since everything changed. It was here that we took our first steps as a family of two.

‌



"It was here that I learnt to be strong when I had no other choice, and it is here that my son has grown up surrounded by memories that I will always carry with me."

The post included black-and-white images of the home Garnacho and Garcia shared, as well as snaps of their son Enzo. She added: "Today we have to pack our bags and leave.

"Not because we want to, nor because we’ve chosen to do so, but because there are circumstances and decisions made by other people and which have ultimately made it impossible for us to stay here.

‌



"And perhaps that’s what hurts the most: knowing that you did everything in your power to avoid a farewell you never wanted. That you tried to keep a home together whilst the decisions of others ended up setting a date for your departure."

Sports.title: Man Utd new signing sends message to Michael Carrick during private friendly
Sports.content:
Man Utd new signing sends message to Michael Carrick during private friendly

Manchester United manager Michael Carrick will be keeping a close eye on Cristian Orozco following the 18-year-old midfielder's recent arrival from Colombian side Fortaleza

View 2 Images Cristian Orozco has joined Manchester United's under-21s (Image: Poppy Townson/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Cristian Orozco has already made an impression after joining Manchester United this summer. The 18-year-old midfielder touched down from Colombia earlier this month and has scored in a friendly win for the club's under-21s.

‌



Orozco agreed to join United last year but was forced to wait until this summer to officially join due to his age. After turning 18, his transfer from Fortaleza took place earlier in August.

‌



The Colombia under-17 international has initially been placed with United U21s so he has time to settle in a new country. He's wasted no time, scoring his first goal in a 5-0 romp for the under-21s against Aston Villa.

‌



Chido Obi also found the back of the net in the behind-closed-doors friendly, while Ashton Missin scored twice and Amir Ibragimov got on the score sheet too.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

All of United's young players will be hoping to catch the eye of Michael Carrick in the 2026/27 season. Unlike his predecessor Ruben Amorim, Carrick has a reputation for bringing through academy players and pre-season has shown that the door is open.

‌



The likes of Shea Lacey, Ethan Williams, Jacob Devaney and JJ Gabriel have all been handed opportunities this summer. However, Orozco knows he will have to bide his time to break into the first team, with central midfield extremely competitive.

United have splashed out a combined £85million this summer to bring Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa and Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Carrick still wants another arrival in the position, along with a left-back.

View 2 Images Cristian Orozco joined the club earlier this month (Image: Zohaib Alam/Manchester United via Getty Images)

‌



Despite scoring this week, Orozco is primarily a defensive midfielder and has leadership qualities, having captained Colombia's under-18s side before.

"I know my strengths are my physicality and my technique," he told ESPN Colombia before joining United. "I have those qualities and, with the gift God gave me, I don't think it will be too difficult. But everything is about adapting. I'm very young and that's what I'll need to do.

"I want to arrive and learn as quickly as possible. That's what's required so I can show my level and everything I'm capable of. I want to adapt to everything that comes my way as quickly as possible."

‌



He added: "I expect to learn a lot of English. When I was there, I realised just how, how important it is."

United's first team have their final pre-season friendly against Amorim's AC Milan on Saturday. They will then focus on preparing for their Premier League opener against newly-promoted Hull on August 22.
