Sports.title: Lankshear double steers Boro to victory
Sports.content:
Marquee signing Will Lankshear notched a second-half double as Middlesbrough fought back to kick off their Championship bid with a hard-fought 2-1 victory and end newly promoted Lincoln's stunning nine-month unbeaten run.

The Imps - playing their first second-tier match in 65 years - made a strong start and opened the scoring in the 12th minute through Adam Reach.

But former Tottenham forward Lankshear marked his first league appearance since his much-hyped move to the Riverside by equalising just after the hour and then stabbing in a stoppage-time winner.

It was a devastating end for spirited Lincoln as a run of 29 games undefeated in all competitions since early December was brought to a halt in their first league match since their new joint head coach partnership of Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw stepped up to take the reins following the departure of boss Michael Skubala to Bristol City in May.

Image: Will Lankshear celebrates scoring for Midlesbrough

Boro boss Kim Hellberg included summer signings Radek Vitek, Sebastian Berhalter, Lankshear and Kyle Joseph in his starting XI while Alpha Kante and Neto Borges were also pitched in after returning from loan stints last season at St Etienne and Bristol City respectively.

The Lincoln side selected for their first Championship match since 1961 bore a far more familiar look, with all 11 starters having been part of the squad that cruised to the League One title last term.

The Imps' high-intensity start paid off when they took the lead with a goal involving both of their wing-backs. Captain Tendayi Darikwa was released down the right and his firm delivery across the box was met by Reach, who arrived from the left to rasp a ferocious left-footed shot beyond Vitek from 15 yards out.

Boro tried to summon a response and Leo Castledine and Kante both threatened from distance, while Adilson Malanda then saw a header held by George Wickens.

The visitors remained a threat, however, and Dom Jefferies had two opportunities midway through the half.

Boro cranked up the pressure towards the interval, with Lankshear threatening on a couple of occasions before Joseph's close-range shot was brilliantly pushed behind by Wickens.

The hosts continued to knock on the door after the break and Lankshear had a shot blocked by Wickens before Morgan Whittaker curled a free-kick just over.

Boro levelled in the 62nd minute when Callum Brittain's cross from the right was headed out by Deji Elerewe but only as far as Castledine whose angled drive across goal was diverted home instinctively from six yards out by Lankshear.

It looked like the hosts were going to be left frustrated when Lankshear hit the bar in the closing stages. But Boro's new striker provided the game's decisive moment as it entered added time when he turned the ball home at the near post after brilliant work on the right by sub Riley McGree to set him up.

What the result means and next fixtures...

Sports.title: West Brom earn controversial win at Norwich
Sports.content:
West Brom launched a smash-and-grab raid to open their Championship campaign with a hard-fought 2-1 win at Norwich.

The Baggies were under the cosh for long periods at Carrow Road but stood firm before scoring twice late on through Aune Heggebo and Jimmy-Jay Morgan to secure an unlikely victory, although Heggebo's opener appeared to come off his hand.

Norwich substitute Mathias Kvistgaarden reduced the arrears in the 90th minute but it was too little, too late for a home side who will wonder how they failed to take all three points, let alone one.

The hosts took the game to their visitors from the word go and went close to taking the lead after just four minutes.

Kenny McLean had a clear sight of goal after playing a sharp one two with Anis Ben Slimane on the right but Albion keeper Max O'Leary made an excellent stop to thwart the City skipper.

Image: Jimmy-Jay Morgan celebrates his goal with team-mates

That proved to be the clearest opening of a tight first half which the Canaries had the better of without seriously troubling O'Leary again.

Defender Kellen Fisher's snap-shot from the edge of the box was comfortably dealt with and, when a cross from left looked set to produce the opener, a brilliant last-ditch clearance from Callum Styles snuffed out the danger.

The Baggies defended well but struggled to produce anything in the final third, with Heggebo dragging their only real opening of the half well wide on 25 minutes.

Norwich were again on the front foot at the start of the second period and it required an excellent block from Nat Phillips to deflect Ben Slimane's goal-bound effort into the side-netting.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player West Brom's Aune Heggebo gives the Baggies the lead over Norwich, but did his hands get in the way?

Phillips was at it again on the hour mark to prevent what looked like a certain goal. This time Paris Maghoma produced some magic on the edge of the box before setting up a glorious chance for Andre Brooks but the big defender got his imposing frame in the way.

The home pressure was now incessant, with Mohamed Toure hitting an upright after wriggling his way through from the left and O'Leary then keeping out Fisher's flick after the defender had popped up unmarked at the back post.

It seemed as though a home goal was inevitable but when the opener eventually arrived on 75 minutes it was at the other end as Albion made their first clear chance of the match count.

Styles did well to put in Morgan through the inside left channel and his low cross was bundled over the line by Heggebo, with the hosts appealing in vain for offside. Although the ball did seem to strike his arm to cross the line.

Vladan Kovacevic made a superb save to prevent Isaac Price from doubling Albion's advantage from long range eight minutes later.

But after Styles had made another fine block, Albion broke upfield to make it 2-0 on 87 minutes. Morgan showed great composure after being given a clear run down the left and worked his way skilfully into the box before drilling the ball home.

Norwich were not finished, however, and pulled one back as the game entered added time. O'Leary made an incredible reflex stop to deny Jacob Wright but fellow substitute Kvistgaarden was on hand to nod home the loose ball.

What the result means and next fixtures...

Sports.title: Swansea strike back to win at Stoke
Sports.content:
Super-sub Adam Idah snatched the winner with his first touch of the game as Swansea bravely battled back from a goal down to stun Stoke 2-1.

The Republic of Ireland international had been on the pitch for barely a minute when he scored in the 66th minute as the Swans claimed their first win at the bet365 Stadium for over five years.

Defeat was a bitter bill to swallow for the Potters, especially after Eric Bocat had fired them into a 10th-minute lead.

The defender grabbed his first goal for the club on his 60th league appearance with a deflected left-foot strike.

But Nigeria international midfielder Joseph Opoku snatched a 23rd-minute equaliser for the Swans, powering in with a sweet right-foot shot after some poor defending.

Image: Zan Vipotnik of Swansea City is challenged by Bosun Lawal of Stoke City

And the hosts' frustrating afternoon went from bad to worse when Idah won it with a smart close-range finish after more questionable defending.

The home side made the best possible start when left-back Bocat fired them ahead.

Svante Ingelsson whipped the ball in from the left wing, Tomas Rigo collected and teed up Bocat who, having turned his marker, unleashed a left-foot shot which was deflected over goalkeeper Lawrence Vigouroux and into the far corner.

But it was not long before the visitors were back on level terms when Opoku took advantage of sloppy defending by the Potters.

Moussa Yeo crossed from the left, Zan Vipotnik got an important flick-on and there was Opoku, unmarked at the back post, to fire home with ease.

Goalscorer Boucat was nowhere to be seen as the 21-year-old summer signing gladly notched his first goal for his new club.

Seven minutes before the break Bosun Lawal attacked a ball at the back post but his header flew high and wide.

Stoke boss Mark Robins made a change at the break with Maksym Talovierov brought on to replace Lawal.

And the hosts started brightly and came within a whisker of scoring a second, but an alert Vigouroux thwarted them with a brilliant save.

Sorba Thomas weaved his way into the box and looked certain to score, but Vigouroux tipped his thunderbolt shot over the crossbar.

That save proved hugely important as the Swans broke on the counter-attack and Idah slotted home with his first touch.

Josh Tymon's cross evaded everyone as the hosts were again caught sleeping and Idah gleefully netted his first goal of the season.

Bocat had a chance to level with six minutes remaining, but his low left-foot drive was saved well by Vigouroux at his near post.

Sports.title: England's Givens breaks LET duck at 210th attempt as rival's ball gets stuck in tree
Sports.content:
England's Eleanor Givens won her first Ladies European Tour title at the 210th attempt with a one-shot victory at the VP Bank Swiss Ladies Open.

The 37-year-old carded a five-under 66 on the third and final day in Zug, retaking the lead at 17 with her fifth birdie of a blemish-free final round and then parring the last.

Alexandra Forsterling - who chipped in for a remarkable par at 14 after her ball got stuck in a tree off the tee - shared second place on 12 under alongside Ireland's Anna Foster and Australia's Whitney Hillier, with Sweden's Kajsa Arwefjaell fifth on 11 under.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Alexandra Forsterling hit her tee shot at 14 into a tree before escaping with a remarkable par

Givens registered just one bogey all week, in her three-under opening round, with the Englishwoman also enjoying a five-under Friday, including three birdies on the trot to finish.

Her gains on Saturday came at two, three, seven and 10 ahead of picking up a decisive shot on the penultimate hole as she became the third English winner on the LET this year.

Sports.title: Bolton beat Preston for first Championship win since 2019
Sports.content:
Sam Dalby and Thierry Gale scored first-half goals as Bolton beat Preston 2-1 to record their first Sky Bet Championship win since March 2019.

Last season's League One play-off final winners have been predicted to struggle on their return to the second tier after seven years away.

But in front of a sellout 26,262 crowd at the Toughsheet Community Stadium, Steven Schumacher's side dominated the long-standing members of this division.

Image: Sam Dalby celebrates his opener

The only nerves came four minutes from time when Jusef Erabi headed in fellow substitute Andrija Vukcevic's cross. Liam Lindsey should have headed a last-gasp equaliser but missed from close range.

That would have been harsh on Bolton. Dalby scored 14 times last season in all competition and he was soon off the mark as Wanderers set a hot pace.

John McAtee did not have the best of times in League One last season but he quickly embraced this step up in class.

However, Daniel Iversen should have dealt better with McAtee's left-footed shot. The goalkeeper's weak save only pushed the ball to Dalby, who side-footed home from 18 yards.

Eleven minutes later, Wanderers deservedly doubled their advantage.

McAtee's latest pass picked out Gale who cut in from the left before unleashing a curling right-footed shot beyond Iversen's despairing dive.

North End had won each of their last three away league games against Bolton but a fourth on the bounce never looked likely.

They looked to have gone three behind as Dalby headed in after 37 minutes. Instead, McAtee was adjudged to have fouled as he challenged for another assist.

A minute later, North End threatened to reduce their arrears as new boy Delano Burgzorg burst into the area. Chris Forino triumphantly celebrated the subsequent block.

Bolton though were dominating opponents playing in the Championship for a 12th successive season.

Just after the hour mark, Preston's 4,400 fans were in unison as manager Paul Heckingbottom introduced his most recent signings Leo Leroy, Odel Offiah and Erabi for Pol Valentin, Jordan Thompson and Callum Lang.

Leroy was immediately fouled by Josh Sheehan, previously cautioned for a cynical challenge on Alfie Devine, who received a final warning from referee Adam Herczeg.

Devine's pass then presented Milutin Osmajic with a shooting opportunity but Jack Bonham was equal to the Montenegrin's tame effort.

Dalby should have settled the contest after 73 minutes with only Iversen to beat. Instead, his left-footed effort was equally soft and the keeper saved.

Preston then wasted a fantastic chance to get back into the game four minutes later. Osmajic beat the offside trap but with only Bonham to beat squared the ball to Erabi who was quickly crowded out.

Erabi made amends but Lindsay's miss ensured Wanderers topped the fledgling Championship table.

The managers

Bolton's Steven Schumacher:

"That's what this division is all about. From being in control of the game we are happy they missed a sitter at the end not to take away our three points. It's going to be an exciting ride so strap in.

"This was a big occasion for us. It was our first game back at this level for such a long time. We were playing a local rival and in front of a sell-out crowd. There was so much riding on it.

"We were ready to be positive and in the first half particularly, we were against a well organised and fully established Championship team.

"There were things in the second half, especially in the last 15 minutes, that we can learn from. Overall, I am pleased how the boys handled it. To step upto this level and play as well as we did is a real positive and I think we deserved them (the points).

"We had to make changes towards the end because this league is demanding. Even our goalie had cramp and you don't see that too often."

Preston's Paul Heckingbottom:

"It was frustrating in lots of ways. Frustrated with the nature of the two goals and the people involved in them.

"The goals were shocking and changed the game and changed the atmosphere. It probably gave them even more energy.

"In transition they had a hunger about them. They hunted the ball much better than us.

"We needed to be better in the second half in lots of ways. It left us a mountain to climb but I said to the players I still felt we could win the game.

"We got in behind them down the sides a lot more than they did us. But we weren't positive or direct enough. We let them off the hook at one end and we gave them the opportunities at the other to get the place rocking."

What the result means and next fixtures...

Sports.title: Oxford 2-2 MK Dons
Sports.content:
Ciaron Brown turned in a Gatlin O'Donkor cross deep into stoppage time to earn relegated Oxford United a 2-2 draw against newly-promoted MK Dons at the Kassam Stadium.

Mark Harris fired Oxford in front in the 20th minute only for Charlie Goode to head Dons level nine minutes later.

Aaron Collins then nodded in Ryan Wintle's cross on 34 minutes to put Dons in front and turn the match around.

When Harris shot the U's ahead, it followed a spell of sloppy defending. Sirike Dembele saw a shot blocked and as Oxford's players appealed for a handball, Dons failed to clear and Harris lashed the ball in from 12 yards.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Aaron Ramsey's Oxford scored a 96th minute equaliser against MK Dons.

Yet the visitors levelled when Goode rose at the far post to head Daniel Barlaser's cross over keeper Jamie Cumming and in.

And Dons quickly struck again - Wintle crossing for Collins to power home a header.

In the second half, Collins headed against a post but the U's refused to give up - and got their reward in the fifth minute of stoppage time.

Sports.title: Scotland hope to name 39-year-old Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approach
Sports.content:
The Scottish Football Association hopes to name the Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke as manager early next week. The 39-year-old, who was sacked by Monaco in June, will become the country’s first non-Scottish manager since Berti Vogts, who was in charge from 2002-04.

Clarke’s abrupt departure came as Scotland exited the World Cup at the group stage. He had signed a four-year contract extension immediately before the tournament. It quickly became clear the SFA would turn towards a foreign manager; Jon Dahl Tomasson and Kasper Hjulmand were linked with the position.

Pocognoli will probably be welcomed by Scotland fans in respect of a fresh approach. Clarke was in position for a generally successful seven years, but was often criticised for a pragmatic style.

After a period in youth coaching, Pocognoli enjoyed a successful time in charge of Union Saint-Gilloise in his homeland. Under Pocognoli, Union won their first title in 90 years in 2025. A move to Monaco followed, but Pocognoli lasted eight months and 38 games in France.

Sports.title: Women’s U20 World Cup boycott may hurt in short term but can send Fifa a vital message | Tom Garry
Sports.content:
“And I say to all the women … Pick the right battles. Pick the right fights. You have the power to change. You have the power to convince us men what we have to do and what we don’t have to do. You do it. Just do it. With men, with Fifa, you will find open doors. Just push the doors. They are open.”

Those were the condescending words of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, three years ago during a tone-deaf speech in Sydney, which left his audience, including some of the most senior women in the game, exasperated. It is a damning indictment of Infantino’s tenure that his patronising monologue on the eve of the Women’s World Cup final now barely even creeps into the top 10 of the most controversial moments since his latest re-election, in March 2023.

Yet, with the Swiss administrator’s future hanging finely in the balance, the power to enforce once-in-a-generation change at Fifa may well be in the hands of women’s teams after all, as the threat of a boycott lingers over September’s Women’s Under-20 World Cup, the Women’s Under-17 World Cup, which gets under way in October, and that month’s senior World Cup playoff ties for next summer’s major showpiece, the Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

This week Lisa Nandy told the BBC that Infantino “should go” and, overall, the culture secretary spoke well on the matter, but she added that she would not support a boycott of the U20 World Cup and said she was “not generally in favour of sporting boycotts full stop – because they unfairly penalise athletes and competitors who are not responsible for the reason that these boycotts take place”. On that specific element, it is important to respectfully disagree with Nandy and the many others who share that view.

Yes, it would feel deeply unjust for football’s political turmoil to have an adverse impact on the development of the world’s best young women footballers through no fault of their own, but that is why any participating countries being prepared to boycott the upcoming under-20 tournament would send such a powerful message.

It is tempting to follow the stance that many working within the women’s game are taking privately, which is that it would be a travesty if women’s football, having been neglected and let down by the authorities for generations, was harmed again by disruption to such a significant tournament, but the painful reality is that the young generation of women’s stars stand to be most affected by the decisions that are made by governing bodies in the days, weeks and months ahead.

View image in fullscreen North Korea celebrate winning the most recent Women’s U20 World Cup, in 2024. Photograph: Julian Medina/SPP/Shutterstock

And yes, is it unfair for women’s teams, and young women’s teams in particular, to shoulder the responsibility of taking a stance against the now-scrapped vision of selling off a stake in Fifa tournaments – which, we should remember, would include all Fifa’s women’s tournaments too – through the murky concept of the Fifa Forward Enterprise subsidiary, but it is their futures, and the organisation of the World Cups finals that will come to define their careers, which are at stake.

And the future of the governance of the sport, and decisions about who runs the game, is a debate that women’s football players, coaches and fans all deserve a much more vocal say in, on far more deep-rooted injustices than those that have dominated the news in recent weeks.

Is it fair that, for example, there are only two women – Paola López of Mexico and Vietnam’s Thi My Dung Nguyen – among the 18 members of Fifa’s disciplinary committee, which hit the headlines amid the farcical Folarin Balogun scandal this summer? Or that all 10 of the members of Fifa’s Future of Football committee are men?

Is it fair that, of the 37 members of Fifa’s council, the organisation’s strategic and oversight body, 29 are men and only eight are women? Or that seven of the eight vice-presidents are men?

Is it fair that the 2023 Women’s World Cup prize money totalled $110m and this summer’s men’s World Cup’s prize pot was around eight times larger, at a record-breaking $871m?

It would be wrong to say that there have not been positive improvements in women’s football across the world since Infantino took office in 2016. The past decade has included long overdue, albeit still very important and welcome, enhancements to provisions for players and coaches at women’s tournaments, a sizeable growth in financial investment and huge uplift in prize money, albeit from a very low bar. It is also fair to say that there are many key figures in the women’s game, across all continents, who support Infantino and are appreciative of the gradual improvements that are being made, while acknowledging that there is still a very long way to go.

View image in fullscreen Lucy Bronze has backed a boycott. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA

But everyone associated with women’s football should be concerned that the 25-page sales pitch that was titled Fifa Forward Enterprise Member Materials contained only one token reference to women’s football. It is why the England defender Lucy Bronze was right to use her voice to say she backed a boycott “for the good of the game”.

On Friday morning, the latest twist in Infantino’s future delivered both positives and negatives for the under-fire president, as on the one hand, the Oceania Football Confederation declared its support for Infantino, while the confederation’s biggest member, New Zealand, withdrew its backing for him. New Zealand, impeccable co-hosts of the most recent Women’s World Cup, will have had plenty of reasons to support Infantino but has chosen to use its platform to call for “stronger governance, accountability and transparency”.

Shortly before that news, on Thursday, a feature article was published on Fifa’s website entitled “Europe’s finest hours at the Under-20 Women’s World Cup”, looking back at dazzling performances of young breakthrough stars such as Spain’s Salma Paralluelo’s in 2022 or the Germany striker Alexandra Popp in 2010. Next month six European teams – including the hosts, Poland – are scheduled to show the world what they are capable of, but – whether the timing of that article was purely coincidental, political or ironic – European women’s under-20 teams’ finest hour may still be yet to come.

Sports.title: Farewell Cristian Romero, you actually always were ‘that type of player’ | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
“He’s not that kind of player” is perhaps the greatest of the co-commentators’ meaningless banalities. Used shortly after a “nice guy” has scythed someone in half about a day after the ball has gone, it is by definition nonsense because if you have scythed someone in half about a day after the ball has gone, then you are indeed that kind of player.

But I don’t recall ever hearing anyone saying “the thing is Clive/Brian, he is that kind of player”. I haven’t analysed every foul in Premier League history to tell if you those kinds of challenges are carried out by players all of us would consider to be “that kind of player” as opposed to the opposite – but the list of players with the most red cards suggests a pattern – Richard Dunne, Duncan Ferguson, Patrick Vieira with eight reds, Lee Cattermole and Roy Keane on seven, Vinnie Jones, Joey Barton and Alan Smith (obviously not that one) among those on six.

This article is about Cristian Romero – who I would have in tier A of “that kind of player” if I had any idea how to do one of those Instagram reels where you rank things (posh hotels you can’t afford, non weight-bearing exercises for middle-aged people, biscuits of the 80s etc). There is not a debate about the category in which he belongs.

A player with a permanent look of mild confusion about the situation he finds himself in – am I really playing for Spurs? Consistently inconsistent. And always just a moment away from just giving the whole game a Falling-Down-full-Michael-Douglas-ing.

Six red cards in his Spurs career. It feels like so many more. The one that sticks in my mind is in the Champions League last-16 exit to Milan in 2023. Hopefully you don’t remember the game, it was awful. 1-0 going into the second leg, it’s goalless in the 77th minute at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Spurs aren’t doing much. Romero’s already on a booking for lunging into Rafael Leão. And then for no apparent reason he flies into Théo Hernandez on the touchline.

It’s peak Romero. That sense that he was just a bit annoyed he wasn’t playing for someone better and so he needed a release. And in this case Hernandez was that release.

His four Premier League red cards feature all your favourites. Two yellows against Manchester City featuring a wild late tackle on Erling Haaland deep in the City half – really letting him know he was there.

There are a couple of straight red get-the-ball-really-get-the-man challenges that he probably would have got away with in 1986. One against Chelsea when Spurs were top of the league and 1-0 up early in the Ange Postecoglou tenure earned a “oh nooooo Romero, you … you … you …” from Gary Neville. The other on Casemiro last season came shortly after he criticised the club on social media prompting calls for Thomas Frank to strip him of the captaincy. It was his second red of the season after getting two yellows for dissent and kicking Ibrahima Konaté on the floor against Liverpool last December. “What’s he doing?” Neville again.

View image in fullscreen Cristian Romero is sent off at Old Trafford last season with his international defensive teammate Lisandro Martínez celebrating in the background for good measure. Photograph: James Gill/Danehouse/Getty Images

It’s often said the great defenders don’t go to ground – but it feels like that is exactly where Romero spent his entire Spurs career.

And yet. And yet – he spent most of the Europa League final win against Manchester United on the floor – hurling himself at shots, and United players, in a man-of-the-match performance. People rightly remember the Micky van de Ven goalline clearance, but Romero was unbeatable in that game. He can’t not be good. Gasperini, Scaloni, Conte, Postecoglou, Frank, Simeone all like him. He has played in two World Cup Finals (if you accept any Argentinians actually played in the last one).

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

All fans like a player who flies into challenges – we like to think we’re subtle, but we evolved from primates – one of your own putting in a reducer, an oof into the turf perhaps it takes us back somewhere deep into our past. And he scored vital goals too.

Atlético Madrid feels so perfect. The people I talk to who watch Spanish football (ie Sid Lowe once he’s actually replied to a WhatsApp) tell me Atléti aren’t the Atleti we want them to be anymore. It’s not all Godín Giménez and Juanfran. Perhaps Simeone is taking them back there. But we should all be thankful that he has arrived in his spiritual home.

As soon as the Atleti rumours began it felt perfect – it is rare for a player to feel like they fit at a club before they’ve even worn the colours. But in the same way James Maddison always looked like he should be in a Spurs shirt, perhaps Romero never did, even when he was wearing it – even when he was playing brilliantly in a gritty backs-to-the-wall job in a Europa League final. Is that really emblematic of what a Spurs centre-back should be? At their best Spurs centre-backs are Gary Mabbutt or Ledley King, Jan Vertonghen or Toby Alderweireld – solid, reliable, measured. At their worst – well there have been lots of them, but not many as rash as Romero.

It is perhaps a fault of mine, or a fault of how we watch and consume football, that I’ve already made my mind up. Watching Romero I was either annoyed by something he’d done, or annoyed that I was going to be annoyed about something he was going to do later. This permanent pre-annoyance rendered an objective judgment impossible.

So when people talk about his leadership and especially his ability on the ball, I was never totally convinced. But good luck Cristian, I get the feeling it will be much less stressful watching you play for a team I am less invested in. He might leave Spurs a club legend, it’s hard to say for sure; but if he does, he leaves as an incredibly infuriating one.

Sports.title: London City Lionesses’ Mapi León: ‘It is a club created for women. It is beautiful and exciting’
Sports.content:
‘No, I can’t, I’m sorry, it’s a secret!” Mapi León roars with laughter, in response to being asked what persuaded her to join London City Lionesses. Does this bode badly for our interview? Fear not, the Spain centre-back is in as banterous and jovial a mood as you could imagine any new signing to be, as she embarks on her first major interview since signing for the Women’s Super League club.

Across the course of our conversation, in bright sunshine outside a quiet hotel near Maidstone, it is evident that the 31-year-old could scarcely be happier about her decision to swap Barcelona for south-east England. She is sorely missing her cat, Bagheera (“Here, you ask for so many things for pets, you can’t [really] fly with them, it’s so many documents, so many things”) but, that aside, she is buoyant, relaxed and clearly embracing English life. She says she likes the “little bread” in the morning, and we eventually establish she is referring to crumpets, and reveals: “I like the beans in the morning. It’s really interesting. My Spanish teammates like Alexia [Putellas] and Jana [Fernández] are like: ‘What are you doing eating beans in the morning? You need to train.’ I go: ‘No, it’s fine I like it.’”

However, English breakfasts were surely not what attracted her to Kent to play for London City Lionesses so, returning to that first question, she explains thoughtfully: “My body was craving something different. I spent many years in a comfortable position, because playing at Barça has been absolutely wonderful and very nice; it is a style of game that suits me a lot and coming to England, the football is very different from the Spanish one, at first glance. So, I think [the reason was] being able to challenge myself and see if I am capable. I am going to make an effort to adapt to this league and also to show myself that I’m able to compete in another style of play that is not the one that makes me stand out the most.”

An undisputed club legend at Barcelona, León certainly stood out in Spain as the best ball-playing centre-back of her generation, and won seven league titles, seven Copa de la Reina’s and – most impressively – four Champions League titles, during a nine-year period of relentless dominance with Barcelona, whom she joined from Atlético Madrid in 2017.

This summer she was one of four members of the Spain starting XI that beat England 4-0 in June in Mallorca to leave Barcelona, together with Arsenal’s new signing Ona Batlle, OL Lyonnes’ new winger Salma Paralluelo and, most notably, her London City Lionesses teammate Alexia Putellas. Together, León and Putellas drew raised eyebrows across the women’s game by swapping the reigning European champions for a lesser-known team that finished sixth in the WSL last term, but they have been joined by a series of other world-renowned names including the former England goalkeeper Mary Earps and the France winger Kadidiatou Diani.

The club’s new signings meet the vision of their ambitious owner, the American businesswoman Michele Kang, of whom León says: “The impression I get is of an empowered woman, with a winning mindset, driven by a desire to see things improve and a drive to win. And that is a competitive and winning mentality. And if in the end, I want to be part of it because it is a club created for women and that is not common, I think it is beautiful and exciting.

“Everything counts when you make this kind of a decision, and of course, [Kang] was an important part because seeing another woman doing so much to help women’s sports, and women’s football grow, I think it’s impossible not to value that. I think it’s something very powerful.”

View image in fullscreen Mapi León hugs the Champions League trophy after Barcelona’s victory over Wolfsburg in 2023, the second of four WCL titles the defender had won with the club. Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images

The club’s signings of Putellas and León were announced five days apart in July, which prompts the question: did they discuss their decision with one another and was it a case of “If you go, I’ll go too”?

“No, not really, no. I think we take the issue of personal matters very seriously,” León says. “It’s a very different challenge. You come from a league where you win every year. Where you have achieved great things internationally and you come to a club that finished mid-table with some different challenges. And I think it is a very personal decision for each individual to make, choosing what is best for you personally.

“[You ask yourself] what do you really need right now? What is your body telling you? What do you think is best for you to keep improving, to keep pushing yourself, and to maintain that ambition? And I think each person needs different things. So, there wasn’t much communication between us. And that the decision wasn’t planned.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The more she reflects on her move, the tactical differences between Liga F and the WSL become clear as a key factor, as the Zaragoza-born defender continues: “The English league can give me a lot. You can learn a lot. The transitions, the style of play, playing with more space. The pressing is different too because I’m used to teams often sitting back in a mid-to-low block, whereas here, it’s probably more of a high press. I’d like to bring a bit of calm to the game.

“I don’t know if that really fits with English football, but no, of course, I don’t want to change the system, but simply the timings as a centre-back. I am a centre-back so I see everything. And I like to control a little bit of the timings so maybe we can try to have a little bit more of the ball. Or there are many spaces, so we can go. So I like to have a bit of control.

View image in fullscreen Mapi León is one of several big summer signings made by London City Lionesses and was attracted by the competitive nature of the WSL. Photograph: Sally Rawlins/London City Lionesses

“The league is so competitive, the commitment the league is making, the clubs, I mean, I think everything makes it very attractive to come because I have been following the English league over these years and it feels like it can’t let you relax even for a second, not in any match, not during the match. Not a single second can relax you, because the English league is much more competitive.”

Her new side open the season at home to Manchester United on 4 September. Until then, she is embracing a comparatively quiet life and enjoying not being recognised in public, adding: “It’s so different [here]. It’s not a bad thing but, I can just walk to buy food, and no one recognises me! And sometimes it’s nice, because in Barcelona we are not ‘famous’ but people know us. It’s one of the many amazing things. But also sometimes you miss this freedom. Like, just go and shop.”

How long that newfound anonymity will continue is hard to tell, as it will surely not take long for León to become one of the most recognisable faces in the WSL if she can bring her form for Spain and Barcelona straight to London City Lionesses. For now, she can enjoy her beans and her crumpets in peace.

Sports.title: Paris Saint-Germain sign Ferran Torres from Barcelona in €50m deal
Sports.content:
Paris Saint-Germain have signed Spain’s World Cup-winning ⁠forward Ferran Torres from Barcelona on a contract until 2031. Financial ​details were not disclosed, but reports said PSG paid €50m (£42.7m) ⁠for the 26-year-old.

“I’m delighted to be beginning a new adventure at such an ambitious ⁠club as Paris Saint-Germain,” Torres said. “I’d like ‌to thank President ‌Nasser al-Khelaifi, Luis Campos [PSG’s football adviser] and coach ‌Luis Enrique for giving me the opportunity to join the team, which I hope to help win as many trophies as possible.”

Spain’s World Cup hero arrives in the French capital after ‌scoring the extra-time winner in the final against Argentina. He scored ​21 goals and provided three assists in 49 appearances in all competitions for Barça last season as they retained their La Liga ⁠title.

Sports.title: Liverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos
Sports.content:
Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.

Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.

Elaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo, and Bryan Baum, co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will also join the Liverpool board. Bezos is considered a passive investor and will not have a seat on the board.

Despite the involvement of Bezos, the third richest man in the world with $272bn (£201bn), Eduardo Saverin, worth an estimated $33bn and the Mittal family, worth around $17bn, FSG will remain in operational control of Liverpool as well as majority owners. 1892 Holdings’ investment remains subject to regulatory approval, which could take up to 90 days, and will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. There is also no change to the leadership or day-to-day running of Liverpool.

FSG insist the deal is not part of an exit strategy from a club they acquired in 2010 for £300m after the near-ruinous ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett. The transaction does not compel FSG to sell more of the club to 1892 at a future date, or include obligations for 1892 to increase their stake, but it does give Bhatia’s consortium options to purchase more of Liverpool should the majority owners eventually decide to sell.

It is the makeup of Bhatia’s consortium, rather than any financial need, that FSG claim attracted them to the British-Indian businessman’s proposal. The FSG leadership team of principal owner John W Henry, chair Tom Werner and president Mike Gordon have spent almost a year getting to know Bhatia and believe the deal will create further opportunities for Liverpool in global business, technology and investment, including in the important markets of India and Asia.

View image in fullscreen The sale will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Gordon, who has resumed a more hands-on role at Liverpool following the departure of Michael Edwards as chief executive of football at FSG, said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.

“As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.”

With Premier League and Uefa financial regulations linking a club’s spending to turnover, the new investment will not have an immediate benefit for head coach Andoni Iraola and his Liverpool team. However, the commercial opportunities presented by the involvement of Bezos, Bhatia and Saverin will enable the Anfield club to grow their annual revenue significantly. Liverpool’s annual revenue increased to a record £703m in the year ending May 2025.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Speaking on behalf of 1892 Holdings, Bhatia said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.

“To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come.”

Bhatia was involved in QPR for almost 19 years and took on numerous roles, from chair of the club to chair of the club’s community trust, until transferring his shareholding in July. He is likely to have a more visible presence at Anfield than fellow members of his consortium or FSG.

Sports.title: Enzo Fernandez BOOED and cheered by Chelsea fans during home friendly against Real Sociedad after Man City failed to meet strict transfer deadline
Sports.content:
Chelsea supporters were divided as Enzo Fernandez returned to Stamford Bridge on Saturday after Friday’s 5pm deadline for clubs to make a £120million offer for the Argentine international passed without a bid.

There were perhaps expected boos when his name was read out before kick-off, with the World Cup runner-up starting on the bench.

But the atmosphere turned bizarre when he was introduced after an hour, with sections of the crowd booing him while others proudly sang his name. That continued when he had the ball in midfield, too, with disgruntled boos followed by encouraging chants.

Fernandez, who replaced Reece James and wore the captain's armband for the final 30 minutes, has been stuck in a complicated situation at Chelsea since he alerted the world in March that he dreams of playing for Real Madrid. Then-manager Liam Rosenior took umbrage and dropped him for two games in response.

Enzo Fernandes was both booed and serenaded by Chelsea fans on his Stamford Bridge return

The feeling this summer has been that his future lies away from Stamford Bridge, but his options are limited by few clubs having the financial capacity to meet Chelsea's valuation.

Manchester City were the front-runners, but Chelsea set suitors an unofficial deadline of 5pm Friday to make a sufficient offer as they want their squad fixed before their season opener against Fulham on August 24.

Although that deadline passed without an offer, it remains to be seen if a £120m bid between now and September 1 would test their resolve. What is for sure, though, is that Chelsea supporters do not know how to feel about it.

Fernandez was unaffected by his contradictory reception, looking comfortable in midfield as he earned his first minutes since returning from the World Cup.

The Matthew Harding stand became a supportive chorus in the 90th minute, chanting and applauding when he took a free-kick near the corner flag which looped over the bar.

Peerless Pedro

With the pantomime out of the way, the picture is much more encouraging on the pitch after Joao Pedro put Premier League defenders on notice.

The forward, with fire blazing in his belly after Carlo Ancelotti snubbed him for Brazil’s World Cup squad, wrapped up pre-season with eight goals in seven games, scoring twice as Chelsea beat Real Sociedad 3-1 in their final match before the curtain-raiser against Fulham. He was by far the best player in Chelsea's pre-season campaign.

It is no surprise after a stellar first season at Chelsea, in which he scored 20 goals in 50 games despite the West London club’s subpar league campaign. But the 24-year-old has looked even brighter under new manager Xabi Alonso.

Joao Pedro scored twice in Chelsea's final pre-season friendly

The tightness of the front three in Alonso’s 3-4-3 allows Pedro to showcase the best elements of his game, both linking up play, using his blistering pace to run in behind and constantly looking for the ball in the penalty area.

A timely cross from James found Pedro at the far post as he scored Chelsea’s second of the afternoon, burying his header past the near post. His second was trademark Pedro, latching on to a ball in behind from Malo Gusto and drilling a low shot with his right foot.

Pedro was lively, eager to get going and better last season’s efforts. Chelsea’s frontline looks lethal with Morgan Rogers joining him alongside Cole Palmer.

Rogers off the mark

Chelsea’s £117m marquee summer signing Morgan Rogers could not have wished for a better start to life at his new club, scoring inside 10 minutes.

Rogers lined up on the left of Chelsea’s front three and showed laser-sharp reactions to pounce on Real Sociedad goalkeeper Alex Remiro. The Spaniard initially denied Pedro inside the box, but could do little to prevent Rogers from tapping home the rebound from a couple of yards out.

Morgan Rogers made a good first impression in front of his new fans at Stamford Bridge

The British record transfer holder played 62 minutes, having only joined Chelsea training this week after spending the summer at the World Cup with England.

He showcased his ball-carrying ability just minutes after putting Chelsea ahead, driving forward to create another chance for Pedro, who was denied by a fine stop from Remiro.

Alonso commits to back three

Xabi Alonso appears to have settled on the back-three formation that served him well at Bayer Leverkusen, using the system in consecutive first-team games after initially leaking goals with a back four.

Alonso debuted the system against AC Milan last week, as Chelsea kept their only clean sheet of pre-season. And while they conceded once against Real Sociedad, a wonderful strike from outside of the box by Jon Aramburu, the set-up offers more defensive stability than a back four.

Xabi Alonso was given a warm welcome by Chelsea supporters pre-match - they even sung his name midway through the first half

With Maxence Lacroix now integrated into the squad, the centre-back trio Alonso is likely to start against Fulham appears clear. Lacroix joined from Crystal Palace, where he played in the centre of a back three.

Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill flanked Lacroix against Real Sociedad, making for an imposing trio. Chelsea’s backline lacked physicality at times last season - Lacroix's physicality and pace could help address that weakness.

Marco Palestra has been efficient at left wing-back, getting up and down the line. Pedro Neto, however, could become a problem on the opposite side with the Portuguese winger lacking offensive prowess.

Missing men

There was an extensive list of absentees for Chelsea's final pre-season outing, with new signings Danny Welbeck, Emmanuel Emegha and Jordan Henderson among those not involved.

Henderson had surgery at the World Cup after a freakish injury celebrating England's win against Mexico at the Azteca, tumbling over the advertising hoarding and fracturing his wrist and arm. Although his match fitness is unclear, he has partaken in Chelsea training this week after arriving from Brentford.

Danny Welbeck topped the list of absentees for Chelsea's final pre-season match

Meanwhile, Mykhailo Mudryk, Tosin Adarabioyo, Liam Delap and Nicolas Jackson - all of whom could depart before the transfer window closes in 16 days - were not involved. Could that, perhaps, indicate they are not part of Alonso’s plans?

Aston Villa have rekindled talks for Parma goalkeeper Zion Suzuki after the collapse of his move to Paris Saint-Germain.

The Japan international was scheduled to have a medical with PSG today but the French club indicated the commission demanded by agents, was considered too high and the deal fell through.

Zion Suzuki has rekindled talks with Aston Villa after his Paris Saint-Germain move fell through

Villa have Emiliano Martinez as their number one who was expected to stay after the World Cup but had been a target for Juventus.

The Italians fell short in their initial offers for Martinez and have been discussing a loan for Guglielmo Vicario from Tottenham.

Newcastle's talks progress with Benfica's Dedic

Newcastle are advancing in talks to sign Bosnia right-back Amar Dedic from Benfica.

Talks are continuing over a £30million fee for the 23-year-old and all parties are hopeful of concluding a deal.

The 23-year-old played under coach Matthias Jaissle at RB Salzburg.

Newcastle have also considered going back into the market for Bayern Munich's Joao Palhinha as they search for a midfielder.

Palhinha has interest from Aston Villa and Benfica but Bayern only want a permanent sale not a loan.

Newcastle are advancing in talks to sign Bosnia right-back Amar Dedic from Benfica

Spurs reach agreement with Boro for Phillips

Tottenham defender Ashley Phillips is ready to complete his protracted move to Middlesbrough.

The deal was held up last weekend after concerns over his medical. However, following further tests and discussions, the clubs have reached an agreement.

He is due on Teesside this weekend to finalise his switch to the Riverside.

Boro kick off their Championship campaign at home to Lincoln City today.

Tottenham defender Ashley Phillips is ready to complete his protracted move to Middlesbrough

Benfica offer for Harwood-Bellis rejected

Southampton have rejected a £17.5million offer from Benfica for defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis.

The Portuguese side, coached by Marco Silva, turned to the 24-year-old after initial interest in Chelsea's Tosin Adarabioyo who wants to stay at Stamford Bridge.

Benfica are considering an improved offer with Harwood-Bellis interested in the move.

Benfica are considering an improved offer for Saints' Harwood-Bellis after having their initial bid of £17.5million rejected, while the 24-year-old is interested in the move

Forest sign former Fulham goalkeeper Benda

Nottingham Forest have completed the signing of former Fulham goalkeeper Steven Benda.

The 27-year-old is being brought in to replace the departed Angus Gunn as third-choice. He had spells on loan at Feyenoord and Millwall last season.

Eagles sign £21m right back Khalaili

Crystal Palace have completed the £21million signing of Union Saint-Gilloise full-back Anan Khalaili.

Khalaili's move to Inter Milan fell through earlier this summer over a health issue, but he passed his medical with Palace last weekend.

The 21-year-old is being brought in to provide competition for Daniel Munoz at right wing-back.

However, there is no guarantee that the £20m-rated Colombian will stay beyond this summer amid interest from the likes of Tottenham and Everton. He has two years left on his deal.

Khalaili, who has won 16 caps for Israel, said: 'I'm happy to be here, I'm excited, and I can't wait to start.

'I’ve followed the Premier League. It's a new challenge for me, and I've followed Crystal Palace for a long time. I'm happy to be here.'

Khalaili's move to Inter Milan fell through earlier this summer over a health issue, but he passed his medical with Palace last weekend

Gourna-Douath 'excited' to join Tigers

Hull City have finalised the £3.5m transfer of French defensive midfielder Lucas Gourna-Douath from RB Salzburg.

The deal is worth £2.9m guaranteed, plus add-ons and a 10 per cent sell-on clause.

The 23-year-old has signed a five-year contract, becoming the club’s 10th summer signing.

Gourna-Douath said: 'I’m really happy because it was such a long journey from the first phone call until I signed. I’m so excited to get started.

'I’m really happy to have this experience. I got a chance to play in the Champions League, Serie A and Ligue 1.

'I've learned a lot and I’m really happy to put this experience on the pitch in the Premier League. The Premier League is the dream of all footballers. Now, I have a chance to play in the Premier League, so I am excited to play.'

Leeds agree £6.8m move for Eveldi

Leeds United have agreed a fee with Borussia Monchengladbach for Nico Elvedi.

The deal is understood to be worth an initial £6.8m plus add-ons.

The central defender was left out of Gladbach’s squad for today’s friendly against Aston Villa.

His arrival would open the door for Sebastiaan Bornauw to join Hamburg.

Gladbach have also negotiated a 15 per cent sell-on.

Black Cats ink Methalie deal

The fee is understood to be £26million including add ons.

Methalie has agreed a five-year contract.
