World.title: As speed cameras spread to more states, so does the backlash from drivers
World.content:
As speed cameras spread to more states, so does the backlash from drivers

toggle caption Joel Rose/NPR

MIAMI — If you've driven in Florida recently, you may have seen the speed cameras springing up in school zones across the state.

Carlos Acosta wishes he hadn't.

"I think it's a money grab," Acosta said. "That's what irks me the most. It's all about making money."

Millions of drivers across the country are encountering automated speed cameras for the first time, or they will soon. Safety advocates say there's clear evidence that these cameras work to make roads safer. But there's also a growing backlash from drivers in Florida and beyond.

Drivers like Acosta, who worked in the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office for 27 years before retiring. This spring, Acosta says he got two speed camera tickets in school zones near his house in a suburb of Miami.

Sponsor Message

"I'm all for protecting the kids coming and going from school," Acosta said.

But he says both of his tickets were issued during the middle of the day, when those kids were inside the school. "So they're basically giving you a citation for going over the regular speed limit," he said. "That's where you get popped."

Florida recently joined the growing list of states where speed cameras are allowed. So have California, Hawaii, Michigan and Minnesota. They're now legal in more than two dozen states , with each taking a different approach in terms of where the cameras are located, and where the money goes.

In general, safety advocates say these cameras are working, and saving lives by forcing drivers to slow down.

"The whole point of the cameras is reducing the speeds, which leads to crashes at lower speeds when they happen, so there's fewer people dying," said Raul Avelar, an engineer with the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, a nonprofit research organization funded by the auto insurance industry.

Avelar points to multiple studies in the U.S. that show cameras can cut speeding by 70% or more. One study in Maryland found speed cameras reduced the likelihood of serious injury by 39%.

Sponsor Message

But some drivers are pushing back. Ted Hollander is a lawyer at The Ticket Clinic, a law firm that is tracking the locations of speed cameras in Florida , and fighting the tickets in court.

"We don't really think it's truly about safety, because if it was, it would only be during the times when the kids are around, not when they are in school," Hollander said. "We feel like it's an illegal tax and we want to do what we can to protect people."

Critics of speed cameras may have found an ally in the Trump administration's Department of Transportation.

Last month, the Federal Highway Administration quietly stripped speed cameras from a list of " Proven Safety Countermeasures ," as they're known, that have been shown to reduce crashes and save lives, along with bike lanes and other speed-related measures.

The FHWA said the changes to its website are part of a broader review of safety recommendations to ensure they align with the Trump administration's priorities, though safety advocates argue the DOT is undermining strategies already proven to work.

Speed camera backers also dispute that these programs are intended to raise revenues.

"We have so many safeguards built into this to make sure it is purely a traffic calming and speed reduction effort and not a money grab, not a surveillance tool," said Rep. Laura Friedman, D-Calif., who represents part of the Los Angeles area.

Before joining Congress, as a member of the state assembly, Friedman wrote California's speed camera law. Any money raised from the speed camera program there has to be invested in safety improvements to the streets where the tickets were issued, Friedman said.

The first speed cameras in the state came online last year in San Francisco, followed by Oakland earlier this year.

But the big test of California's law is looming over the next few months, when speed cameras are set to be activated in Los Angeles — a city that has long been defined by its love of cars, especially fast ones .

Sponsor Message

Still, Friedman says many of her constituents welcome the cameras.

"When people come forward and they say, 'I've been scared to cross the street in this area, or we have had street racing constantly all night long,' seeing them have a chance now to do something about it" has been satisfying, she said. "It is going to make it harder for people to speed, and that's a good thing."

World.title: Is there a summer COVID-19 surge this year? Yep, it's ramping up again
World.content:
Is there a summer COVID-19 surge this year? Yep, it's ramping up again

toggle caption Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Hantavirus. Ebola. West Nile. Measles. And, of course, cyclospora — that stomach parasite making people miserable across the country. Americans have plenty to worry about this summer.

But remember COVID-19? It may not be surprising that many people may have almost forgotten about COVID. Unfortunately, COVID hasn't forgotten about us.

"We're now in the midst of a growing summer surge of COVID here in the United States," says Dr. John Brooks , an infectious disease doctor at Emory University in Atlanta, Ga., who used to work at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "I think most of us kind of feel like it's fading away and are certainly very grateful for that. But nationally we're seeing it ticking up pretty much everywhere."

Sponsor Message

The virus is spreading the most again in the South and West, but is also on the rise in the Northeast and Midwest. The good news is the virus is still at very low levels. And so far this summer's wave seems to be continuing the trend of getting milder each year, sending fewer people to the hospital and causing fewer deaths.

"What we're seeing is very likely evidence of growing herd immunity if you will," Brooks says. "More and more people have had one or more infections that give them some immunity against the virus and have had more than one vaccination, or maybe both. And all of that really has begun to offer us a lot of protection."

Now, that doesn't mean people don't have to worry about COVID at all anymore. The disease still makes lots of people feel awful for a week or two, foiling their summer vacations and forcing them to miss work and school.

And COVID can still cause serious disease for some people, sending them to emergency rooms, causing hospitalizations and even sometimes still causing death.

"COVID-19 is still dangerous, particularly for older adults, infants and people who are immunocompromised," says Caitlin Rivers , an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Md. And that is a lot of Americans. "In a typical office, if you have 20 colleagues, it's likely that one or two of them have some degree of immunocompromise. So it's very common that people have risk factors that make COVID-19 dangerous."

Sponsor Message

Unlike the flu, which only surges during the winter each year, COVID sees spikes twice a year – both in the summer and winter. The reason for that remains unclear.

"It's a big mystery as far as I'm concerned. It is the only seasonal respiratory virus that has a summer season," River says. "To my knowledge, we don't know what is causing this seasonality."

Rivers says she still masks up when she's in crowded places like busy airports, and recommends that people stay up to date on their vaccines. The next shots look like a good match for the dominant strain of COVID that's circulating and should start becoming available soon.

Unlike previous years, the CDC hasn't issued updated recommendations for the vaccines because of litigation over the Trump administration's efforts to overhaul immunizations in the U.S. The administration no longer recommends that everyone aged 6 months and older routinely get an annual shot.

But major medical groups still do recommend it. And insurers have indicated they will keep covering vaccines. The shots are likely to remain available for free through government programs like the Vaccines for Children program.

Public health experts worry that conflicting messages will cause confusion, discouraging people from getting another shot.

"The message is that COVID vaccine and flu vaccine will be available, they're covered by insurers, they're recommended by medical societies. People should get them and get them for their kids," says Clare Hannan , executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, which advocates for immunization programs.

There's also even a new drug , called Xocova, that people can take right after they've been exposed to the virus to cut their chances of actually getting sick from COVID.

"It is something for people to just have in the back of their mind," Brooks says. It is expected to be a useful tool in hospitals and nursing homes when exposures happen to vulnerable people.

World.title: Mangione pleads guilty in federal court, leaving fate of state trial uncertain
World.content:
Mangione pleads guilty in federal court, leaving fate of state trial uncertain

toggle caption Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post

Luigi Mangione, the 28-year-old accused of killing a health care executive on a Manhattan street, pleaded guilty to stalking charges in federal court Friday.

Mangione faced those charges in connection with the December 2024 shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

"I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione said in court Friday. "I knew what I was doing."

Thompson's family was in the courtroom sitting in the front row watching as Mangione entered his plea. Mangione voiced no remorse and repeatedly referenced his concerns with the U.S. health care system.

Mangione, who arrived in court wearing what appeared to be tan-colored prison fatigues rather than the business suit he's worn to previous hearings, said he stalked Mr. Thompson, posing as an investor to gain information about the conference where Thompson was scheduled to appear.

Sponsor Message

According to Mangione, he traveled to New York after using a 3-D printer to make a gun, which he equipped with a silencer and a magazine. Throughout that process, he said, it was his "intent to shoot Brian Thompson."

Speaking during the hearing, federal prosecutors said they had an overwhelming amount of evidence, including DNA and fingerprints from the murder scene.

"Today, Luigi Mangione admitted to stalking and murdering Brian Thompson on a Manhattan street in broad daylight," said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in a statement. "No grievance, political belief, or ideological cause can justify murder."

Earlier this year, a federal judge struck down charges that might have brought the death penalty.

Mangione still faces murder charges in a state trial set to begin next month, but his guilty plea in federal court is expected to have significant impacts on the state trial. New York state's strict double jeopardy law could potentially upend those proceedings. That law says that a defendant can't be tried twice for the same thing.

Mangione's defense team cited that law in a motion filed Friday, shortly after his federal guilty plea, urging state court Judge Gregory Carro to dismiss state charges against him, including a count of 2nd degree murder. If successful, that legal maneuver could spare Mangione a longer prison term.

Sponsor Message

State prosecutors have argued their case is distinct, and that double jeopardy should not apply. In a statement to NPR, a spokesman for the Manhattan district attorney's office said they would fight efforts by Mangione's defense team to derail the state's prosecution.

"We are encouraged that Mr. Thompson's family received a measure of accountability today," DA spokesman Douglas Cohen said. "While federal sentencing is pending, we are prepared to litigate the defense motions. The Manhattan D.A.'s Office remains committed to seeking justice for Mr. Thompson and his family."

If the state murder trial is allowed to move forward, prosecutors would be able to use Mangione's admission of guilt against him.

The case has drawn global attention and media scrutiny. Elected officials across the political spectrum have condemned what they described as politically-motivated violence but Mangione has won strong public support .

He's viewed by many as a vigilante whose actions against an unfair health care system were justified. Supporters have donated more than $1.5 million to his legal defense fund, according to a website run by pro-Mangione volunteers.

Thompson was a 50-year-old father of two. He was walking alone in midtown Manhattan hours before he was to host an investor conference at a hotel when he was fatally shot.

toggle caption Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images North America

In a statement Friday, Thompson's family said Mangione's guilty plea marks an important step toward justice.

"While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable. Now we look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime."

Mangione will be sentenced on federal charges in December.

World.title: Tropical storm Lala closes in, hitting Hawaii's Big Island with rain, wind
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tropical storm Lala was already whipping and soaking Hawaii's Big Island early Saturday, with forecasts saying it could strengthen into a hurricane or, at the least, bring hurricane-force winds as it approaches land.

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) issued a rare hurricane warning for the island, which hasn’t experienced a direct hurricane landfall in 155 years.

Forecasters said higher elevations could get as much as 635 millimetres of rain. That could cause life-threatening mudslides in a mountainous area where people live off the grid in improvised housing, and authorities urged them to find safe shelters quickly.

"This is an enormous storm," Gov. Josh Green said. Tropical storm force winds extended outward for as much as 350 kilometres and were expected to hit the islands of Oahu and Kauai by Sunday morning.

Destructive flooding and even wildfires kicked up by the strong winds were possible in the islands.

Men fill sandbags on Friday in preparation for the arrival of tropical storm Lala in Captain Cook, Hawaii. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/The Associated Press)

A hurricane warning was issued for the Big Island, and a tropical storm warning was in effect for Maui County, which includes the islands of Maui, Molokai, Lanai and Kahoolawe. A tropical storm warming was also in effect for Oahu and Kauai County, including Kauai and Niihau islands.

Even if the storm remains just shy of a hurricane as it approaches land, the NHC said wind speeds atop mountains and on the windward and leeward slopes "are often up to 30 per cent stronger than the near-surface winds" indicated in its advisory, suggesting nearly hurricane-force winds in Hawaii's higher-altitude communities.

According to a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist’s research of newspaper accounts, a Category 3 hurricane hit the northeast corner of the island in 1871. The latest forecast has Lala striking "very close to the southern tip of the Big Island," said Vanessa Almanza, a weather service meteorologist in Honolulu.

Officials and residents braced for Lala regardless of whether Hawaii takes a direct hit. Shelters were scheduled to open, and various events were canceled.

"It doesn’t take landfall to create destruction," Almanza said, noting that a lot of the impacts are felt outside the hurricane's centre.

Sandbags are seen on Friday at a Hawaii County Department of Public Works sand pile ahead of tropical storm Lala in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/The Associated Press)

The NHC predicted 203 to 305 millimetres of rainfall totals across Maui and lower elevations of the Big Island, and 102 to 152 millimetres across the island chain.

It also warned that the storm could cause "life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," along with a dangerous storm surge and ocean swells "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."

As of 5 a.m. local time in Hawaii, tropical storm Lala was located about 175 kilometres southeast of South Point, Hawaii, with maximum sustained winds of 100 km/h and was moving toward the west-northwest at 20 km/h, the hurricane centre said.

Officials urge taking the storm seriously

State Rep. Jeanné Kapela travelled from Honolulu to be closer to her constituents on the Big Island and urged people to remain alert.

The southern end of the island is remote and rural, with agriculture including coffee and cattle, but it's growing in population because of its affordability. Kapela said she was especially worried about people who live off the grid in unpermitted structures.

"If you feel now that your house doesn’t have a great roof or might not be able to withstand hurricane force winds, then first things first: you go to a family or friend’s house and you kind of hunker down there," she texted to The Associated Press as her flight took off Friday. "We're hopeful the storm moves through quickly, but we're preparing for whatever comes."

Many parts of Hawaii are still dealing with the aftermath of devastating flooding in March, Kapela said. "We know how quickly heavy rain and flooding can impact our rural communities."

WATCH | Hawaii's devastating spring floods: Hawaii hit with worst floods in 20 years | Duration 1:51 A storm brought more than 100 centimetres of rain to Hawaii, causing the worst flooding in 20 years. The floods have forced thousands from their homes, and the National Guard has been brought in to help get people out of the floodwaters.

Growers still recovering from the spring floods, including on Oahu's North Shore, were worried about suffering more damage, according to Brian Miyamoto, executive director of the Hawaii Farm Bureau.

Coffee farmer Bruce Corker said it was "sunny and beautiful" Friday in Holualoa, on the west side of the Big Island, and the island's only Costco seemed normal a day earlier, but the prospect of "streams overflowing and high winds" was worrisome.

Wildfire risks increase during windy weather

As winds ramped up across the islands, Almanza said dry and breezy conditions outside the storm would elevate fire concerns.

In 2023 the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds as a hurricane passed far to the south.

"Since the fire, everybody is way more aware of weather in general and our environment and things that are happening," said Archie Kalepa of Lahaina, who is well known in the area for his surfing, paddling and other ocean skills and has been watching the storm closely.

Kauai, which is several islands northwest up the archipelago from the Big Island, saw Hurricane Iniki make landfall as a Category 4 hurricane in 1992. That, like this year, was an El Nino year, when a warming of the Pacific near the equator increases Pacific hurricane activity and affects weather patterns across the globe.

World.title: How AI is bringing the dead back to life — for better or worse
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

About two years ago, audio producer Rebecca Nolan decided to take on a unique experiment: she built an AI chatbot of her late father using ChatGPT and hours of recordings of his voice.

Her father was a physician who had been in denial about his death, but had left behind oral histories he made for Nolan, her mother and sisters to listen to after he passed when Nolan was 14.

"Going in, I 100 per cent knew that this was fake and that this was not going to work. I knew that I was going to come out the other side of it not feeling the catharsis that something like this promises you," she said.

"But there's like that teeny tiny part of you, like the teeny voice in the back of your head that goes but like, what if it does work? What if I do, somehow, through the magic of technology reach across the void and make contact with something?"

Storytelling had been a huge part of their relationship, so Nolan was hoping the chatbot might be a way to recreate those conversations.

Instead, after two hours of talking to the creation she dubbed "dad bot," Nolan said she ended up in tears, yelling at it in frustration.

"And ChatGPT took that moment to kind of break the spell and to step back and go, 'hey, just so you know, remember, I'm a chatbot. I'm not really your dad. I can never be your dad,'" said Nolan, who has done freelance work for CBC.

"And the line that they use, which I thought was a really beautiful line, which they most definitely stole from an artist somewhere, was, 'I'm an echo, an imitation, not the real thing.'"

Rebecca Nolan is an radio producer and sound designer based in St. John's who created an AI chatbot of her late father. (Submitted by Rebecca Nolan)

It may seem like something ripped directly from an episode of Black Mirror, but generative AI and large language models are now being used to conjure up the dead using the massive digital footprints many of us leave behind when we die.

While Nolan built the AI chatbot of her father on her own, start-up companies are now offering to provide that service to people looking for ways to connect with their lost loved ones and grapple with their grief.

That includes You, Only Virtual, a California-based start-up that creates AI replicas of the deceased using their texts, voice recordings and digital traces that promise to "learn, evolve, and remember — keeping that unique connection alive, just like a real relationship."

Another company, re;memory, allows users to create lifelike avatars of their loved ones using photos and voice recordings.

Study looks at how people interact with AI 'ghosts'

A recent study out of the University of Colorado offers a glimpse at how people interact with AI-generated representations of deceased relatives and close friends — commonly referred to as generative ghosts or grief bots.

To do this, researchers recruited 16 people between the ages of 22 to 50 who had lost a close relative or friend. The participants each chatted with two iterations of a text chatbot based on their late loved one for about 20 minutes: one that spoke in first-person as the participant's loved one and another that spoke in the third person about the participant's loved one.

In interviews afterward, participants said they preferred what researchers dubbed the "reincarnation" version that acted like the deceased person, saying this iteration of the bot felt real and comforting.

One woman who took part in the study with a bot speaking like her mother even said the experience gave her the closure she needed.

"A fair number of people were surprised that it actually was better than they expected, a little less creepy than expected," said Jed Brubaker, an information science professor at the University of Colorado and one of the study's authors.

Brubaker said he thought that participants who went into the experiment skeptical would not be won over by the bots.

"What we found instead is that a lot of people would come in skeptical and maybe like, 'oh, this could maybe do some harm,' or 'I could see ways that this would be maybe a little bad,' and then they left it being like, 'Actually, no, that was OK, and I think I would be totally fine interacting with it again.'"

Still, he said, participants did express worries about potential consequences of using bots long-term, like becoming overly reliant on them, or that they might interfere with the grieving process.

Concerns over commodification of grief

Going through grief is extremely personal experience that has no right or wrong trajectory or ways of coping with it, said Elaine Kasket, a psychologist and professor at the Centre for Death and Society at the University of Bath in England.

"What is helpful for you is helpful for you, you know, and it's not for somebody else to come along and tell you what's going to be useful or not useful to you in grief. That's wrong to do."

WATCH | How people are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support: People are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support | Duration 1:45 Warning: Mention of suicide and self-harm. Millions of people, especially teens, are finding companionship and emotional support in using AI chatbots, according to a kids digital safety non-profit. But health and technology experts say artificial intelligence isn’t properly designed for these scenarios and could do more harm than good.

However, Kasket does worry that companies offering grief bots as a service you pay for could be commodifying grief.

"We've been dealing with normal human loss infinitude, for the entirety of our human existence. It's not a problem, but it has to be rendered a problem in order for these companies to sell you their products," she said.

"Normal loss is being pathologized and products are being sold to solve for it, and I find that amoral."

While the aim of these AI ghosts is to help grieving people connect with their loved ones, for Nolan, the experience with the AI ghost of her father had the opposite effect.

She said it robbed her of the ability to have imagined conversations with him in her head, as many people do with those they have lost.

"I used to have this very, what I felt was at least a strong bond still with the memory of my father and the spirit or whatever was out there," she said.

"But when I built the bot, it felt like it exorcised him for me in a way."

Now, Nolan says, it's like her father lives in ChatGPT, so she needs ChatGPT to have those conversations.

"And that felt like a really massive loss to me."

World.title: Multiple shooters at Virginia State University, with 5 people shot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A shooting involving multiple suspects and five people shot at Virginia State University prompted a campus lockdown early Saturday.

The shooting happened near the university’s Quad Annexes, and both campus police and Chesterfield County police are actively investigating. County police said officers discovered five people suffering from gunshot wounds outside campus dormitories when they arrived.

The five victims were transported to hospitals, and one initially listed as having life-threatening injuries has been upgraded to critical condition, county police said. The other victims sustained non-life-threatening injuries, police said.

The university said in a statement that the shooting involves “multiple suspects.” The statement asked people to avoid the immediate area.

“VSU Police and the Chesterfield County Police Department are actively investigating,” the university statement said. “The campus community should continue to avoid the area and follow all law enforcement instructions.”

Residence halls opened just a week ago

The campus had a large law enforcement presence on Saturday morning. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Hanover County Sheriff’s Office were assisting, county police said.

Virginia State Police deferred questions to local police, who they said are leading the investigation. County police and campus officials said there would be more information later in the day.

Virginia State University is a historically Black university located in Ettrick, Va. The public university has about 5,700 students and was the first fully state-supported four-year college for Black Americans. Most of its students are undergraduates.

The shootings happened just before the start of the academic year at Virginia State. According to the university’s website, residence halls opened for students a week ago, and classes are set to begin on Monday. Many students had just completed the university’s “New Trojans Experience” for incoming students.

World.title: Homes across B.C. have been decimated by wildfires. Here's what to know about your insurance
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's been five years since Tricia Thorpe's home was razed to the ground with hundreds of others in the deadly 2021 Lytton wildfire.

"When you come home and there's nothing left standing and everything is levelled, you don't know where to start," she said.

Thorpe, who has since rebuilt, faced a daunting challenge: her home wasn't insured.

"I was told flat out that fire was an insurable event. And because I had no insurance, not to expect any government help, which was really harsh at the time," she said.

"My situation is not unique in this province."

There's still no official tally of how many homes have been lost to wildfire so far this year. But the number of families who have lost everything could number in the hundreds.

Experts who have worked through the aftermaths of wildfires say even those who are fully insured will face a long, complex process as they begin to rebuild.

"The best thing you can do for yourself is make sure you understand your insurance policy," said Liam Corcoran, a lawyer and adjuster with Pythe Navis MDP.

"Nobody really spends the time to read or look at it unless something goes wrong."

Tricia Thorpe lost her home in a fast-moving fire that devastated the village of Clinton and surrounding areas in 2021. Her home, which she has since rebuilt and fireproofed, was uninsured at the time. (Submitted by Tricia Thorpe)

Corcoran said most policies insure on an "all risks" basis, which covers damage from fire, including wildfires. But that doesn't mean the replacement process will be quick or easy.

"You're going to get what's called actual cash value ... you're not going to get the cost to fully buy, rebuild a brand new home unless you actually rebuild a brand new home," he said.

"So you're now in the midst of a construction project and that that could take years."

'Videotaped every room'

Annick DeGooyer lost her West Kelowna home in the 2023 McDougall Creek wildfire.

Her family had painstakingly documented their property in advance of the fire, a decision that assisted her insurance claim.

"We videotaped every room and opened every drawer and every cupboard, and so when we had to go back and do the claim for our contents, we were able to go through each room, freeze the video and write down all the things we saw," she said.

"It's an endless process, but without the videos, you're relying on memory."

The McDougall Creek wildfire destroyed nearly 200 homes as it tore through West Kelowna and the surrounding areas in 2023. (Chris Corday/CBC)

Even so, she says the recovery process was slow, with multiple steps — a process that can be further delayed if a slew of wildfire-related claims creates a bottleneck in the system.

"It is a real test of patience, and some days you think we're not any closer than we were six months ago," she said.

Some costs of evacuating covered

Insurance Bureau of Canada vice president Aaron Sutherland said even if your home isn't damaged by fire, your insurance policy can help with other costs associated with the emergency.

"Insurance is also there to provide support with things like hotel costs, food — any additional living expenses you're incurring," Sutherland said.

He said the amount you're entitled to will vary by circumstance — for example, Summerland residents forced to flee with little to no notice may be entitled to a higher dollar amount than some others.

Evacuees from the Bald Range wildfire are pictured in Penticton, B.C. Experts say even if your home isn't damaged by fire, your insurance policy can assist with the costs of being evacuated, including hotels and food. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Sutherland said if your home has been damaged or destroyed by fire, it can take weeks to months for authorities to let people back into the area, let alone begin construction.

Still, he said, it's important to contact your insurer to start the process of filing a claim immediately.

'Nightmare scenario'

A worsening challenge, Corcoran said, is that many homes in remote areas are underinsured or uninsured entirely.

Thorpe's home was uninsured because it was outside a fire protection zone — meaning it was far from a hydrant or official fire hall — and had a wood burning stove, she said.

In some areas, residents are uninsured because policies have become prohibitively expensive.

Corcoran saw this first hand working with people who lost their homes in the Bush Creek East wildfire, which forced the evacuation of more than 8,000 people in the Shuswap region.

"Insurance companies are going to charge increased premiums to right risk in those areas," he said.

"These are private companies, so there's no requirement for them to offer people insurance at all."

World.title: Why more clothes donated to charity are going in the garbage
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kathy Broussard pulls back a curtain to reveal a mountain of plastic bags stuffed with used textiles. It’s a quarter — no, she self-corrects, an eighth — of all the donations her store has recently received.

The basement is also full, and two custom-made extra-large donation bins outside the store fill up every day.

“It’s a treadmill. It doesn’t end, it keeps coming and going,” she said.

Broussard’s staff and volunteers sort through the bags and sell what they can. Items that do not sell within about a month are put into bins where people can take them for free. Garments spend a day in the free bins before going in the dumpster.

“We need to find somewhere for it to go besides the landfill and I don’t know where that’s gonna be,” said Broussard, executive director of Hand in Hand, a non-profit thrift store in Halifax whose proceeds go to the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul.

For decades, many charity thrift stores across the country sold their surplus clothes to other non-profits, which would in turn sell the goods in bulk to support their own charitable causes. But in recent months, those arrangements have been falling apart.

Kathy Broussard, executive director of Hand in Hand thrift store in Halifax, is pictured in the store in July 2026. (Jeorge Sadi/CBC)

Hand in Hand hasn’t had a buyer since February, and Broussard said she’s searched high and low for an alternative, without success. Dumpster pickups at her store have increased 50 per cent, and every pickup comes with a fee that eats into the charity’s bottom line and undermines Broussard’s desire to be a good environmental steward.

“Clothes really shouldn't go in the dumpster. But there's just so many clothes being generated now with fast fashion,” she said.

CBC News spoke to four other charity thrift operations that are in the same bind as Hand in Hand, but did not want to speak about it on the record.

‘That market is rupturing’

Charlotte Genge, a textile circularity consultant, works with people in the used clothing industry across Canada. She said charity thrift stores are facing the same problem coast to coast: options are dwindling for getting rid of unsold stock.

“We're seeing just such an abrupt end to that collection mechanism. And it's really throwing people off, not only because they want to be environmentally friendly, but also because it costs them money to do it,” she said, referring to dumping fees.

Without a fix, she said she expects the volume of textiles going to local landfills to swell in the coming years.

“It almost needs to get worse before it's going to get better because it's been so out of sight, out of mind for so long.”

Hand in Hand thrift store has operated in the community of Spryfield in Halifax for about two decades. The problem of having no outlet for excess stock started about six months ago. (Jeorge Sadi/CBC)

Genge said used clothes in Canada have historically cycled through thrift stores until they’re deemed unsellable, and then followed two possible paths: they’re repurposed (usually into industrial rags, stuffing or insulation) or they’re exported .

“But that market is rupturing and because of that, it's having all of these downstream effects,” she said in an interview.

The National Diabetes Trust, which is the clothing donation program that supports Diabetes Canada, collects used clothing from donations bins and from charity thrift stores to sell it wholesale and support its cause.

The National Diabetes Trust said it has "temporarily paused” pickups from thrift stores in five provinces: Nova Scotia, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia.

“Like many organizations involved in textile collection and reuse, we are experiencing changing market conditions that have affected inventory levels and processing capacity,” they said in a statement, adding they’re seeing increased donation volumes.

Value Village’s role

A common buyer for non-profit collectors is Value Village. While it is not a charity, it is enmeshed with the charitable used clothing sector. Purchases from non-profit partners used to account for nearly half the items Value Village took in, but in recent years, it’s been shifting how it sources its goods.

Recent annual reports from the company say it's cheaper and therefore more profitable to supply stores with items that are donated directly to Value Village, rather than buying bulk from non-profits.

Charlotte Genge, textile circularity consultant, is based in Halifax but works in the used clothing industry across Canada. (Jeorge Sadi/CBC)

Last year’s report said the company has been “strategically focused” on getting more donations, and demonstrates the strategy bearing out: direct donations to the thrift giant grew from 53 per cent of all the goods it processed in 2019 to 78 per cent in 2025.

CBC News made multiple interview requests but the company would not make anyone available. In email exchanges, a spokesperson did not directly answer questions about changing its buying practices or about sending textiles to landfills.

On buying practices, they said they value working with their non-profit partners.

On landfilling, they said “most” of the items that don’t sell in Value Village stores continue “through the global reuse economy.”

The global context

Steven Bethell says his company, Bank & Vogue, is the biggest exporter of used clothing in Canada, buying from charities across North America and shipping to more than 30 countries around the world.

“Canadians are buying more and more clothing,” he said in an interview from his Ottawa head office. “There's more and more of a problem out there.”

His company’s mission is to find solutions to that problem, which he calls “the crisis of stuff.” He said the export business is “very strong,” but he also described some acute challenges that help explain why some thrift stores are struggling with a backlog.

Steven Bethell, co-founder of Bank & Vogue, a used clothing export company based in Ottawa, says the market is under pressure, but he expects that it will normalize and thrift stores will adapt. (Patrick Louiseize/CBC)

One challenge is that the cost of rounding up used clothes for export is rising because of inflation and this year’s war-driven spike in fuel prices, he said.

“To go around and collect the product and bring it back to a central place, the costs have literally doubled or tripled in the last few years.”

He said exporters are also grappling with new “war risk” fees for freight going through or near the Middle East and Eastern Europe, new levies on used clothing imports to some African countries, and increasing competition in the international used clothing marketplace.

Bethell said the Chinese, in particular, have made the used clothing market more competitive, having rapidly shifted from consumers of second-hand clothes to producers of it.

“About 10 years ago, 70 to 80 per cent of the clothes in Kenya were either from the U.S. or Canada. Now 70 per cent of that clothing is not from the U.S. or Canada, but comes from China,” he said.

He described the current challenges as “dramatic,” but said he expects the international marketplace will normalize and thrift operators will adapt.

“It is always a dynamic environment and especially when you're working with the developing world, markets are in continual flux. It's just part of the nature of the trade,” he said.

The solution

For Genge, the bottom line is that Canadians are consuming too much new clothing, making it increasingly unrealistic to keep up with the ever-growing volume of donated garments.

“The real problem, it's just that we need to turn off the tap,” she said.

Bales of sorted second-hand clothes are seen at a facility in New Taipei City, Taiwan, on July 15, 2022. (Annabelle Chih/Getty)

Genge said every level of government needs to take action. She pointed to extended producer responsibility — a policy that puts responsibility for end-of-life management of products onto the manufacturers — as one possible solution. Another, she said, would be to enforce the use of recycled content.

“There are very limited recycling operations happening in Canada right now,” said Genge.

Recycled textile materials cannot compete on cost with virgin materials, but a government mandate could change that, she said.

“Waste is a resource. And we should be looking at not waste management, but resource development from the waste perspective.”

WATCH | Why more clothes donated to charity are going in the garbage: Fast fashion surge forces second-hand stores to send excess clothing to landfills | Duration 2:20 Charity thrift stores are sending more used clothes to landfills. Industry insiders say the cause is layered. But at the core is the growth of fast fashion and fluctuating textile markets. The CBC's Taryn Grant has the story.

World.title: This Ontario farm uses bees for relaxation therapy. Is it a buzzkill for stress?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Half a million bees are buzzing in a southwestern Ontario farm to offer visitors a way to help them relax and reduce stress.

Inside a small hut on Diana Graham's 28-hectare Comber-area farm, where she runs Bees and Bloom Wellness, four beehives are underneath each of two wooden beds, with screens separating the insects from clients who lie over them to experience bee bed therapy.

Graham and others who offer the therapy say it can be beneficial in reducing anxiety and stress.

But there’s still a dearth of scientific evidence around it.

Graham said sleeping while surrounded by bees is therapeutic, and her visitors have reported feeling “amazed” and “breathing better” after spending time in the presence of bee pheromones. She said it’s built perfectly safe, so the insects can’t sting her clients.

Graham says she's known as 'the queen bee' in her inner circle. People using her bee bed therapy have reported a drop in their anxiety levels. (Pratyush Dayal/CBC)

“The pheromones from the bees help with your immune system, lungs and their buzz, the frequencies, helps with anxiety, depression, PTSD, sleep disorders and overall health,” Graham told CBC News.

“Your anxiety will go down because the hum of these bees is absolutely amazing.”

The air inside the cabin is rich with honey and beeswax scents. Graham said it adds to the wellness.

There are a handful of such centres across Canada.

Visitors say time at bee farm helped them relax

Christine Brady of Petrolia, a town southeast of Sarnia, is among visitors to Graham’s farm who were contacted to talk about their experiences there.

Brady, who recently was at the farm with her mother and recommends the therapy, said she's elated there's a bee bed facility in Ontario.

Before she came across Graham's far, Brady said, she could only find one in Italy.

“I just went there to kind of zone out and relax. It was just more for the vibration, the smell and the frequency of the bees,” she said.

“I probably got into an almost meditative trance. You kind of go into that mental zone where you're aware, but you have kind of gone within.”

Bees are 'hard at work' on Graham's farm. While people offering bee bed therapy say it helps reduce anxiety, there’s a lack of scientific evidence around it. (Pratyush Dayal/CBC)

Annette Bourassa of Barrie, Ont., visited Graham's farm a couple of week s ago and plans to go again with her friends in the fall.

“It was incredible. I can see the benefits of doing it often. I wish I lived closer because I would probably go once a week to get this,” she said.

“The hum of the bees is so relaxing and therapeutic. I just felt very, very relaxed and soothed when I left. It was excellent…. While I was lying there, I wasn't thinking about my stressors, or my clients or my deadlines.”

Bourassa said the experience was not claustrophobic and assured it’s safe, as people can also wear a protective jacket.

The cost for each 60-minute session, according to Graham's website, is $85 for one person, $120 for two people, and $300 for a group of four to six people.

Bee bed buzz started in Ireland

Known as “the queen bee” to her friends, Graham inspects the hives, pulls frames with honey and checks in on the bees weekly to ensure they have space.

To set up the bee beds, Graham turned to Paul O'Neill in Ireland for guidance.

O'Neill and his partner, Anton Tovarnitskyi, a Ukrainian beekeeper and refugee, built Ireland’s first commercial bee bed houses on Valentia Island, drawing inspiration from bee beds in Ukraine.

“It's very new and unique around the world,” O’Neill told CBC’s Windsor Morning. “It's an old form of therapy and relaxation whereby you sit or lie on top of an active beehive.”

O’Neill said bee beds have become popular across Europe, and they have been approached by many people globally — including in the United States, Germany and Canada — to teach them how to build and manage their bee cabins. His facilities are frequented by tourists from around the world.

In bee bed therapy offered at Graham's farm, a couple of wooden beds have beehives underneath each one. Under the wooden slats, there are screens that separate half a million bees from people who lie atop them. (Pratyush Dayal/CBC)

Amid more awareness and concern about the significance of bees, O’Neill said, the concept has been gaining traction.

“The concept of the bee beds relies around energy, microvibration, the sound of the bees and the air from the hive. It's about this kind of connection with bees that is the key concept of why we do it.”

While Graham and O’Neill shared experiences of people feeling relaxed using the bee beds, there’s still little scientific evidence that this form of therapy helps with mental health issues.

Health Canada was contacted for comment on bee bed therapy, but the federal department declined to comment.

CBC Windsor also reached out to the Ontario Ministry of Health to ask questions including if bee bed therapy is a recognized therapy in the province, if certification is needed to practise it and if there's any provincial health coverage.

An emailed response from a spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones said all insured services under the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP) are spelled out in the Health Insurance Act (HIA) and regulations, and bee bed therapy isn't an insured service under OHIP.

Bee sound helps reduce anxiety levels: researcher

In Turkey, Yanki Tandircioglu, whose research is published in Apis , a scientific journal on honey bee-related sciences, has been looking into the effects of bee bed therapy on anxiety levels.

When she started digging into the topic, Tandircioglu said, “there was no scientific study” around bee bed therapy. While doing her master’s degree, she and her research partners designed an experiment to understand the impact of bee beds on anxiety levels.

She said two groups of participants, totalling 60 people, were chosen. One group was made to experience the bee beds, while the other group was just asked to listen to bee buzzing sounds. They filled out an anxiety questionnaire before and after the exposure, and their brain electrical activity was recorded with a portable electroencephalogram (EEG) device.

“So, we got significant results from both groups that we can say the buzzing sound affected people's anxiety levels and it reduced it,” Tandircioglu said, referring to what was reported on the questionnaires.

This small hut on Diana Graham's 28-hectare farm near Comber in southwestern Ontario contains two wooden beds with four beehives underneath each one, and screens separating the bees from people lying over them. Graham, who runs Bees and Bloom Wellness, says up to six people can enjoy the bee bed therapy. (Pratyush Dayal/CBC) (Pratyush Dayal/CBC)

But she also noted they could not “observe any significant change” in the brain activity based on EEG readings.

In her paper, she writes this study is “a first investigation” into the effects of bee beds on anxiety levels, laying the groundwork for further exploration in this area.

Since it’s still a relatively new field of research and there is no amassed scholarship around it, Tandircioglu said, she understands why bee bed therapy is still not mainstream.

The sound of the colony is different from a single bee buzzing, and the microvibrations and smell of the beehives, Tandircioglu said, add to the overall relaxing experience. She said the bee sound was found to be closer to pink noise, like waterfalls and rain, rather than white noise.

“Nature always heals, and so do the bees.”

World.title: U.S. company's 'sunlight on demand' project worries N.B. astronomers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some New Brunswick astronomy experts and enthusiasts are joining a chorus of opposition against a U.S.-based company’s big goals of using mirrors in space to provide artificial sunlight to people interested in paying for it.

The company, Reflect Orbital, calls its project proposal "sunlight on demand," and would sell it as a service.

It said this “sunlight” could be used for a variety of things like agriculture or solar power infrastructure, for search and rescue efforts, construction projects and other benefits.

“It's kind of a disaster,” said Mount Allison University astronomy professor, Catherine Lovekin.

“It would basically kill ground-based astronomy and backyard stargazing, which is already in trouble from the huge number of satellites that have been launched — and they're not nearly as bright as these.”

The company was founded in 2021. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission gave the project its approval in July, despite hundreds of public voices speaking out in opposition.

The approval is for one mirrored “demonstration” satellite which, the company said, will be used to test its technology and safeguards.

Mount Allison University, Catherine Lovekin, says the Reflect Orbital project will have negative impacts for ground based astronomy, sleep cycles and more. (Mount Allison University.)

The company’s goal is to put 50,000 of the satellites in space by 2035. They would be used to reflect sunlight that would span five kilometers back down to Earth, including potentially at night.

“With 50,000 of them, that's basically going to make the night sky invisible even for our big telescopes,” Lovekin said.

The project also comes with a number of risks and potential impacts to anything that relies on a steady day and night cycle, she said, including circadian rhythms, nocturnal ecosystems and wildlife.

She also isn’t the only one speaking out.

Astronomy group says light pollution is getting worse

Stéphane Picard, who owns an astro-tourism organization called Cliff Valley Astronomy, shares Lovekin’s concerns.

Picard said the province currently has four dark-sky sites. These are areas largely free of light pollution — like light coming from street lamps, cars or city buildings — that allow an unhindered view of the natural night sky.

He said the province hired him to add eight more sites to the list by next year, which according to Picard, would make New Brunswick the province with the most dark-sky locations.

Astronomer, Stéphane Picard says rural parts of the province are dependent on the tourism that comes from their natural spaces, which include the natural night sky. (Emily Brass/CBC)

The province’s smaller rural communities can be dependent on the tourism that the province’s natural landscapes — and skies — can bring, he said.

“Traditionally, most people would discover by accident that we have dark skies,” he said.

“80 per cent of Americans right now can't see the Milky Way from where they live; in Canada, it's creeping above 60 per cent. It's becoming harder, and people have to travel further to find a natural sky.”

On Wednesday, New Brunswickers had the chance to witness two astronomical events, a partial solar eclipse and a Perseid meteor shower. Picard watched these from one of the province’s dark-sky sites, Mount Carleton Provincial Park.

On Wednesday, New Brunswickers were able to witness a partial solar eclipse during the day and a Perseid meteor shower that night and into the following Thursday. (Peter Dawson/CBC)

Chris Curwin, who runs an astronomy group called Astronomy by the Bay in Saint John, also held a viewing event for the same occurrences at Irving Nature Park, another of the province’s dark-sky sites, which is called an “Urban Star Park.”

He said it will become increasingly difficult to enjoy these natural phenomena with more objects added to space.

“The next generation is not going to be able to appreciate the night sky like we can today,” he said at the watch event.

While eclipses can be seen by people in more urban areas, something like a meteor shower or even just a clear view of the stars isn't as easy to spot in a well-lit city.

Chris Curwin, a local amateur astronomer in Saint John, says light pollution is getting worse and will make astronomy events more difficult to witness. (Submitted by Chris Curwin)

And light pollution, Curwin said, is getting worse.

“It's very seldom that we find dark-sky preserves. New Brunswick has a large number of them, but we're a very rural province. So we have that opportunity.”

Light won’t impact most places, company says

Reflect Orbital declined an interview with CBC News, but sent a statement that said the company aims to make clean, abundant renewal energy available on demand.

The company said “most places will never see this light” and it will be targeted towards customers who would require permits for the service and be turned off when idle. It will also, according to the statement, have exclusion zones “to cover astronomical observation sites.”

The statement said the company engaged with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and others whose feedback informed the project. The brightness levels would be “calibrated to levels humans and animals already tolerate,” the statement said.

Astronomy professors in British Columbia and Australia along with agencies like the U.S.-based Dark Sky Consulting and the American Astronomical Society have also expressed concerns.

The international agency, the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, which deals with matters related to space including law, said in recent comments to CBC News, there isn’t anything prohibiting placing a reflective object in orbit.

But, the group said, objects are still subject to “due regard and consultation obligations owed to every other state,” and it would be up to countries to create laws around this type of service.

World.title: In Canada's largest honey-producing region, beekeepers brace for U.S. tariffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Harvest is in full swing at a family-run honey farm in central Alberta — but there's a cloud hanging over this year's sweet crop as producers watch the clock tick down on a trade agreement with the United States.

“It's just one more frustration,” said Lorne Prins, who owns Gull Lake Honey, located about 130 kilometres south of Edmonton. The operation has nearly 3,000 hives spread across roughly 90 locations in the heart of Canada’s largest honey-producing province.

The looming Aug. 19 deadline has thousands of local producers like Prins bracing for a major sting. A proposed 50 per cent U.S. tariff on honey could effectively close off their biggest export market, he said.

The U.S. administration threatened the levy in July on hundreds of Canadian goods, citing what it describes as unfair trade practices. The threat caught industry stakeholders off-guard, given that Canadian honey was previously exempt from tariffs under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) on trade.

Inside Gull Lake honey's facility in central Alberta. (Kevin Sabiston/CBC)

The wet summer had already created stress about honey production levels this year, Prin said. "Now to even consider the possibility of our honey prices being squashed by U.S. tariffs.”

Rod Scarlett, executive director of the Canadian Honey Council, expressed “surprise and shock” over the inclusion of honey among new goods potentially facing tariffs.

Nationally, the industry generated more than $241 million in revenues in 2025

“Alberta is Canada’s biggest producer,” Scarlett said. “The Prairies are about 60 per cent of the honey production. Alberta represents 40 per cent of that.”

Gull Lake Honey owner Lorne Prins opens a super, a wooden box where bees deposit honey, on one of his hives in central Alberta. (Kevin Sabiston/CBC)

Though Prins solely sells locally, he will still be hit by new tariffs, saying he expects domestic prices will plummet if Canadian exporters lose their top international buyer.

“It will strand an enormous amount of honey on the Prairies and it could be really, really damaging to our price this year,” Prins said.

A rush to the border

Canadian beekeepers typically send about 70 per cent of their honey exports to the United States. Scarlett said that volume likely surged over the last fortnight as producers raced to move their shipments south before the tariffs take effect.

‘“[The] U.S. packers were quite worried that they wouldn't be able to get Canadian honey. They moved up their contract delivery dates and prices,” Scarlett said.

Jeremy Olthof, owner and operator of Tees Bees, about 150 kilometres south of Edmonton, said the tariff threat is an added stress in a year where wet weather has already disrupted timelines and delayed extraction schedules.

“I know of a lot of beekeepers that are scrambling,” he said. “And because this year … everything is so much later, there just isn't enough honey in barrels right now to get moved in time.”

While his own operation doesn't export a lot to the U.S, Olthof echoed Prins concerns that his business would be hit hard by a potential drop in prices.

Beekeeper Lorne Prins stands in the barrel room of his central Alberta warehouse, where he stores the honey crop from the season. (Kevin Sabiston/CBC)

Ripple effects

Barbara McKenzie, executive director of the Alberta Beekeepers Commission, said losing access to the U.S. market would be “catastrophic” for Canadian producers.

A survey of local producers conducted by the organization last week found many expect exports will immediately collapse, she said.

“Many of our producers would not be able to have the funds to be able to purchase what they need to overwinter their bees. Nor would they be able to restock their bees after winter hive losses.”

And those ripple effects wouldn't stop at honey, McKenzie added.

Alberta accounts for about 40 per cent of Canada's total honey production, according to federal statistics. (Kevin Sabiston/CBC)

“We have effects on pollination. We have effects on other food crops,” she said, noting the industry's crucial role in pollinating canola, fruit and vegetable crops.

“This isn't just a few hundred million [dollars] in honey that's being affected. It's billions of dollars across the agriculture industry that would be affected by these tariffs,” she said.

The ticking clock

In an email statement to CBC News, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada(AAFC) said it has met with the Canadian Honey Council and industry groups about the potential impacts.

If a deal isn't reached, AAFC said there are existing federal programs like AgriInvest and AgriStability to help cushion losses.

AgriInvest covers smaller income dips, while AgriStability handles larger losses. The deadline for the latter has already passed for this year but it would still be allowed if requested by a province or territory and approved by the AAFC, it wrote.

Producers that apply after the enrolment deadline would be subject to a penalty of 20 per cent of their total payment, AAFC said.

A photo of Tees Bees Inc., a commercial beekeeping operation located about 150 kilometres south of Edmonton. (Kevin Sabiston/CBC)

A spokesperson for Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in a statement to CBC News that Canada is "engaging intensively with the United States to address outstanding trade issues," but declined further comment while negotiations continue.

Back on the farm, Olthof said all that's left for local producers to do now is wait and hope a deal is reached before time runs out.

“The mood is just hoping and praying that they get this figured out, and hoping this doesn't go through,” he said.

World.title: The trouble with backup cameras: Here’s what we know about the many recalls
World.content:
How have backup camera systems performed in Canada?

Like in the U.S., there are myriad media reports about vehicle recalls in Canada over faulty backup cameras. Here are a range of recalls reported in just the last few years.

In late July, more than 17,000 Volkswagen vehicles were recalled, requiring the owners to take them back to a dealership. Transport Canada officials said that “(u)nder certain conditions, a software problem could cause the rearview camera image not to display when the transmission is shifted into reverse.” As a result, it “could reduce a driver’s ability to see behind the vehicle while backing up. This could increase the risk of a crash.”

In early July, Honda Canada recalled 32,289 Odyssey minivans due to an issue with the rearview-camera-image display.

In late May, Honda recalled nearly 1,000 vehicles due to an issue that could affect the rearview cameras.

In April, General Motors recalled more than a quarter of a million Chevrolet Malibus in Canada and the U.S. due to potentially defective rear-view cameras. The number of affected vehicles in Canada numbered 10,098. At the time, the Associated Press reported that a letter from the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration stated that the rearview camera on certain Malibu vehicles could display distorted or blank images when they were reversed, increasing the risk of a crash.

In late January, Transport Canada issued a recall notice for 12,179 Toyota Tundra trucks from the years 2024 and 2025 due to an issue that could affect the vehicle’s backup camera.

In early January, Transport Canada announced an update regarding an earlier recall involving more than 40,000 Volvo cars and SUVs. Again, the issue cited was a software problem that could cause the rearview camera images not to display when the vehicle was reversed. Even vehicles recalled previously required a new fix.

In late December of 2025, Porsche recalled more than 25,000 vehicles in Canada because of the possibility that the rearview camera image might not appear on the display.

In October 2025, Toyota recalled 32,733 vehicles in Canada due to rearview camera safety concerns, according to Transport Canada.

The month before, on Sept. 9, Ford issued a massive recall. It affected more than 120,000 vehicles in Canada due to potentially faulty rearview cameras. The notice from Transport Canada was part of a broader recall affecting around 1.9 million vehicles worldwide.

In November 2024, Hyundai recalled 48,509 SUVs and small cars in Canada because of a potential issue with the rearview camera imaging not showing up on the driver’s screens.

An even larger recall in June 2024 by automaker Stellantis involved more than one million vehicles, including minivans, SUVs, and pickups, in North America due to a software problem that could affect the display from the rearview camera. Transport Canada listed 126,530 affected vehicles.

World.title: Conrad Black: A comprehensive plan for Canada to survive Trump’s trade war
World.content:
Article content

There was absolutely no reason for the United States to be running a trade deficit of $1.3 trillion and although the American administration has imposed tariffs in a gratuitously blunderbuss manner, there is nothing wrong with that country straightening out its accounts and putting the welfare of its own workforce ahead of others. The world owes the United States more than the United States owes the world. However, and as I have also had occasion to tell Mr. Trump and reported here, his assimilation of Canada’s conduct to Mexico’s was an outrage. The U.S. does not really run a deficit with Canada; this has always been a fair-trading country, and Mexico was in active collusion with the most violent gangsters in the world in the introduction of huge numbers of destitute people into the United States including hundreds of thousands of hardened criminals bringing with them dangerous quantities of lethal narcotics. Mexico also engaged in a systematic pattern of attracting American manufacturing with tax breaks, cheap labour, and abuse of trade arrangements to sell product back into the U.S. that had formerly been made there. We did none of this and were defamed by the comparison.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
