Fernández has made confronting organized crime one of her government’s central priorities, promising a tougher response to narcotrafficking and violent crime while seeking changes to Costa Rica’s policing and justice systems.

Today’s call suggests Washington will remain a major partner in that effort. What remains unanswered is what “deeper” security cooperation will mean in practice. Neither government announced new operations, personnel deployments, equipment transfers or financial commitments following the conversation.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves Immigration Applications Online for Some Foreign Executives
World.content:
Costa Rica has moved several immigration procedures for foreign executives and their families online, allowing eligible applicants to complete and track the process through the Ventanilla Única de Inversión, or One-Stop Investment Window. The new service became available yesterday and is aimed specifically at people connected to companies operating under Costa Rica’s Free Trade Zone Regime.

For now, the online system covers three immigration categories: Free Trade Zone Executives, Dependents of Company Executives and Free Trade Zone Stays. Applicants using the platform can review requirements and applicable regulations, submit their cases, follow the progress of their applications and receive notifications and approvals online.

The system also provides a record of each stage of the process and allows applicants to interact with the government agencies handling their cases. The change is particularly relevant for international companies that regularly bring managers, executives and other specialized personnel into Costa Rica.

The General Directorate of Immigration and Foreigners developed the service with Costa Rica’s foreign trade promotion agency Procomer, with support from the Ministry of Foreign Trade. The immigration procedures have been added to the Ventanilla Única de Inversión, commonly known as VUI, an existing digital platform designed to bring government procedures required by businesses into one system.

The platform already centralizes dozens of processes related to opening, expanding and formally operating companies in Costa Rica. The government has been expanding the platform as part of a broader effort to reduce the amount of paperwork and in-person processing required from companies operating in the country.

For foreign companies, immigration procedures can be an important part of establishing or expanding operations in Costa Rica, particularly when businesses need to relocate executives or specialized employees from other countries. The online system should make it easier for participating companies and their employees to see where an application stands instead of relying entirely on separate communications with government offices.

However, the change does not mean Costa Rica has introduced online processing for all residency applications. The service announced this week applies only to the three designated categories connected to qualifying companies and the Free Trade Zone Regime. Foreign residents applying through other immigration categories should not assume their residency applications can now be submitted through the VUI.

Costa Rica’s Free Trade Zone Regime is a major part of the country’s strategy for attracting foreign investment. Companies operating under the program receive tax and customs incentives in exchange for meeting investment, employment and other requirements. The addition of immigration procedures to the VUI is therefore aimed as much at companies as individual applicants. The government wants businesses bringing foreign talent into Costa Rica to have a more predictable and trackable process.

The three newly available immigration procedures can now be started through the VUI platform.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Wild Capuchin Monkeys Are Using AI Touchscreens
World.content:
Wild white-faced capuchin monkeys in Costa Rica are learning to use a touchscreen in the middle of the forest, giving researchers a new way to study animal intelligence without taking the monkeys out of their natural environment. The system, called CapuchinAI, combines artificial intelligence, cameras, a touchscreen and an automatic food dispenser at the Taboga Forest Reserve in Guanacaste.

When a capuchin approaches the station, the technology can detect the animal, record its interaction and present a task on the screen. Successful interactions can trigger a food reward, typically a slice of dried banana. During a two-week field test involving two groups of wild capuchins, 16 monkeys voluntarily interacted with the device. Ten learned how to trigger food rewards, while eight developed and retained a clear association between touching the screen and receiving food.



Some figured it out faster than others. The first monkey to seriously investigate the device was a large male named Trompudo. After initially hitting different parts of the apparatus, he touched the screen and received a piece of banana. He quickly repeated the action.

Other monkeys eventually began using the station as well, with some discovering that the touchscreen responded not only to their hands but also to their mouths. A few learned to effectively “kiss” the screen to get a reward. The research, published in the American Journal of Primatology, is intended to solve a longstanding problem in animal cognition studies: scientists can tightly control experiments in laboratories, but captive conditions do not fully reproduce the social pressures, competition and environmental challenges that animals face in the wild.

CapuchinAI is designed to bring some of that experimental control into the forest. An early facial-recognition model trained on images of six known capuchins was able to identify individual monkeys with more than 97% performance across still images, video and live field footage. During the latest field deployment, the system was adapted to recognize when a capuchin approached the station, allowing researchers to automatically collect more video and build a larger database for identifying individual animals.

That distinction is important as the pilot study primarily tested whether wild monkeys would approach the technology, interact with the touchscreen and learn the connection between touching it and receiving a reward. The next stage is intended to recognize individual monkeys automatically and give each one cognitive tests suited to its progress.

Researchers are developing experiments covering learning, impulse control, cognitive flexibility and short- and long-term memory. Once an individual is recognized, the system could eventually determine which test that particular monkey should receive and track its performance over time.

The portable unit is built around a Raspberry Pi computer and includes a webcam, touchscreen, motorized food dispenser and battery. It can operate for about eight hours on a lightweight battery pack, making it practical for field conditions where normal laboratory equipment would be difficult to use.

The work is particularly well suited to Taboga since the reserve contains about 2.97 square kilometers (1.15 square miles) of protected tropical dry forest and supports one of Costa Rica’s larger concentrations of white-faced capuchins. More than 14 groups have been identified in the area, while long-term researchers concentrate on four groups.

Years of observations also mean scientists already know the histories, social relationships and behavior of many individual monkeys. Combining those records with controlled cognitive tests could help researchers examine why some capuchins learn faster than others, whether social experiences influence problem-solving and how different environments shape intelligence.

The technology is not intended to replace researchers following monkeys through the forest. Instead, it gives them another way to collect standardized information while the animals continue moving freely through their normal habitat. If the approach proves successful, similar systems could eventually be adapted for other wild primates, allowing scientists to compare cognition across animals and environments without relying as heavily on captive populations.

For Costa Rica, the experiment puts one of our most familiar wild animals at the center of an unusual meeting between conservation research, artificial intelligence and behavioral science.

World.title: Latin American Players Make Early Push at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Latin American players made an immediate impact as the Cincinnati Open main draw began Thursday, with Argentina’s Mariano Navone and Thiago Agustín Tirante advancing while several more players from the region prepared to take the court Friday. Tirante produced the most dramatic result of the opening day, outlasting Britain’s Jan Choinski 7-6(9), 6-7(7), 7-6(4) in a match that lasted just under three hours. All three sets were decided by tiebreaks, with the Argentine finally pulling away in the deciding breaker.

His reward is one of the biggest matches available at this year’s tournament. Tirante will face third-seeded Novak Djokovic in the second round after the Serbian received a first-round bye. Navone had a more straightforward opening victory, defeating Belgium’s Raphael Collignon 6-3, 7-6(3). The Argentine will next face No. 28 seed Alexander Blockx.

Not every Argentine advanced. Román Andrés Burruchaga pushed Germany’s Jan-Lennard Struff to three sets before losing 7-6(4), 2-6, 6-3. Camilo Ugo Carabelli was also eliminated, falling 6-3, 6-3 to Miomir Kecmanovic. On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio won the opening set against American Taylor Townsend but could not hold the advantage. Townsend recovered for a 3-6, 6-3, 6-3 victory, ending Osorio’s Cincinnati run in the first round.

The Latin American presence continues Friday with a busy schedule across the grounds. Argentina’s Sebastián Báez faces former world No. 3 Grigor Dimitrov on P&G Stadium Court. Juan Manuel Cerúndolo meets qualifier Mark Lajal, while Marco Trungelliti, who came through qualifying, faces Hamad Medjedovic.

Colombia will have two players worth watching. Nicolás Mejía takes on Australia’s Adam Walton, while qualifier Emiliana Arango has one of the highest-profile assignments of the day against seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams on Grandstand. Paraguay’s Adolfo Daniel Vallejo will also make his Cincinnati main-draw appearance against French qualifier Kyrian Jacquet.

Several of the region’s better-known players received first-round byes and are waiting for the second round. Brazil’s João Fonseca is seeded No. 23, Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo is No. 22, Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo is No. 20 and Tomás Martín Etcheverry is No. 26. Their presence gives Latin America several opportunities to remain deep in the draw once the seeded players begin joining the tournament.

Fonseca, one of the most closely watched young players in men’s tennis, will face the winner of the first-round match between Tallon Griekspoor and Botic van de Zandschulp. Tabilo will open against Struff, while Francisco Cerúndolo and Etcheverry are also awaiting their first matches after receiving byes.

With Navone and Tirante already through and another group of Latin American players beginning their campaigns Friday, the region has plenty at stake during the opening weekend in Cincinnati.

World.title: International News: World Meteorological Organization record heat, drought, wildfires and flooding across globe
World.content:
International News: World Meteorological Organization record heat, drought, wildfires and flooding across globe

By Zoila Palma: Record-breaking temperatures, drought, wildfires and flooding continued to affect countries around the world through July and early August 2026, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

The agency said the latest extreme weather events highlight the growing need for reliable forecasts, early warnings and climate monitoring to reduce the impacts on communities and economies.

July 2026 was jointly the warmest July on record globally, tying with July 2024, according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The Copernicus Climate Change Service ranked July as the second-warmest on record, with global surface air temperatures averaging 1.47°C above the estimated pre-industrial baseline. Both datasets also recorded the highest global sea surface temperatures ever measured for the month of July.

The WMO said the ten warmest Julys on record have all occurred since 2016, with 2023 through 2026 occupying the top four positions. North America, Africa and Asia experienced their warmest July on record, while Western Europe endured its hottest June-July period on record.

Persistent heat, exceptionally low soil moisture and drought have affected agriculture, ecosystems, river levels, transportation and energy supplies while increasing the risk of wildfires.

Extreme weather has also brought deadly flooding to several regions.

Heavy monsoon rainfall caused severe flooding in India, Bangladesh and other parts of South and Southeast Asia, while Afghanistan and Kyrgyzstan experienced flash floods.

China faced severe flooding and mass evacuations linked to tropical cyclones, including the evacuation of approximately 700,000 people following Typhoon Noul in late July.

In Western Europe, low rainfall contributed to exceptionally low river flows in major waterways including the Seine, Rhine and Danube.

WMO climate information chief John Kennedy said the recent extremes reflect the combined effects of long-term global warming and persistent high- and low-pressure weather patterns across the Northern Hemisphere.

World.title: Southern Region police hold mid-year CompStat to review operations
World.content:
Southern Region police hold mid-year CompStat to review operations

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department’s Southern Region held its CompStat Mid-Year 2026 on Thursday, August 13, at Blue Reef Resort in Seine Bight Village, bringing together senior officers and commanders to assess crime trends, policing initiatives and operational needs across the region.

The session, held from 9:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., was chaired by Sgt. #98 Aretha Gordon, Officer in Charge of the Seine Bight Community Oriented Policing Unit.

Deputy Commissioner of Police, Operations, Alden Dawson; Deputy Commissioner of Police, Administration, Sandra Bodden; Southern Region Commander Superintendent Brent Hamilton; and other senior officers were in attendance.

Commanders and representatives from formations and sub-formations presented updates on crime statistics, community policing initiatives, officers’ welfare, operational activities, station management, and the availability and use of resources.

They also raised concerns regarding operational capacity, resources and other needs within their respective formations, which were addressed by Deputy Commissioners Dawson and Bodden through guidance and clarification.

The CompStat provided a platform for accountability, collaboration and strategic decision-making, with discussions emphasizing teamwork, effective resource management, communication and proactive policing.

World.title: The side hustle Economy: How Belizeans are turning weekends into extra income
World.content:
The side hustle Economy: How Belizeans are turning weekends into extra income

By Zoila Palma: In Belize, having one job is increasingly no longer the only way people are making ends meet.

Across the country, workers are turning to side hustles to supplement their regular incomes, using evenings, weekends and even holidays to sell food, clothing, household items and other products.

From weekend chicken dip and ceviche to online orders from Shein and Temu, these small ventures have become a familiar part of everyday economic life.

For some Belizeans, the side hustle is something they operate only on weekends, while others have transformed their extra-income activities into small businesses.

Office workers may spend their Saturdays preparing wings or burgers for sale, couples may operate small drink bars or food stands, and others set up booths at night markets to sell everything from snacks and desserts to clothing and imported goods. These ventures allow people to earn additional income while keeping their regular employment.

Night markets have become one avenue where these small entrepreneurs can test their ideas and reach customers.

At a recent night market at Falcon Field, BBN’s Zoila Palma encountered a businessman who already owns an ice cream shop in Orange Walk but had also started a wing business as a side venture. His experience reflects a growing trend among Belizeans who are not necessarily starting a business because they have left their jobs, but because they want another stream of income alongside their main source of earnings.

The reasons behind the side-hustle culture are varied, but for many families, the additional income can help cover groceries, bills, school expenses and other rising costs.

Some entrepreneurs may eventually turn their weekend operations into full-time businesses, while others are simply looking for a way to earn extra money without giving up the security of their primary employment.

World.title: International News: Five shot at Virginia State University as campus begins new academic year
World.content:
International News: Five shot at Virginia State University as campus begins new academic year

By Zoila Palma: A shooting involving multiple suspects left five people wounded at Virginia State University early this morning, prompting a campus lockdown and a police investigation just days before the start of the new academic year.

Campus police and Chesterfield County officers responded to the area near the university’s Quad Annexes shortly before 1:30 a.m., where they found five people suffering from gunshot wounds outside campus dormitories.

The five victims were transported to hospitals for treatment, AP reports.

Police said one person who was initially reported to have life-threatening injuries was later upgraded to critical condition, while the other four sustained non-life-threatening injuries. The university said the shooting involved “multiple suspects” and urged people to avoid the immediate area as authorities investigated.

The campus lockdown remained in effect for several hours before being lifted at approximately 9 a.m. Saturday. Following the lockdown, the university said a significant law enforcement presence remained on campus as investigators continued working to determine the circumstances surrounding the shooting.

World.title: Minister Usher: Corozal Free Zone supports 3,000 jobs and more than 300 businesses
World.content:
Minister Usher: Corozal Free Zone supports 3,000 jobs and more than 300 businesses

By Zoila Palma: The Corozal Free Zone continues to play an important role in Belize’s economy, particularly for communities in the north, with approximately 3,000 people employed and 333 businesses currently operating in the area, according to Minister of Enterprise Henry Charles Usher.

Usher described the Free Zone as a major area of economic opportunity, emphasizing its contribution to employment and business activity. “The free zone is an important economic area for the country, especially for the north,” he said.

The minister said the government wants to see the Free Zone continue to grow by attracting additional investors and expanding the range of products and services offered there. “It is an area of economic opportunity. It is an important area for business, and we have to make sure that we continue to invest in the zone,” Usher said.

Usher also pointed to the potential for diversifying the Free Zone’s economic activities, including the introduction of light manufacturing. He said creating opportunities for investors to establish different types of businesses could further strengthen the zone and generate additional economic benefits for northern Belize.

World.title: Minister of Enterprise says Government working to keep illegal activities out of Corozal Free Zone
World.content:
Minister of Enterprise says Government working to keep illegal activities out of Corozal Free Zone

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Minister of Enterprise Henry Charles Usher says the government remains focused on preventing illegal activities in the Corozal Free Zone while strengthening the facility as an important economic hub for northern Belize.

Usher said the government is aware of concerns surrounding activities in the zone and is maintaining regular patrols while working with international partners.

Usher said the government continues to monitor the Free Zone and collaborate with authorities in neighboring countries to address potential illegal activities.

“We have to make sure that there’s nothing illegal happening in there, that we continue to have regular patrols in the zone, outside the zone to make sure that there are no illegal activities happening,” he told 7News Belize.

At the same time, Usher emphasized that the Free Zone remains a significant source of employment and economic activity for the country.

He noted that approximately 3,000 people work in the zone, with 333 businesses currently operating there. “The free zone is an important economic area for the country, especially for the north,” Usher said.

The minister said maintaining the balance between economic development and security will require continued cooperation with Belize’s international and regional partners.

World.title: Belize Tourism Board opens nominations for 2026 National Tourism Awards
World.content:
Belize Tourism Board opens nominations for 2026 National Tourism Awards

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Tourism Board (BTB) has officially opened nominations for the 2026 National Tourism Awards, which will recognize individuals, businesses and organizations demonstrating excellence and contributing to the growth and sustainability of Belize’s tourism industry. The awards ceremony is scheduled to take place in November 2026.

Nominations are open across 11 categories, including Hotel of the Year, Small Accommodation of the Year, Tour Operator of the Year, Tour Guide of the Year and Frontline Tourism Professional of the Year. Other categories include Cultural Experience of the Year, Restaurant of the Year, Local Eatery of the Year, Sustainable Tourism Champion of the Year, Site of the Year and Wellness Experience of the Year.

The BTB is encouraging the public and tourism stakeholders to nominate deserving individuals and businesses that have made outstanding contributions to Belize’s tourism sector.

The awards seek to highlight the people and enterprises helping to strengthen Belize’s reputation as a tourism destination while promoting sustainable practices.

Nominations must be submitted by September 4, 2026.

World.title: International News: Mexico slams US ‘Interference’ after visa revoked for Ex-President’s son
World.content:
International News: Mexico slams US ‘Interference’ after visa revoked for Ex-President’s son

By Zoila Palma: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has criticized the United States government’s decision to revoke the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, calling the move interference in Mexico’s domestic politics.

“This amounts to interference in Mexican politics,” Sheinbaum said on Friday, adding that she could see no other reason for the US decision.

López Beltrán, 39, confirmed the visa revocation on social media, describing it as a “crude and perverse act” by US State Department officials.

In an open letter addressed to US President Donald Trump, López Beltrán accused American officials of targeting him for political and propaganda reasons.

He specifically criticized Secretary of State Marco Rubio and argued that there was no justification for what he described as “arrogant behaviour.”

The visa decision comes amid reports that several members of Mexico’s ruling Morena party have also had their US visas revoked in recent months.

World.title: NOT TRUE!
World.content:
ANDERSON... perhaps the most serious wound is the suggestion that panels of the court have been constituted or altered in order to secure a particular outcome in a case

Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) President Justice Winston Anderson on Friday broke his silence on allegations surrounding his leadership of the regional body, describing as “entirely unfounded and untrue” suggestions that he interfered with the composition of panels and sought to influence judgments.

At the same time he characterised the disclosure of a series of e-mail between himself and colleague judges to the

Sunday Express newspaper in Trinidad and Tobago “as the most troubling aspect of this entire episode”, and condemned, “in the strongest possible terms, the unauthorised disclosure and publication of confidential material relating to the internal deliberations and confidential correspondence of the court”.

According to Justice Anderson, “such disclosures and their publication are wholly unacceptable and strike at one of the fundamental principles upon which every independent judiciary depends”.

“It erodes trust in the sanctity of judicial deliberations and judicial collegiality. It erodes public trust and confidence in the Third Branch, and it does untold harm to the people we are sworn to serve and betrays the trust and confidence placed in us,” the CCJ president stated.

The Sunday Express had reported that in the e-mail exchanges, a majority of the judges accused Justice Anderson of governing the regional court in an “authoritarian” and “dictatorial” manner.

The complaints, as reported by the newspaper, range from accusations of Justice Anderson unilaterally imposing a judicial dress code to allegations of “panel fixing” and attempts to influence the outcome of cases.

Addressing the allegations further, Justice Anderson said, “Perhaps the most serious wound is the suggestion that panels of the court have been constituted or altered in order to secure a particular outcome in a case.

“Such an allegation strikes at the very heart of judicial independence and public confidence in the administration of justice. It therefore warrants a clear and direct response. The allegation is wholly untrue. No judge of this court can or should be restrained from expressing his or her judicial views, or from deciding any matter according to his or her independent assessment of the law and the evidence,” Justice Anderson stated.

He said that it was “with particular concern” that he “noted suggestions in the public domain” that he has sought to influence the outcome of cases before the court.

“Those allegations are entirely unfounded and untrue,” Justice Anderson declared while explaining that a little known fact is that, “in the original jurisdiction of the court, no dissenting judgments are published”. However, the CCJ president maintained that, “the principle of unanimity is a standard practice in international courts exercising jurisdiction of this type”.

“The suggestion that judicial views were suppressed, or that any judge was directed to reach a particular conclusion, is therefore wholly without foundation. Throughout my judicial career, both as a judge and now as president, I have regarded judicial independence as inviolable. It is a principle that I have consistently defended and will continue to defend,” Justice Anderson said.

Detailing the constitution of panels within the court, the CCJ president pointed out that “the inferential leap required to elevate the issue of Bench attire to an allegation of panel-fixing is irresponsible, intellectually dishonest, injudicious and, quite simply, malevolent!”

“Accordingly, I reject entirely the suggestion that panels of this court have been constituted or altered to secure predetermined outcomes. Such allegations are unsupported by the facts, inconsistent with the court’s long-established practices, and contrary to the principles upon which this court has operated since its establishment,” Justice Anderson stated.

He however said, in putting that matter to rest going forward, “every judge of the court will be required to sit on every panel, unless the judge opts out for a legitimate reason and is excused”.

Responding to reports that he had taken a high-handed approach in deciding on the judicial dress code, the CCJ president provided the background to that development. He conceded that while he “may have approached the matter of the handling of the issue of the dress code too strongly”, he did so because he “regarded it as an institutional issue concerning the appearance, consistency and tone of the court, rather than a question directed at any individual judge”.

Said Justice Anderson: “The CCJ is the apex court for a diverse Caribbean region and population. Dress codes set by the CCJ will have implications for all courts of member states as well as for the region. The idea of individual judges adopting their own interpretation of national or traditional dress would seem to be at odds with the very concept of a Caribbean court.”

He added that “if it is the view of the region that national dress is appropriate for judges to wear on the Bench, the inevitable question of what is ‘national dress’ in a Caribbean context of diversity must be determined”.

“This must be determined by the people of the region and toward this end I propose to engage all national courts in this consultation,” Justice Anderson said further.

Addressing commentary about his meetings and discussions with the president and leader of the Opposition of Guyana regarding the prolonged acting appointments of the chancellor and chief justice of that country, Justice Anderson made it clear that he had “no personal interest or preference in who is appointed” to both positions.

“My concern has always and only been confined to the constitutional principle that the judiciary should be headed by substantively appointed office holders enjoying the full constitutional protections intended by the framers of the constitution,” Justice Anderson insisted. He said while in retrospect he believed “another course would have been much better” his actions were fed only by his concern about “the preservation of judicial independence and the constitutional integrity of the Guyanese judiciary”.

“Those considerations alone informed my actions and comments. They were not motivated by any political or other preference, personal interest, or any desire to intervene in the domestic affairs of Guyana beyond what I regarded as my responsibility as president of the final appellate court for that jurisdiction to ensure constitutional protection of the judiciary,” Justice Anderson said.

On Wednesday, the heads of judiciary of Barbados, The Bahamas, Belize, Guyana, the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, Jamaica, and Trinidad and Tobago — which subscribe to the original and/or appellate jurisdictions of the CCJ — in a media release said, while they “do not consider it appropriate to comment upon the merits of statements or allegations attributed to individual judges, nor upon matters arising within the internal deliberative or administrative processes of the court”, they were gravely concerned “about the breach of confidentiality which resulted in the disclosure of what appear to be internal communications”.

Said the heads of the judiciary: “We remain confident in the Caribbean Court of Justice as a vital regional judicial institution and in the commitment of its judges to the principles which underpin the administration of justice throughout the Caribbean”.

World.title: ‘Dream Supreme’
World.content:
Wards of the state listen during a session at the Child Protection and Family Services Agency Transitional Living Programme Higher Education Day for Youth in State Care and Expo, held inside the Douglas Orane Auditorium, Wolmer’s Boys’, School on Thursday. Photo: JIS

TWENTY-FIVE adolescents leaving State care will receive full scholarships for tertiary education, from Supreme Ventures Foundation under its latest investment in the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) Transitional Living Programme (TLP).

The announcement was made by Chloleen Daley-Muschett, assistant vice-president of public relations and corporate affairs at Supreme Ventures Limited, as she delivered greetings to the TLP Higher Education Day Expo held at Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Thursday.

According to Daley-Muschett, when the foundation first partnered with CPFSA’s TLP in 2021, it awarded 20 youths with full-ride scholarships while it was celebrating its 20th anniversary.

Now that the organisation is celebrating 25 years, Daley-Muschett argued that it was only fitting to award 25 excellent and deserving adolescents with full scholarships to fulfil their academic dreams.

“When we say full [scholarship], we mean full. So tuition, accommodation, expenses, housing, everything, miscellaneous, we provided for them,” she said.

“To date, I can tell you that the foundation has invested more than $100 million. That’s $100 million into the students who have gone through the programme so far. So you can do the math; if it was $100 million for 20, you can do the math to know how much we’ll be investing for the 25 students,” said Daley-Muschett.

That investment, she said, will cover whichever path a recipient chooses, noting that even a traditionally more pricey degree, like medicine, is supported.

“So when I say dream supreme, I mean dream supreme. Don’t limit yourself… If it is something that you’re interested in and you have an aptitude to do, go out there, get the information, make yourself visible, and you never know what can happen for you, because the success of our investment depends on you,” she said.

Daley-Muschett encouraged youth at the TLP Expo to be bold and pointed out that hard work and dedication are the values that will allow them to achieve their goals.

“It depends on your drive, your focus, your own ambition. Those are the qualities that will turn the opportunity that we give to you into achievement for life for you. So to all of you today who are a part of the TLP, this day is for you. The CPFSA has gone all out to have all of these executives here for you. Use the opportunities to ask questions, explore your options, and imagine your future. Don’t limit that imagination. Dream supreme,” she reiterated.

Described as an exit-readiness project, the TLP was implemented through the collaborative efforts of the CPFSA, The University of the West Indies Open Campus, the Caribbean Child Development Centre, and the United States Agency for International Development, which provided the funding for the initial implementation.

The aim of the project is to facilitate a smooth transition to independent living for adolescents who have reached 18 years and are leaving State care.

Under the programme, the TLP youngsters are exposed to different pathways to aid in their readiness for independent living. These include life skills, coaching, entrepreneurship, vocational and technical skills training, house accommodation for two years, as well as tertiary enrolment.

Wards who are unable to transition directly into tertiary programmes after leaving State care are provided the opportunity to participate in the agency’s Transition to Work Programme, under the vocational skills component of the project.

According to director of alternative care services at the CPFSA Larenzo Badalo, some 300 youths are currently benefiting from the many pathways offered by the programme.

He expressed hope that the youth present at the expo took the opportunity to make themselves visible and to become more knowledgeable about the paths available to them under the TLP.

“We want them, today, to understand that a derailment is not the end. Going through State care is just a stop on your journey to where you’re going. But while you’re in State care you’re not defined by being in State care. You should be able to have the access to all the opportunities that other persons who are not in State care are supposed to have. So what we do for them is bring services to them,” he said.

“So today we want them to see that there are educational opportunities for you. Here are scholarship opportunities, here are skill-based opportunities, or if you’re also considering an essential service programme. We have the JDF [Jamaica Defence Force] out there who are going to present their services. So our hope is that at least a significant number of them would see that they can have an education. They can get a skill and they can be gainfully employed so that they can support their independent lives,” said Badalo.

World.title: Modern $760-million Christiana tax office officially opened
World.content:
The $760-million Christiana tax office in north-east Manchester. Photo: Kasey Williams

CHRISTIANA, Manchester — Three years after ground was broken here for the Christiana tax office, Finance Minister Fayval Williams on Friday officially opened the facility which has increased efficiency for taxpayers in north-east Manchester and adjoining areas.

“This tax office here is not only about taxes, it is about trust, it is about access and ultimately it is about how the Government shows up for its people. Today the Government of Jamaica is showing up. [A] modern tax office brings public service closer to the people of Christiana and the surrounding communities,” Williams told her audience at Friday’s opening ceremony.

Among those in attendance at the ceremony was former Finance Minister and Manchester North Eastern Member of Parliament Audley Shaw, who has been credited for his vision in lobbying for the modern facility. Christiana is located in north-east Manchester.

“I want to acknowledge Minister Shaw and the role that he played in this, in terms of getting this office here to serve the people of Christiana,” Williams said.

“When Government brings service closer to the people we are not simply opening another office. We are making lives better for you. We are opening another door between Jamaican people and the Government they support,” Williams added.

She said the $760-million state-of-the-art facility actually opened its doors in February, offering a wide range of services, greater convenience, and a more modern customer experience.

“This moment has been in the making for some time. Our journey began in 2023 when we broke ground for the construction of this new tax office to address the challenges experienced by staff and the taxpayers at the previous location. Three years later we can see the result of that investment,” said Williams.

“The significance of this investment extends beyond Christiana, it serves residents across Manchester and provides another option for neighbouring communities in Trelawny, Clarendon, and even St Elizabeth; if you do not want to use the Santa Cruz tax office we will welcome you here,” the finance minister added.

She said additional work is needed to reach more taxpayers at their convenience.

“We know that distance can be a barrier to accessing Government services. A trip to another parish can mean additional transportation cost, time away from work or business, and inconvenience for families, that is why investments such as this one today matters,” she said.

“We recognise that for many Jamaicans their most direct interaction with Government happens when they need a public service, whether it is obtaining a taxpayer registration number, completing a motor vehicle transaction, processing a driver’s licence, filing taxes, or making a payment. That interaction should be efficient, straightforward, and respectful of the citizens’ time”.

“Imagine we are asking you to pay a fee and we have you waiting in line. What can go so?” Williams added, evoking laughter.

World.title: Kirkledove bares his soul
World.content:
Kirkledove

BY KEDIESHA PERRY Observer writer entertainment@jamaicaobserver.com

For Grammy-nominated musician, producer, and songwriter Kirk “Kirkledove” Bennett, music has always been more than rhythm and melody. It has been a source of healing, reflection, and expression.

Those emotions take centre stage on his latest album, Analog Heart Digital Mind, which was released on June 4.

While Bennett has built a prominent career as one of Jamaica’s most respected session drummers, the project sees him stepping further into the spotlight as a recording artiste, blending reggae, dub, and soulful influences to tell a deeply personal story.

The inspiration for the album came during one of the most difficult periods of his life.

“The inspiration behind this album came from a time in my life when I was in a vulnerable situation, or at least I felt that way. When my grandma passed away, she [had been] that person I could share anything with, and she was no longer around. I became very emotional towards creating, which put me in a different perspective and process mood towards my music. Luckily, I had some friends who supported me through the process and journey,” Bennett said.

The result is an album that Bennett describes as a “soulful vibes dub reggae fusion”, created with the hope of uplifting listeners despite its emotional origins.

“My main objective is to make the people in this world feel joyful and upbeat towards my music,” he said.

Although Analog Heart Digital Mind is his latest release, Bennett is no stranger to recording projects, having released a few albums throughout his career. However, he says this one stands apart from his previous work.

“My other albums are straight dub music. This album is more about being on a musical journey, with more grooves, more of my vocals, and showing more emotions,” he explained.

The album also features collaborations with long-time friends and musical associates Anthony Red Rose, Dean Fraser, Jah Man, and Mr Vegas.

“These are my close friends who I’ve been working with for years, so it was ordained to be that way to finish the puzzle,” Bennett said.

Known affectionately throughout the music industry as “Drummy”, Bennett has spent decades behind the scenes helping to shape the sound of reggae and dancehall. Born in Trelawny and raised in Montego Bay, St James, his musical journey began at Muschett Comprehensive High School before he refined his craft with the Trelawny Marching Band, and later on the north coast hotel circuit and aboard Royal Caribbean Cruise Line. His life changed when reggae icon Beres Hammond spotted his extraordinary talent and invited him to join the renowned Harmony House band. Bennett went on to serve as the band’s principal drummer for more than 17 years, performing on songs including

I Feel Good, Come Down Father, and Who’s That Sound. Today, Bennett is widely regarded as one of Jamaica’s premier session drummers. His résumé includes work with Beres Hammond, Marcia Griffiths, Toots Hibbert, Busy Signal, Tarrus Riley, Queen Ifrica, Maxi Priest, Elephant Man, Julian Marley, Jesse Royal, among many others. He also served as principal drummer for the legendary Roots Radics band and was ranked among the top 10 reggae drummers of all time in a LargeUp.com poll. Despite those lofty achievements, Bennett remains grounded. “My biggest accomplishment is life. Just to wake up every day and make music is an achievement. I have to give thanks to the Most High for what I have accomplished and for what is coming next for me,” he said. Since the album’s release, Bennett said the response has been overwhelmingly positive, with encouraging feedback coming through social media, YouTube, radio stations, and disc jockeys. “I’ve been getting a lot of good feedback and comments from this album. Big up to the DJs and radio personnel who are giving me the ‘strength’,” he said. As for what’s next, Bennett says fans can expect plenty more music. “I’m always working on different projects in the studio and playing music all over the world. I like to surprise my fans with music and whatever I’m doing through my label,” he said.

World.title: S Hotel celebrates Jamaica’s resilience with new sculpture
World.content:
Work ongoing on the new sculpture at S Hotel in Montego Bay..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — The S Hotel, located on Jimmy Cliff Boulevard in Montego Bay, continues to make an impression with its visual artwork, this time with the construction of a sculpture that pays tribute to the resilience of the Jamaican people following the devastation wrought by Hurricane Melissa last year.

The new statue will serve as a landmark and an expression of gratitude to the Jamaican people and everyone who contributed to the country’s ongoing recovery from the Category 5 storm.

“After we put up the 46-feetbDoctor Bird on the side of the S hotel in Montego Bay in August 2025 we received such positive feedback that we decided to put a statue in Kingston,” S Hotel Chief Executive Officer Christopher Issa told the Jamaica Observer.

“But after Hurricane Melissa we decided to do another one in Montego Bay on the Hip Strip as an inspiration, and in recognition of the resilience of the Jamaican people, and as a thank you to all those who help with the recovery locally and overseas,” he continued.

The 62-foot sculpture is now in its final phase of construction and sits prominently in the commercial area of the S Hotel property, allowing locals and visitors to interact with and view it.

Issa declined to comment on the cost but said more than 35 people were involved at different stages of the construction over a period of more than six months.

The sculpture is expected to become a new point of attraction on the famed Hip Strip, although the hotel mogul was quick to point out that it is separate from plans already in place to upgrade the area.

“The statue was done independently of any plans for the Hip Strip,” he said, explaining that it was meant to be an added attraction.

A statue of sprint king, Olympian Usain Bolt was shifted slightly to the side to accommodate the new structure.

“When completed we hope that the statue will be visited by locals and tourists [who] will appreciate not only the message behind it but the scope and level of artistic talent that our country has,” he said.

The sculpture is the work of local visual artist Scheed Cole, the man behind the massive

Doctor Bird statue that spans one side of the S Hotel building. He explained the inspiration behind the project after being commissioned to take on the task.

“I felt very heavy in my heart to do something to help the Melissa recovery, and something to really give hope back to a nation and to rebuild a country, and a thought came of Jamaica rising, or together we rise,” Cole told the Observer.

The sculpture, described as dynamic, is made up of several different parts that tell the story of a country that faced great peril and is bouncing back.

“I came up with the tree of life, of giving back life to Jamaica, and on the tree itself, which is the highest point, it has 14 different leaves representing the 14 parishes. Each leaf is a healing plant — coming back to the tree of life in the

Bible having different fruits on it — and of course the herbs are [for] the healing of the nation,” he explained.

The height of the sculpture represents Jamaica’s 62 years of independence from British rule.

“Everything has a meaning,” said Cole.

Working with his core team and with support from the S Hotel over the last six months, Cole has been putting together a very complex piece of art.“I wanted to show the people that helped along the way. At the bottom of the sculpture you have the trauma that is taking place during the hurricane — people trying to survive. As you can see there is a soldier trying to help a lady who is at the point of giving up, so you can see the anguish on her face, and he’s begging her, ‘Please, don’t give up,’ “ he said about another section of the sculpture.

“I have the construction worker; the man with the banana represents agriculture coming back, and it’s a reviving and a rising — and that’s really where the tree came into being. I wanted to show a sculpture that kinda symbolises a refreshing, a revitalising, and a springing back,” he added.

There are also tributes to the international support received. Cole insisted that he wanted the message of revitalisation and recovery to be expressed as clearly as possible, and therefore thanked those who commissioned the piece for the opportunity.

“I give kudos to Christopher Issa who really is the one that has backed it 150 per cent [with] his belief in having the Montego Hip Strip revitalised as well as something iconic for the world to see,” he said.

His dream is for Jamaica — long known for athletics, its food and music — to make a name for itself in the visual arts.

Cole said the piece should be completed in the coming weeks, with plans for an official unveiling in October to mark the passing of Hurricane Melissa.

World.title: UP AGAINST IT!
World.content:
Jamaica Kingsmen player Andre Russell celebrates the dismissal of Guyana Amazon Warriors batsman Shimron Hetmyer during the Caribbean Premier League Twenty20 match at Sabina Park in Kingston on Thursday.

CAPTAIN Rovman Powell says the Kingsmen will need to lift their game in every department as they turn the page to Saturday’s crucial clash versus Trinbago Knight Riders, after the Jamaica franchise slumped to a third Caribbean Premier League (CPL) defeat with a six-wicket loss to Guyana Amazon Warriors at Sabina Park on Thursday.

“Obviously if you’re 0-3 down and you’re going to play such a strong Trinidad team it’s always an uphill task, you know,” Powell said in a post-match interview.

“But, as I keep on saying, it’s just for us as players to spend some time together and just work on those areas. I think all three areas need a little bit of touching up. If us as individuals can be 10-15 per cent better, then I think we can collectively put it together as a team,” he added.

Sent in to bat, Jamaica Kingsmen were bowled out for 117 in 19.4 overs. Reeza Hendricks made 40 from 38 balls with two fours and two sixes. Powell contributed 24 runs, Kirk McKenzie 16, and Vitel Lawes 14 runs, but no other batter reached double figures.

Mohammad Nabi did the damage with both bat and ball for Guyana Amazon Warriors. He took 4 for 22 from 4 overs, then returned to make 19 from 15 as the visitors cruised to 118-4 in 14.1 overs.

Shai Hope top-scored with an unbeaten 56 from 41 balls, including two fours and four sixes, and Glenn Phillips added 28 from 17 at the top. Andre Russell was Jamaica’s best with two for 12 from two overs, while Nabi was named Player of the Match.

Powell was blunt about the performance in front of the home crowd.

“It is disappointing when the people come out and support us and we haven’t turned up. But, a lot of credits have to be given to Guyana; I think they found their lines and lengths as a bowling group early. And it’s just for us to lift our heads up, you know? Nobody is going to come into the dressing room and lift our heads up for us,” Powell said.

The Kingsmen captain pointed to consistency as the missing piece.

“I think we’re playing cricket in patches. The guys are still a little bit lackadaisical, you know; they are not 100 per cent in. If you should look on the fielding, a lot of simple errors [were made], and that goes into the batting and it goes into the bowling.

“It’s for us as a group to be a bit more consistent, you know? When we get partnerships with our batters, it’s not long enough, it’s not big enough. And when we approach it as a bowling group, we’re not bowling good overs,” Powell explained.

Batting has been a particular concern. After getting starts in back-to-back games, Powell knows he has to go bigger.

“That’s something that I will look on tonight,” he said of his own dismissal in the 20s.

“But if we’re 50, 60 runs in 10 or 15 overs, the game is going nowhere. Somebody has to sometimes hold the bull by the horn, and that’s what I tried. Hopefully, over the 24 hours I will sit down and come up with a better batting plan,” he said.

There are positives to take into the Trinidad and Tobago match, and Powell highlighted Russell’s bowling, Lawes’ emergence, and some runs for Hendricks.

“Obviously the first game at home, the guys fought. You know, Andre Russell played well, young Vitel Lawes played well also. He’s a young talent, still young and inexperienced, but he’s coming into his own. He showed glimpses of what he can do in the first few games. It’s good to see one of our overseas batters, Hendricks, get some runs under his belt. You know, that should go well for us in the next game,” Powell stated.

With a young squad still adjusting to CPL cricket at Sabina, Powell asked fans to stay with the team.

“It’s a team with a lot of youngsters. CPL cricketers haven’t played at Sabina Park, the franchise haven’t been at Sabina Park for quite a time and so, therefore, the talent pool [has] kind of dwindled down. A lot of guys haven’t played CPL before now and so it’s a young team. It’s for you guys, as fans, to keep on supporting us. I’m sure we’ll turn it around,” Powell ended.

World.title: NWA stresses bypass solution to Lucea’s traffic woes
World.content:
Backhoes clearing drain outlets to the sea adjacent to the Seaview Drive main road in Lucea on Wednesday. Anthony Lewis

LUCEA, Hanover — The National Works Agency (NWA) has revealed that while concrete paving of the heavily trafficked Seaview Drive in the coastal town of Lucea remains on the table, a bypass road is the ultimate solution to the problem.

“The long-term [goal] right now is to build a bypass to the town of Lucea; that is the intention. But at Seaview [Drive], we are looking to put a bit of concrete road in that space. Because the road is pretty close to the sea and you have a combination of tidal waves on the one hand, and then you have a situation where the drain and the road act pretty much like a basin that collects water. Those two things are not good for that area,” manager, communication and customer services at the NWA Stephen Shaw said Thursday.

He was responding to queries, from the Jamaica Observer, about long-term plans for the problematic roadway, which is susceptible to water damage from the sea and has been repaired several times over the years. Apart from minor works, major repairs were carried out by the NWA in 2023.

A bypass road for the town of Lucea was first mentioned by Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness nearly a decade ago.

While they wait for that project, road users struggle to navigate the pothole-riddled Seaview Drive which has resulted in severe daily traffic jams.

On Wednesday, the

Observer reported that while the NWA had started drain- cleaning and patching works the night before, stakeholders were calling for a permanent fix. The NWA had indicated, last September, that there were plans to make a significant shift from asphalt road surfacing to concrete pavement on the roadway.

On Thursday, Shaw noted that concrete paving will have to be planned in a way that minimises the impact on the motoring public which uses the heavily travelled road.

“Concrete is something that [when] you pour it, you cannot drive on it at the same time. With asphaltic concrete, you can drive on it immediately. With Portland-type cement concrete, you have to allow a curing period,” explained Shaw.

He did not provide a date for the concrete paving to be done but gave an assurance that the public will be provided with ample time to make preparations.

“When that time comes, we are going to make sure that the public is apprised well ahead of time, so whatever changes, [and] modifications are necessary, they can deal with it,” stated Shaw.

World.title: UN warns sanctions chill is stopping Cuba aid
World.content:
MATANZAS, Cuba — Residents carry containers while queuing for potable water from a water tanker in a neighbourhood of Matanzas, Cuba, on August 6, 2026. Recurring water shortages and power outages have forced many residents of Matanzas to rely on water deliveries and public water distribution points. Photo: AFP

HAVANA, Cuba (AFP) — The top United Nations official in Cuba has warned vital humanitarian aid is not reaching the island because shipping and financial firms fear United States (US) reprisals, stranding deliveries of cancer drugs and water-treatment equipment.

Francisco Pichon, the UN resident coordinator in Cuba, told AFP on Thursday that a climate of fear over US sanctions among shippers, insurers, and banks had led to “over compliance” that was forcing aid agencies to re-route cargo and delay deliveries intended for hospitals and schools.

“They respond to the risk of sanctions by simply withdrawing from providing those services,” he said.

Since January the US has imposed a virtual fuel blockade on the communist-run island, worsening rolling blackouts that make normal life impossible.

Washington has also threatened sanctions on companies doing business with Cuba’s Government, deepening shortages of basic goods.

“There is no food for us elderly people,” said 68-year-old Havana resident Jose Antonio Ortega, a retired truck driver.

“My pension isn’t enough for anything,” he said. “I have nothing to eat or drink in the morning.”

Only one fuel tanker is known to have arrived in Cuba in the last seven months — although limited private sales of fuel tanks from the United States have risen.

“What initially affected the most vulnerable groups is now affecting the population much more broadly,” Pichon said.

Firms are wary of anything that may risk vital access to the US banking system or the world’s largest economy.

Pichon said one recent delivery of a medicine used to treat childhood cancer had failed to arrive because refrigerated transport could not be secured in time.

He also pointed to reproductive health kits for pregnant women that were returned to suppliers, and containers carrying medicines and school materials that were diverted rather than shipped on to Cuba.

Cuban Government data show the crisis is rapidly accelerating.

Infant deaths are believed to have more than doubled, while survival rates among children with cancer have fallen from 85 per cent to 65 per cent.

Water shortages are also worsening. According to the UN, around 3.5 million people face disruptions to drinking water supplies, while about one million depend on deliveries by tanker trucks because pumping systems lack sufficient fuel and electricity.

Pichon said the crisis is affecting not only Cuban institutions but also the UN’s own relief effort, which has been forced to rely on increasingly scarce fuel supplies obtained through private channels.

With the Atlantic hurricane season under way, UN officials are particularly concerned about the vulnerability of water and sanitation systems and the potential for disease outbreaks.

“What we are seeing is that humanitarian risks are being translated into humanitarian impacts,” Pichon said, warning that conditions had continued to deteriorate over recent months.

World.title: Hungary uses sunken barges to raise Danube River to keep nuclear plant going
World.content:
Magyar said on X that the current water level near Hungary's only nuclear energy facility is 122 cm lower than normal and it is projected to drop below 132 cm on Monday, which would force one of the plant’s two turbines to shut down.

On Wednesday, Magyar announced that they would be building a riverbed sill with 150,000 cubic meters of stone and was considering sinking the two 80-meter barges. A sill is an underwater dam meant to slow down the current and raise water levels. Hungary’s Defense Ministry has assigned 100 troops to work around the clock on the project, the prime minister said on X.

Nuclear energy facilities across Europe have been affected by this summer’s droughts and soaring temperatures. Romania shut down a nuclear power plant earlier this week due to the Danube’s water levels.

France — one of Europe’s biggest producers of nuclear power — has seen its fleet of nuclear power plants affected throughout the summer. Le Monde reported authorities had to shut down six of the country’s 57 nuclear reactors as yet another heat wave broiled much of the country. Earlier in the week, a climate change-fueled jellyfish invasion forced workers to bring parts of a different plant offline.

Magyar has also cast doubt on completing an expansion of the Paks plant by a Russian state-owned firm in a deal signed by Magyar’s predecessor, the Kremlin-friendly Viktor Orbàn, citing the water issue.

World.title: EU ready to send satellite system to help Indonesia after 7.7 magnitude earthquake
World.content:
A rescue team searches the ruins of a building in Maumere, Indonesia on Aug. 15, 2026. | Arnold Welianto/AFP via Getty Images

The European Commission is ready to offer “eyes in the sky” via the Copernicus program to support Indonesian search and rescue operations after the country was hit by a 7.7 magnitude earthquake, President Ursula von der Leyen said Saturday.

“Indonesia, we stand with you,” von der Leyen said in a post on X.

Copernicus is an observation system that can provide mapping services useful for search operations and damage assessments.

World.title: US threatens EU over its green reporting rules
World.content:
The dispute centers on two pillars of the EU’s corporate sustainability rulebook: the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, which requires large companies to address human rights and environmental harms linked to their operations and supply chains, and the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, which requires companies to disclose sustainability-related information.

Brussels has scaled back both laws in its drive to cut red tape, but has stopped short of Washington’s demand to shield U.S. companies from their reach.

Last week, Puzder similarly attacked the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism as a tariff on U.S. exporters. On Thursday, the White House also accused the EU and more than 40 countries of enabling Chinese goods to skirt U.S. tariffs by rerouting them through their markets.

A European Commission spokesperson told POLITICO that Brussels had made “considerable efforts” to explain its rules and highlight "its willingness to cooperate with the US to increase trade where possible," but drew a line at changing its regulatory regime in response to U.S. pressure.

“We have been very clear and consistent on the fact that neither our rules framework nor our regulatory autonomy are up for negotiation,” said the spokesperson.

This story has been updated.

Koen Verhelst contributed reporting.

World.title: Le Conseil constitutionnel censure la loi interdisant les réseaux sociaux aux mineurs
World.content:
“L’interdiction instituée par la loi est susceptible de s’appliquer à des services de communication en ligne dont les risques pour la santé et la sécurité des mineurs ne sont pas établis”, estime encore le Conseil constitutionnel, insistant sur l’imprécision autour du champ d’application de l’article.

Le risque avait été soulevé au moment de l’examen du texte au Sénat, certains élus de la Chambre haute ayant tenté d’imposer l’établissement d’une “liste noire” qui définirait plus précisément les plateformes concernées par cette limitation d’accès aux mois de 15 ans – et éviterait ainsi le risque de censure par le Conseil constitutionnel.

Un élément du texte retiré au moment de son examen en Commission mixte paritaire pour assurer sa conformité avec le droit européen.

Le Conseil constitutionnel estime par ailleurs que le texte ne définit pas les garanties légales propres à assurer le droit au respect de la vie privée des utilisateurs qui seront contraints de faire vérifier leur âge par les plateformes pour prouver leur majorité.

“Le gouvernement n’a pas assez écouté le Sénat et le risque d’inconstitutionnalité que nous pointions depuis des mois. Désormais, le risque, c’est que le texte soit vidé de sa substance”, a réagi, sur ce point, la rapporteure du texte au Sénat, Catherine Morin-Desailly, auprès de POLITICO.

Un constat partagé par le député socialiste Arthur Delaporte, à l’origine de l’une des saisines du Conseil constitutionnel. L'autre émanait du groupe de la France Insoumise (LFI).

World.title: French court blocks social media ban for under 15s
World.content:
The French president has also pushed restrictions to the top of the EU agenda, with an expected announcement of bloc-wide measures by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September.

In a statement late Friday, the French presidential office said the government would not be giving up on the bill. It has set a new target date for spring 2027, which coincides with when Macron will leave office.

The statement said Macron “has instructed the Prime Minister to work, as quickly as possible, on a legally sound draft that takes into account” the court's decision. The ruling hinted at what would make the age restriction align with fundamental rights: giving parents more flexibility.

Peter Craddock, a senior Brussels-based attorney advising social media firms, said the French court decision could have far-reaching implications.

"What they're basically saying here is: 'Listen, government, if you want to get this to succeed, you can't just work on the basis of a general ban. There have to be limitations," said Craddock, a partner at Keller & Heckman. "There have to be ways for people to say, 'well, actually, in my case, my son, my daughter is of a certain degree of maturity and is able to use this properly.'"

The government bill had passed through the French legislative procedure after a lengthy back-and-forth earlier this summer. It was set to bring forward Europe's first social media age restrictions, with Greece and Denmark planning to follow suit.

World.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
World.content:
Latvia's military warned that similar incidents may happen again in the future. "While the Russian aggression in Ukraine is ongoing, the recurrence of such cases when a foreign unmanned aircraft enters or approaches Latvian airspace is possible," it said.

An air raid alert was declared in four eastern Latvian municipalities at around 4 a.m. local time. The military urged people to stay indoors and away from exterior walls.

After the drone was downed, Sandra Kapteine, head of the Rugāji village administration, told the Latvian Information Agency that the incident “caused no casualties,” as the drone wreckage fell in a “wooded area.”

There has been an uptick in similar incidents over recent months in countries close to the war-zone. A week ago, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said a Ukrainian-made drone crossed Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded near the village of Kardam.

World.title: Spain and Morocco reinforce border amid fears of fresh Ceuta migrant surge
World.content:
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska traveled to Ceuta on Thursday to inspect border infrastructure and a new sea barrier designed to keep people from swimming into the city. The exclave’s security personnel has also been reinforced with an additional 300 police officers and 2,000 soldiers.

“We do this to dissuade anyone who aspires to enter Ceuta and Melilla irregularly,” said Grande-Marlaska. “None of them will remain in Ceuta, none of them will make it to the Iberian Peninsula, none of them will be given legal status.”

The rumored mass crossing has been cited by critics of Spain’s migration policies.

Austria’s conservative Europe, Integration and Family Minister Claudia Bauer, last week mentioned the rumored Aug. 15 surge in a written statement, demanding Madrid “immediately and significantly reinforce border protection in its African enclaves and ensure that this time it will hold.”

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government also cited the possibility of a mid-August mass arrival last week while justifying its decision to maintain border checks on travelers from Spain.

World.title: Deceased academic Jason Arday's family decries 'campaign of harassment' against him
World.content:
The family of British academic Jason Arday, who was found dead at a South London address on Friday night amid a high-profile plagiarism storm, have denounced what they called years of "sustained abuse".

 

In an overnight statement following Arday's death, his family said he had been "subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University".

Arday had himself alleged a "racially motivated" campaign against him.

Speaking to reporters on Saturday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said "it's a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends."

Burnham also said it was not the time for "any rushing to judgement", and that now is "a moment for reflection... reflecting on how things came to this."

A 'campaign of misinformation'

Arday resigned from his post at the University of Cambridge last week shortly after it announced a probe into the various accusations against him.

He made headlines when the university appointed him as its youngest black professor in 2023, but subsequently faced growing claims he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis.

Questions also emerged about some of his stated life achievements, including that he once ran 30 marathons in 35 days and raised millions for charities.

The allegations were seized on by British right-wing newspapers and commentators, who claimed he unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.

Media outlets including The Times, Guardian and the Telegraph have published several investigative articles into Arday's academic work and personal life.

In their statement following his death, Arday's family alleged "the campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

Diagnosed with autism, Arday said he was non-verbal until age 11 and only learnt to read and write at 18, before becoming Cambridge's youngest black professor at age 37, teaching sociology.

In an interview with The Times earlier this month, Arday admitted making academic "mistakes" but said he was being wrongly "portrayed to be a liar and a fantasist and an academic fraud".

He said that some errors in his early academic work were because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to understand information.

Simon Baron-Cohen, a Cambridge professor and director of the Autism Research Centre, told BBC radio that he spoke to Arday on Friday morning.

"He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life," he said.

"He wasn't coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he could not go on. He used those words in voice notes."
