World.title: NSW launches gun buyback scheme in wake of Bondi terror attack
World.content:
New South Wales will become the first state to begin a gun buyback scheme promised in the wake of last year's Bondi terror attack, with shooters to be compensated up to $10,000 per firearm.

The push to strengthen Australia's gun laws was the first commitment made by the Commonwealth following the December 14 attack on Sydney's Jewish community, in which 15 people were killed.

From November 2, those who exceed new limits on the number of firearms a person can possess, or whose licences will no longer allow them to have certain types, can surrender their guns for payment.

As many as 274,000 firearms — about a quarter of those registered in NSW — and 50,000 licence holders are estimated to be affected by the state's gun reforms.

The buyback scheme will start on November 2. (ABC News)

"We want those guns handed in, compensated for and safely destroyed," NSW Premier Chris Minns said in a statement on Saturday night.

" This is a big undertaking, but the principle behind it is simple: fewer dangerous guns in our community means a safer New South Wales. "

In December, NSW brought in acquisition limits of four firearms for most licence holders, and 10 firearms for others, like farmers and sports shooters.

Firearms that are quicker to reload, such as those with a straight-pull action, were reclassified to require a more restricted licence, but those changes are yet to take effect.

Compensation for gun owners

In the initial stage of the buyback, there will be a fixed price schedule ranging from $450 for an air rifle to $1,000 for a centre-fire rifle or revolver.

From early next year, owners of more expensive firearms with an "indicative market value above $3,000" can apply for compensation, which will be capped at $10,000 per gun.

There will be a flat fee for associated ammunition handed in.

Grants of up to $25,000 and licence fee relief worth $500 will be available to dealers.

Firearms type Firearms Sub-type Compensation Handgun Revolver $1,000 Semi-auto $850 Shotgun Double barrel $850 Single barrel $650 Rifle Rim-fire $600 Centrefire $1,000 Air rifle $450

While the Commonwealth will foot the cost of destroying the surrendered firearms, the buyback and administration expenses will be funded evenly between the state and federal governments.

"We must do everything we can to make sure the antisemitic terrorist attack in Bondi doesn't happen again," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement.

"That includes meaningful nationwide gun reform."

But the buybacks will not be implemented nationwide, with most other jurisdictions opposed or uncommitted to the scheme.

Queensland and Victoria have outright rejected the measure.

The scheme was announced after the Bondi Beach terror attack where 15 people died. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

While South Australia flagged "in principle" support for a buyback in January, it has since said it has no plans to change firearms laws.

The Northern Territory said it would not contribute any funds towards a buyback.

Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory have committed to the national scheme, but negotiations about funding remain ongoing.

While Western Australia completed its own two-year buyback scheme in January, it said it was "keen" to participate in a national one.

The NSW agreement comes several months after the federal government missed its own March deadline to agree with states and territories on firearm reforms.

A national buyback scheme was recommended in the royal commission on antisemitism's interim report in April, with the Commonwealth and states and territories urged to "prioritise efforts" to implement it.

After a One Nation-led community forum in Central NSW on Saturday afternoon ahead of the announcement, leader Pauline Hanson reiterated her general opposition to any gun buyback scheme, in response to an ABC reporter.

"I don't think there should be a buyback. These are law-abiding Australians that want their guns," she said.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, who also attended the forum, said such a scheme would be "an intrusion of the state into the right of the individual".

"Why are we buying back rifles from people who have never committed a crime? Are you going to start buying back golf clubs?" he told the ABC.

World.title: NRL updates: Metcalf, Walsh injured as Warriors thrash Broncos
World.content:
Luckless Warriors half Luke Metcalf has suffered yet another injury in a 40-6 defeat of Brisbane, who lost their own superstar Reece Walsh to a possibly season-ending ankle issue.

The third-placed Warriors drew level on competition points with Penrith in second place, but are now poised to lose another playmaker on the run to the NRL finals.

Metcalf clutched at his right hamstring after landing the conversion for the Warriors' third try, and cut a devastated figure leaving the field in Brisbane on Saturday night.

Overlooked for most of the season, Metcalf had been playing only his second game since April after starring in last week's defeat of the Panthers.

But the St George Illawarra recruit's dream of leaving the Warriors as a premiership winner is now in doubt, just when he appeared back in favour at the Kiwi club.

It is the latest injury blow for Metcalf, who returned from his second anterior cruciate ligament rupture earlier this season, only to suffer a hamstring injury two weeks later.

Minutes before Metcalf's new injury, Walsh was crunched in a hip-drop tackle that landed Warriors fullback Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad in the sin bin.

Walsh initially attempted to play on, but in his next involvement he threw an intercept that allowed winger Alofiana Khan-Pereira to streak away and score.

He left the field as Khan-Pereira's try put the Warriors up three scores and on the way to a fifth victory in six games.

Brisbane's finals hopes are well and truly over, but Walsh's injury may also impact his hopes of playing for Australia at the World Cup from October.

Earlier, the Warriors made a fast start and scored first as Jacob Laban grabbed Wayde Egan's pass and snuck outside Ezra Mam to the tryline.

Warriors halfback Metcalf is learning to carry a nation The halfback of the New Zealand Warriors plays with an entire nation on his shoulders and Luke Metcalf won't shy away from carrying the weight.

Metcalf batted the ball on for five-eighth Chanel Harris-Tavita to step twice through traffic and nab the Warriors' second try.

The Warriors took a 20-0 lead into half-time and never looked likely to be chased down.

The Warriors' Maori stars electrified after the break in Indigenous Round, with Nicoll-Klokstad touching down from a kick and Dallin Watene-Zelezniak finishing acrobatically in the right corner.

Left centre Leka Halasima crossed in the final five minutes to put the icing on the cake as the 16th-placed reigning premiers dropped a 12th game from 13 starts.

The Warriors may need to call on Luke Hanson for a second NRL game next week, given fellow halfback options Te Maire Martin (hamstring) and Tanah Boyd (knee) are both out.

Another option is to shift Nicoll-Klokstad from fullback and into the halves until Martin returns in coming weeks.

Cowboys lose to Eels after late penalty

The race for the NRL's top eight is still alive after a controversial late penalty consigned North Queensland to a 32-30 loss to Parramatta at CommBank Stadium.

With a chance to lock in a finals spot beckoning, the Cowboys' defence crumbled on Saturday night, allowing in six Eels tries.

The defining moment then came with four minutes to play, when Mitch Moses set up for a Parramatta field goal with scores locked at 30-30.

The Eels halfback eventually ran it on the last, was ankle-tapped by Heilum Luki and spilled the ball forward while falling.

But Moses reviewed the call, and the bunker found he had been collected in the head by Tom Chester while just inches above the ground.

The result means Canterbury are still alive in the race for the finals, albeit still two points behind the Cowboys and with North Queensland having a bye next week.

Manly also remain in the hunt, but would need to win their last three and have the Cowboys drop their final two games at home against Wests Tigers and Canberra.

As tough as the late penalty may have been for North Queensland, their defence remains a massive issue just weeks out from the finals.

A fortnight after leaking 82 points to the Sydney Roosters, it was poor again on Saturday night.

The tone was set when Parramatta winger Brian Kelly went 60 metres from the opening kick-off, while the Cowboys also conceded six first-half penalties.

The Cowboys lost to the Eels at Commbank stadium. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Luki could also find himself in trouble with the match review committee, after being sin-binned in the opening half for a high shot on Luca Moretti.

There is no doubt North Queensland's attack has the spark to put points on, with halfback Jaxon Purdue again impressing.

He put on a long cut-out ball for a Braidon Burns try in the first half, then stepped Teancum Brown and fullback Apa Twidle for a second-half try of his own.

Reed Mahoney also starred out of dummy-half, burrowing over for the night's first try, before going short to Reuben Cotter and putting him over after the break.

The Cowboys also put on one of the tries of the year with scores locked at 24-24, with the ball going from right to left and back to the right through five passes and two kicks before Chester crossed.

Not to be outdone, Parramatta also had plenty of attacking flair.

It was big prop Junior Paulo who responded to level the scores at 30-30, with a lofted 35-metre cut-out ball in the lead-up to a Jordan Samrani try.

Moses also had three try assists and broke through the line in the lead-up to a Tallyn Da Silva penalty try.

And his off-contract halves partner Ronald Volkman again pushed his case for another deal, scoring one try and putting a grubber-kick in for a Josh Addo-Carr four-pointer.

Sharks stumble as Dolphins stay in NRL's vital top four

Cronulla have blown a huge opportunity to move back into the NRL's top four with a painful and potentially fatal 24-20 loss to lowly Canberra.

Star Sharks playmaker Braydon Trindall also suffered a dislocated shoulder as the Dolphins held on to the all-important fourth spot with three rounds remaining before the finals.

Cronulla will rue not finding a match-winner despite being camped on Canberra's line, set after set, for the final 10 minutes.

But the Sharks' mounting injury toll will be of equal concern for coach Craig Fitzgibbon, who has now watched his faltering side fumble and bumble their way to consecutive losses to sides well out of finals contention.

Trindall lasted less than 10 minutes before trudging off.

Initial reports were promising, with the shoulder quickly put back in.

But with the Sharks leading 8-0 and looking strong, Fitzgibbon opted not to risk their key playmaker any longer.

It may have been the wrong move as the Raiders wrestled back control and momentum.

Already without suspended forward enforcer Addin Fonua-Blake and injured centre Jesse Ramien, suddenly the Sharks were looking significantly understrength and vulnerable.

The afternoon had started brightly enough for Cronulla, with a Nicho Hynes penalty preceding a lovely chip-and-regather try for Trindall in the fifth minute.

But from 8-0 up, the Sharks lost their way after Trindall was forced off.

First, winger Xavier Savage steamed on to a beautiful long ball from Kaeo Weekes, then Owen Pattie wriggled his way over to suddenly put Canberra ahead 12-8 after 15 minutes.

Things were looking grim for the Sharks when winger Jed Stuart collected a double cut-out pass from Ethan Strange to stroll over and extend the Raiders' lead to 10 points.

But with their top-four hopes — and history would suggest — title prospects on the line, the Sharks regrouped with a much-needed reply from Teig Wilton off a short ball from Nicho Hynes.

The hosts should have snatched the lead after the half-time siren, only for Briton Nikora to ignore a three-on-one overlap on the right edge.

The Sharks, though, were first to score after the break when Will Kennedy swooped to score, before handing the momentum back to Canberra through a soft Joseph Tapine try under the sticks.

There was a huge moment with seven minutes remaining when video replays looked to have shown Ronaldo Mulitalo contorting his body and planting the ball down for a match-levelling try.

But The Bunker went with referee Gerard Sutton's on-field "no try" call.

The near-miss proved Cronulla's last chance as consecutive defeats to last-placed St George Illawarra and now Canberra leave the Sharks likely needing to beat Gold Coast, Parramatta and Melbourne to earn a double-chance in the play-offs.

No team has ever won the premiership in the NRL era from outside the top four.

ABC/wires

World.title: Quick hits: Smith sets review record after horror drop, Warner jinxes Marnus
World.content:
Steve Smith reviews a decision before he's given out, Marnus Labuschagne gets desperate and then jinxed, while Josh Hazlewood provides a bright spot in an otherwise pitch-black day for Australia.

As it happened: Australia fighting to save first Test as Bangladesh claim top order wickets

Here are the quick hits from day three of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Marnus's desperate, ugly appeal

The ball clearly bounced before reaching Labuschagne. (Fox Cricket)

Marnus Labsuchagne is rarely shy in making an appeal.

But even he seemed a little sheepish about this one.

With Josh Hazlewood having snared the crucial early wicket of Hasan Mahmud, the Australians, already well behind in the game, were hopeful of wrapping up the Bangladeshi innings quickly.

But tailender Taijul Islam was finding some sweet timing in the middle, and was profiting with some quick, elegant runs.

In the 117th over, he creamed one straight into the ground and then into the covers, where Labuschagne made a fine diving stop.

But the inner-ring livewire came up holding the ball like he'd claimed a prize at the Easter Show.

Labuschagne made a desperate appeal early on day three. (Fox Cricket)

No-one seemed particularly convinced by the appeal, but umpire Kumar Dharmasena decided to send the decision upstairs.

And sure enough, the television replays confirmed what even Marnus surely must have known — the ball had clearly bounced between the batter and fielder.

Desperate, ugly stuff from the Australians.

2. Smith's inconceivable drop

Smith dropped a sitter in the morning session. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

In a morning of serious lows for Australia, this was surely the nadir.

Steve Smith, just one take away from becoming Test cricket's all-time leading catcher, settled underneath a Taskin top edge.

The Bangladeshi tailender took his eye of the ball as he played his pull shot, and the Australian vice-captain seemed destined to carve out another piece of history.

But the ball was in and then out of Smith's usually so-reliable hands, leaving the best since Bradman looking to the heavens for some sort of explanation.

Only a matter of balls later, it was Travis Head's turn to put one down.

Head's chance was a lot more difficult, retreating at full pelt, but it was the kind of catch we've seen him take in the past.

Australia was forced to wait until after lunch to belatedly see the back of the fighting Bangladeshi tail, which added another 24 runs after those fumbles, with the tourists taking an enormous 228-run lead into the second innings of the match.

3. Hazlewood passes 300

Hazlewood became the ninth Australian to pass 300 Test wickets on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

A bright spot for the Australians in an otherwise pitch-black morning was Josh Hazlewood.

Playing his first international cricket since October last year, the big fast bowler ran in admirably all innings, looking amongst the fittest and most disciplined of his teammates as he returned figures of 6-89.

His fifth wicket of the innings, which was earnt by nicking off the excellent Mehidy, was his 300th in Test cricket.

He was the ninth Australian to reach the milestone, and after picking up the wicket of Ebadot Hossain to finish off the Bangladeshi innings, moved within nine wickets of Brett Lee on Australia's all-time leaderboard.

How high can Hazlewood get?

Well, Lee (310) is certainly in his crosshairs, as is Mitchell Johnson, who took 313 wickets during his Test career.

Then it's captain Cummins on 316 and the great DK Lillee on 355, which you'd imagine, given Hazlewood's injury record, may be a step too far.

Regardless, Hazlewood will finish his career of one of Australia's finest.

Not that that will be of any consolation to the Australian today.

4. Jake's horror homecoming

With 23 runs, Jake Weatherald was Australia's second-highest run scorer in the first innings, an accolade that carries as much credibility as being the English bowler with the best economy rate during the last Ashes.

But through almost all of his 37-ball, 56-minute stay at the crease, he looked skittish and nervous and wholly unsuited to opening the batting at Test level.

It made his second innings all the more crucial personally, even without accounting for the perilous situation Australia found themselves in, over 200 runs in arrears.

How disappointing then, that Weatherald seemingly learned nothing from his first-innings failure, playing with an angled bat outside off with minimal foot movement to be dismissed bowled off the inside edge by Hasan Mahmud.

The ball was too close to play a cut to, he still attempted it and was on his way.

The dismissal raises more uncomfortable questions for Australia's selectors, about whether they stick or twist ahead of a very busy 12 months.

5. Smith reviews before being given out

Smith surely set a new record for the fastest review on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Steve Smith might have got away with one in the first innings, admitting that he hit the ball on its way through to Litton Das.

He got away with that one, but he was going to make doubly sure that he wouldn't be dismissed when a similar event happened when he was on just three runs in the second innings.

The ball beat the outside edge from a superb Ebadot delivery, and umpire Kumar Dharmasena wasted no time in raising the finger after hearing an edge.

Not quick enough for Smith though, who was shaking his head and reviewing before the umpire even put his finger up.

Dharmasena did nod at Smith, in his defence, but even so, it was an odd and extraordinarily self-consciously performative action.

It was not necessarily a surprise that Smith, never one to go willingly from the middle, was so quick to review, but he was proven to be vindicated, the sound coming from hitting the ground with his bat.

6. Warner puts the mockers on 'the Marnus of old'

Labuschagne departed after prematurely glowing praise from a former teammate in the commentary box. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

One of the Australians in desperate need of a big score, Marnus Labuschagne began his innings like he was cripplingly aware of just that, scratchy and anxious, struggling for any sort of rhythm.

But things were slowly improving, with the idiosyncratic first drop playing a few nice drives through the covers and finding some stability in his stance.

On commentary for Fox Cricket, David Warner was glowing in his praise for Labuschagne.

Even at the time, it felt like the former Australia opener was both jumping the gun and tempting fate.

“He’s confident in his game, he’s hitting the ball well ... now he’s in, he looks like the Marnus of old," Warner said while comparing images of Labuschagne's stance early in his innings against footage from after he had found some form.

"He’s confident, he’s got his whole rhythm back. And it’s exciting to see, and I’m happy for him.

" I really hope he goes on with it, and he'll be able to go back today and say 'I feel good, what was it?' And hopefully he can identify that. "

Labuschagne added just one more run after Warner's glowing review, being promptly yorked by spinner Taijul, the Australian playing all around a straight one and departing for 31.

World.title: Resources Minister King weighs in on WA GST furore
World.content:
Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King has slammed as "unbalanced, highly speculative and clearly incorrect" an interim report that recommended a cut to Western Australia's share of the GST, reassuring voters that the Labor government was committed to supporting the resource-rich state.

Minister King was speaking a day after state Premier Roger Cook called the Productivity Commission report on GST distribution an "attack on Western Australians", and dubbed its authors "east-coast clowns".

"I want to make it clear to all Western Australians that the Albanese Labor government has your back," she said today as Labor officially launched its campaign for the hotly contested suburban seat of Secret Harbour, south of Perth.

" We will always ensure Western Australia gets its fair share of the GST, we will always support Western Australia's ambitions to be the resources capital. "

The explosive report, which was released on Friday, recommended the government scrap 2018 changes to how the goods and services tax was carved up among the states, saying Western Australia was the only state or territory to benefit from it and that it was a "costly mistake".

GST alarm bells ringing in the west Premier Roger Cook said "east coast clowns" attacked Western Australia's federal GST deal. It set alarm bells ringing in WA government offices, literally, as state political reporter Keane Bourke witnessed.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose government has endorsed and extended the deal to at least 2029, has said that WA would "get [its] fair share" of GST but signalled he would wait for the final report in December to comment on specifics.

Cook says he has PM's assurances

Minister King said Mr Albanese had assured Mr Cook that there would be no change to the current arrangements.

Minister King said the Productivity Commission's report was speculating about things "that won't happen". (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

"The report itself is not only unbalanced, it is highly speculative and is clearly incorrect. It fails to take account of the enormous contribution Western Australia and Western Australia's resources industry provides to the whole of the nation," she said.

At the same Secret Harbour event, Mr Cook also said he had the prime minister's assurances that the GST deal would remain.

Mr Cook says he has assurances from the prime minister about the GST deal. (ABC News: Lauren Smith )

"He knows that Western Australia is the engine room of the national economy," Mr Cook said.

" And that's why he's backing our team and he's back in our state and he's backing our situation when it comes to the GST. "

The deal struck by then-treasurer Scott Morrison ensures WA gets a bigger slice of GST revenue every year than it would under the national formula, which is meant to give more money per person to states with the highest need and lowest financial means.

The formula has always been contentious, but became particularly so in WA when successive mining booms made it by far the richest state in the federation, resulting in very low GST relativities because the formula assessed the state as very high means.

Mr Cook's government, however, has maintained that changing the GST distribution would unfairly punish WA for its success, with state Treasurer Rita Saffioti saying that unravelling the deal would unfairly disadvantage the state.

World.title: Charity drive charges on despite boggy conditions
World.content:
Torrential rains and flooded roads have not deterred more than 70 cars from taking part in this year's Variety Bash — though the wet did cause a major detour.

The annual event, which raises money for children's charity Variety SA, was originally set for a route from Mildura to Gawler, via Queensland and far north South Australia.

But with outback roads still underwater after record-breaking rains in May, the route was changed to be entirely in SA — what the charity called a "pivot to Pirie".

Bash entrants have been raising money for children experiencing sickness, disadvantage, or living with disability. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

Kicking off at Gawler on August 8, the drivers turned the usually 200-kilometre trip to Port Pirie into a 2,304km trek, via Kimba, Streaky Bay, Port Lincoln, and more.

The change took a "monumental effort", said event chair Darren Greatrex.

"This wasn't supposed to happen this year. We were always going to come to the West Coast next year," he said.

The cars will need to visit an industrial car wash once the bash is over. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

"But 12 weeks ago, we realised we couldn't get to our original destination, which was Birdsville, just because of the volume of water up there.

"Not easy to do with 300 crazy people behind me and rolling into these small towns, and so it's been a monumental effort to do a total flip of the bash.

"[But] we got there and we've had an absolute ball."

A wet road ahead

Despite the bash kicking off just as a major weather event reached the state, Mr Greatrex said the drivers held up "surprisingly well".

Travelling along a diverted route due to flooding on the Birdsville track, rally entrants still found plenty of mud. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

"When we started and left Gawler, the clouds opened up and didn't stop for about 72 hours," he said.

" It threw us into a little bit of disarray, but the farmers out there loved it. But not so good for our bashers who've been swagging for the last seven nights. "

With some particularly soft — and underwater — roads along the way, there is a car wash or two in the future of the 72 cars taking part.

Late August rains provided some particularly soft roads. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

Over the past 12 months, the 231 bash entrants have been raising money for children experiencing sickness, disadvantage, or living with disability, funding more than $480,000 in grants delivered during the eight-day drive.

"They get the opportunity to let their hair down and have a week away and celebrate all the hard work, but also then they get to see the impact of that hard work and where that money goes," Mr Greatrex said.

These colourful characters travelled more than $2,000km on a charity run that raised over $2 million. (Supplied: Variety/Keryn Stevens)

"Some of the grants have been substantial, and it just makes a huge difference to people with disabilities and special needs to just have a much better life."

Grants delivered include $150,000 each for all-abilities playgrounds at Penong Primary School and Port Lincoln Primary School, and funding for sensory equipment, scholarships, and sports facilities in several towns.

Port Lincoln Primary School received a grant to fund an all-abilities playground. (ABC News: Luke Lay)

Port Lincoln Primary School principal Kathy Davison said the grant was "incredible" for the community.

"We had a playground removed and now we can reinstate one for students with disabilities and all abled students. It's great," she said.

South Australian Variety Bash rally driver Sandra Lukin has been taking part in the annual run for 20 years. (Jodie Hamilton)

This year the SA Bash was able to raise just over $2 million, and seeing that money bring joy to kid's faces is what keeps rally goers coming back.

"This is my 20th bash and including this year of fundraising, it's just over $1.3 million [we've raised]," Sandra Lukin said.

"This year, to see how much has come back onto Eyre Peninsula in the way of grants and helping kids and schools and everything, that's what warms all our hearts and keeps us going for next year."

World.title: Fraud officials charge another over alleged $5 million NDIS dishonesty plot
World.content:
A 38-year-old Adelaide man has been charged over an alleged $5 million dishonesty plot against the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).

The man, who is a director of a registered NDIS provider, was arrested and charged by Australian Federal Police (AFP) officers at Adelaide Airport on Friday as he prepared to leave the country.

It follows an investigation by the federal government's Fraud Fusion Taskforce (FFT), which began in March in response to the NDIA's finding that unauthorised access to protected records of NDIS participants had taken place.

In June, a 48-year-old woman was the first person to face charges over the same alleged plot after FFT investigators searched premises in Adelaide's northern suburbs, including a business in Prospect and homes in Mawson Lakes and Blakeview.

The AFP charged the man with one count of dealing with the proceeds of crime, fraudulently claimed from the NDIS.

He was also charged with one count of soliciting protected agency information from a National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) staff member.

The offences carry maximum penalties of 25 years's and 2 years's imprisonment, respectively, according to the AFP.

The man has been remanded in custody and is expected to appear before the Adelaide Magistrates Court on Monday.

World.title: First H5N1 bird flu death recorded in Phillip Island penguins
World.content:
A Phillip Island penguin has died from H5N1 bird flu in the first detection among the island's little penguin colony.

The new detection is one of three announced by Victoria's chief veterinary officer, Graeme Cooke, on Saturday.

It comes ahead of plans to begin vaccinating the Phillip Island penguins against the virus on Monday.

The Phillip Island penguin parade is a major attraction that draws national and international visitors.

Authorities found the dead penguin away from the area where the penguin parade takes place.

A great crested tern found in Lakes Entrance in East Gippsland and another in Dromana, on the Victorian Mornington Peninsula, also died of bird flu.

It brings the total number of bird flu cases in Victoria to 74, but Dr Cooke said there were likely more birds sick or dead in the state.

"We … recognise that this is distressing for Victorians to see and to hear," he said.

Dr James Todd says the latest bird flu detections could lead to large losses of wildlife. (ABC News)

Victoria's chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said the latest cases were significant because the areas hosted several at-risk bird species that would congregate for the upcoming spring breeding season.

"It's highly likely the conditions are conducive for H5N1 spread in those areas that would lead to large losses of wildlife," Mr Cooke said.

"There's little we can do to minimise that impact.

"Having said that, we are working as hard as we can to protect at-risk species and to continue to respond to detections as they come on hand."

The vaccination of Phillip Island's penguins against bird flu will continue as planned. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

No halt to vaccinations

He said the recently announced vaccination program of the little penguin colonies on Phillip Island and St Kilda will begin on Monday despite the detection there.

"We know that little penguins are iconic and highly valued by Victorians, and for that reason, we are working as a priority to protect those communities," he said.

Phillip Island Nature Park, which operates the penguin parade, will also remain open while the vaccination program is rolled out.

"We are rolling out the vaccination program as quickly and urgently as was possible after the federal authorities released the permits and released the vaccines to the jurisdictions," Dr Cooke said.

"We are very concerned … about this detection, but it does represent early surveillance and early vigilance."

He said large groupings of penguins were historically more susceptible to infection.

"At this time of year, the penguins are not at their full capacity in terms of numbers, so it's a good time to start vaccinating," Dr Cooke said.

World.title: Why the Hawks and Pies both won out of their historic draw
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Why the Hawks and Pies both won out of their historic draw Andrew Wu August 16, 2026 — 2:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

This was the draw where there were two winners. On a night the same two clubs played in their second draw in the same season for the first time in VFL/AFL history, both Collingwood and Hawthorn had reason to celebrate – even though they could not sing the song. The Hawks salvaged two precious points, which keeps them in control of their fate, though they did much wrong. For the second time this season, Dylan Moore had a shot after the siren against the Magpies. AFL Photos Even if Dylan Moore’s shot on the siren was not heroically cleared on the line by Sam Swadling, it would not have changed the equation for the Hawks. They still need to beat West Coast next week to remain in the top four.



There is a silver lining to the two points “lost” and the slide to fourth. A qualifying final against Fremantle in Perth, as seems likely, would spare them a preliminary final in the west when they would not have the safety net of a second chance. They will need to improve significantly in the next three weeks to challenge Fremantle, Sydney or any of the other leading flag fancies. In a mid-August encounter that had the feel of a final, the Hawks fell short everywhere but the scoreboard. Moore after his shot on goal after the siren was spoiled on the line by Sam Swadling - reducing the Hawks and Pies to a draw for the second time this season. Fox Footy Jarman Impey papered over many cracks. Their midfield had individual highlights – like Josh Ward’s two quick goals to start the last quarter – but was beaten, losing clearance by 12 and giving up big scores from their losses at stoppage. It remains a weakness, as it was on preliminary final night last year.



Hawks pair Jai Newcombe and Josh Ward. Getty Images Tom Barrass, 30, is playing like a defender who has aged four years in four months. He is not inspiring confidence in the air, and is out of the game once the ball hits the deck. He made Tim Membrey look like an Olympic sprinter in one ground-ball contest. Barrass, who has strained a hamstring this year, is not carrying an injury, Mitchell said, but his coach concedes he is in a trough. “If you’re full-back, [and] you make a couple of mistakes, they usually cost goals, and he had a couple of those tonight,” Mitchell said. “He’s not physically carrying anything, but he’s he’s just not been quite as consistent as he’d like to be. I don’t think everyone plays well every week. It’s just the difference is when you’re the full-back, everyone notices because your errors cost goals.”



This was both one of the games of the season, and its most bizarre. In April, scores were locked at 93 apiece. This time it was 92 each. The final 70 seconds after Roan Steele’s levelling point was full of drama and what ifs. Lloyd Meek had his back to Harry Morrison, who was streaming up the MCC wing, then coughed up a lasso free kick with his handball. Ed Allan, superb for much of the night, will wonder why he bombed the ball long to several Hawks, instead of handballing to Nick Daicos on the run. Jack Gunston had the chance to send the ball to the goal square for his teammates to rush a behind when Collingwood’s defence was not organised. Pinpointing Dylan Moore, albeit in a difficult spot, was still a satisfactory result. Sam Mitchell and the Hawks have plenty to work out before the finals. AFL Photos



Moore was the saviour in April when he kicked a goal after the siren to draw the game for the Hawks. Here, his shot from 45 metres out on the boundary went across the face of goal and was touched on the line. If he had his time again, he may have erred to miss on the near side, as Gunston had done minutes earlier, the precious metres saved being the difference between a score or a spoil. Such was the drama, even Mitchell could not compute what was happening. “Do we want a draw, or do we need to win this game?” Mitchell said. “It was quite an odd moment. When you’ve been in the game a long time, you sort of feel like you’ve seen most things, but [I] certainly haven’t seen that.” Rarely has a coach celebrated a draw with as much gusto as Craig McRae, who was fist pumping the crowd moments after Swadling’s game-saving heroics.



Craig McRae pumped his fist after the Magpies came away with a draw. Getty Images There was good reason for McRae to respond in such a manner, even if the result officially consigned the Pies to the long route to the premiership cup. Despite a 23 including nine players who have played fewer than 50 games, the Pies served it up to one of the leading flag contenders. Missing premiership heroes Brayden Maynard, Jeremy Howe, Steele Sidebottom and skipper Darcy Moore just to name a few, the Pies rescued a game that appeared gone three times in the second half. The most stunning act was saved for after the final siren when Swadling, in just his seventh game, out-jumped Hawthorn triple towers Mitch Lewis, Mabior Chol and Lloyd Meek to prevent a match-winning point.



This may be one of the youngest sides the Pies have fielded under McRae, but they still have the muscle memory to do the right thing at the right time. As Moore took his kick with seconds left, Jack Crisp was one of the senior players organising teammates so they would be in position to spoil a short kick. The attention to detail was so meticulous they made sure players were coming from the correct angle so that any spoil would send the ball away from goal. View post on X “I think everyone got the gist of what we had to do,” Crisp said. “The big boys on their fellas, just making sure were coming from the fence side.



“As you saw, our celebration at the end, our fight to get back in it after we were up, and then we just got Hawthorn back in it. They had some serious momentum. To fight back to get back in front again and give ourselves a chance, it’s good – it’s a great group.” McRae gave the Magpies’ reserves players a stern talking to in June, warning them time was running out for several to make their mark. A young Collingwood side lost no fans on Saturday night. Getty Images Within two months, youngsters such as Swadling, Allan, Harvey Harrison, Will Hayes and Charlie West have taken big leaps. It’s not quite an overnight rebuild, but the future is looking brighter for the Pies’ list than it appeared mid-season. The Pies have now won seven of nine since the King’s Birthday long weekend. Winning five knockout finals in a row to win the flag is improbable, but they are a team no rival will want to face in September.



“There’s a spirit in the whole squad right now,” McRae said. “Winning creates an energy.” Related Article AFL 2026 Why ‘one of the nicest blokes you’ll meet in footy’ is set to face MRO heat With an MCG wildcard final guaranteed, and no prospect of breaking into the top six, the Pies now have the luxury of managing their team in the final home-and-away round when they host Brisbane off a six-day break on Friday night. McRae said Maynard, Patrick Lipinski, Howe and Harry Perryman are all in contention to return from injury. Veteran Scott Pendlebury is likely to be one who will be rested after playing off six days coming back from Perth. “I was pretty deliberate with [high-performance boss] Jarrod Wade that we’ll manage them if they need to be managed, not just for the sake of it,” McRae said.



“If they’re really sore, and they can’t perform well, they won’t play next week. But right now, there’s an energy everyone wants to play, so that’ll be interesting how that plays out.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Why ‘one of the nicest blokes you’ll meet in footy’ is set to face MRO heat
World.content:
Melbourne forward Jacob van Rooyen is “one of the nicest blokes you’ll meet in footy”, according to Demons premiership star Bayley Fritsch.

But even with that glowing character reference, van Rooyen is in grave danger of missing Melbourne’s first final since 2023 after an ugly hit that ended Aliir Aliir’s 200th game prematurely.

The Demons’ clinical 76-point demolition of Port Adelaide was overshadowed by the van Rooyen incident, in which he leapt in the air and made heavy contact with his hand to Aliir’s head.

World.title: Watch: Socceroos star announces new club in epic Michael Jackson-themed video
World.content:
SportSoccerSocceroos Watch: Socceroos star announces new club in epic Michael Jackson-themed video Roy Ward August 16, 2026 — 12:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Socceroos star Nestory Irankunda and Sporting Lisbon have lent into his love of Michael Jackson in a spectacular video posted to social media announcing his official move to the club. The Portuguese giants released the video late on Saturday evening (AEST) showing dancers performing to Michael Jackson’s Bad in a parking garage before Irankunda emerges from a car wearing a glittering Jackson glove. He then dances with the group before the lights flicker, and he emerges in Sporting’s famous green-and-white home jersey. Irankunda made headlines at AAMI Park earlier this year when he scored in a friendly against Curacao and, in a pre-arranged move, a photographer handed him a glittering glove and he performed a Jackson-style dance move.



He also brought out the dance moves during a photoshoot for Good Weekend in the lead-up to the World Cup. Big clubs will often produce videos for their major signings, but most involve a player sitting on a couch or perhaps performing some tricks with a ball. To have the 20-year-old Irankunda dancing is an eye-catching way to introduce the Adelaide United product. Nestory Irankunda throws on a silver glove and performs a Michael Jackson dance after scoring against Curacao. Getty Images The video also confirms Irankunda has signed with Sporting for five years, while reports in Europe suggest his transfer from English Championship club Watford was for €16 million ($26 million) plus add-ons that could take it to €18 million ($29.5 million). The Socceroos forward was greeted by droves of fans and media when he arrived in Lisbon last week to do his physical and finalise the move.



Irankunda has had a mercurial off-season, scoring against Turkey in the Socceroos’ 2-0 win at the FIFA World Cup, and performing strongly in the other matches as the team went out in a heart-breaking penalty shootout loss to Egypt in the round of 32. Editor's pick A-League Men The 12-year sacrifice behind Socceroo’s life-changing decision Mentor and Socceroos teammate Awer Mabil praised Irankunda’s move to Lisbon and urged his dear friend to continue to be himself, advice he must have taken in agreeing to the MJ video. At Sporting, Irankunda will have the chance to play in the UEFA Champions League, and in high-profile league matches against Portugal’s other leading sides, Porto and Benfica. “It’s a very good move for him,” Mabil said after his own move home to Melbourne City.



“It’s a perfect club also for him to take that next step, and then from there on he will make a bigger step for sure. “You are playing a game very three days, so you have to manage your body well and secondly, you might have one or two bad games, but that doesn’t mean you should change who you are. “You just keep working hard. He will learn these things. There is much more attention now but my advice is not to change, keep being himself as that is what has got him there.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: How our region cracked the secret to the ultimate luxury stay
World.content:
InspirationTravel tips How our region cracked the secret to the ultimate luxury stay Jane Richards August 16, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Flat whites, the pavlova, Crowded House and even the much-loved late Sam Neill: Australia and New Zealand have a long history of inventing, claiming and adopting each other’s inventions and heroes. History, character, and adventure … Holme Station Homestead. Guests can dine alone or together. But when it comes to luxury lodges, New Zealand may win the origin contest thanks to its long history of creating spectacular getaways such as the iconic Huka Lodge in Taupo on the North Island, established – albeit on a more rustic scale – in 1925, and Blanket Bay Lodge in Glenorchy on the South Island. Of course, Australia has well and truly joined the party with groups like Beckons (formerly Baillie Lodges), which has built a reputation for standout properties like Southern Ocean Lodge, Longitude 131 at Uluru, and Capella Lodge on Lord Howe Island – (plus they’ve now also hooked Huka). The truth is both countries excel at providing this type of world-class exclusive getaway that is increasingly difficult to replicate, mainly because luxury like this is not simple, no matter how much money and expertise you throw at it.



Tom Gibson, an Australian who recently moved to Queenstown on New Zealand’s South Island – a gateway to some of the world’s finest luxury lodges – has been involved in luxury stays across the world, including Huka, Silky Oaks Lodge in the Daintree and Clayoquot Wilderness Lodge on Vancouver Island. 



Guests also expect the culinary and service standards of the world’s best hotels, delivered in a much more intimate, tailored way, plus real access to world-class or unique local experiences. “This could be fly-fishing, wine, golf, hiking, or cultural experiences nearby.” And another clincher? They must also be able to connect guests to something special beyond their boundaries. History meets luxury at Holme Station. Suite success … Holme Station Homestead is a new addition to New Zealand’s acclaimed luxury-lodge catalogue. One newly opened New Zealand property that has cemented a place in this true luxury realm is Holme Station Homestead, a beautifully restored 1912 South Canterbury sheep station set on more than six hectares of private gardens and surrounded by farmland just two and a half hours from Christchurch. As well as providing all the must-haves such as luxurious suites, an onsite chef, expansive views and privacy, it is carving a place in lodge luxury by also offering unique adventures in the alpine landscapes of the Mackenzie and Waitaki districts, home to Aoraki/Mount Cook, turquoise glacial lakes, and the Alps 2 Ocean Cycle Trail.



Guests can arrive at Holme Station by chopper if they choose and visit the Southern Alps’ highest altitude whisky hut – with optional hot tub. They can also enjoy a round of eco golf, teeing off at almost 2000 metres; ski on private fields, or try fly-fishing in glacier-fed river systems. On the walk to view ancient rock drawings. But one of Holme Station’s most amazing exclusive guest outings is a guided hike to see charcoal drawings of the extinct Giant Eagle (or Haast’s eagle), located on private land. Related Article Luxury holidays Australia’s highest non-alpine lodge will leave you on a high This formidable bird, believed to have been the biggest eagle to have ever existed and weighing up to 18 kilograms, dined out on the also gargantuan moa birds which once stomped across this island nation.



Guests can also hike to the nearby Valley of Moa to view 700 to 1000-year-old drawings of the moa. World.title: ‘Trying to be a superstar’: The mindset shift behind Ashcroft’s latest exploits
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Trying to be a superstar’: The mindset shift behind Ashcroft’s latest exploits Nick Wright August 15, 2026 — 10:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Chris Fagan was desperate to avoid the fanfare as he passed Leigh Matthews as the longest-tenured Lions coach, but it was fitting his side put in the sort of physical performance that would have made his great mate proud. The two-time reigning premiers were forced into an arm wrestle by the Suns for much of the 14.11 (95) to 6.17 (53) triumph at the Gabba, in a Q-Clash far from the lopsided affair of last year’s 53-point semi-final demolition. Will Ashcroft was at his brilliant best against the Suns. Getty Images But ultimately, the class of Brisbane’s all-conquering group stood up when it counted, as Will Ashcroft clinched his second Marcus Ashcroft Medal – named in honour of his father – with a goal, 31 disposals and four clearances. It continued a rich vein of form for the 22-year-old, who overcame an inconsistent – by his standards – first half the year, to pass the 30 disposals milestone in his past nine games.



“I think he’s taken a bit of pressure off himself, to be honest. I think he was trying too hard to live up to the reputation of being a two-time Norm Smith medallist, and was probably trying to be a superstar,” Fagan said. Related Article AFL 2026 As Fagan surpasses Matthews, he has a mission. But it’s not another title “He’s gone back to having a narrow focus every time that he plays and has simplified things, and that’s helped his form.” Fagan had already surpassed Matthews’ 142 wins as Lions coach last week against the Hawks, and on Saturday night went beyond the legend of the early 2000s for most games at the helm (238). And while Brisbane have established a reputation as one of the AFL’s most lethal attacking outfits – second in the competition for points scored heading into the contest – it was a renewed focus on their defence that ultimately reaped the rewards against their M1 rivals.



The Lions ranked last in the league for average tackles per game (48) before round 23 began, but affected 69 – the majority coming before the final quarter, and including 18 inside 50 – to register the 15th win of their campaign and just about secure a top-four berth following Adelaide’s defeat to Fremantle. “It felt like a much closer game; the margin was 42 points, but it felt a tough game all night. It was on their terms in the first-half, but I liked we didn’t get the game played the way we wanted it and were still able to win,” Fagan said. “We know that [pressure] is important to us, we’ve just got to bring it. That’s not system-based, that’s just energy-based because we haven’t changed our system at all, but we get different results in different weeks. View post on X “We have to try and tap into that energy.”



Neither side were able to generate much momentum in the opening half – heading into quarter-time locked at 2.3 (15) apiece, before the Lions slowly but surely began to win the moments. Despite the Suns dominating the clearance battle early – Ned Moyle, Matt Rowell, Noah Anderson and Touk Miller combining for 24 clearances and providing plenty of chances for their forward line – their inability to execute inside 50 plagued them. While Jed Walter came up with two strong finishes, the Gold Coast’s 52 entries compared to the Lions’ 45 did little to impact the scoreboard – Brisbane’s finishing with an 84.4 per cent efficiency inside 50 compared to the Suns’ 51.9. View post on X “There were ample opportunities. Inside 50s – win, clearances – win, contested possession – win, post-contested possession – win. You know what they won? Polish,” Suns coach Damien Hardwick said.



“I thought we had really good opportunities to score, we just made it look hard.” Ryan Lester kept Christian Petracca limited to just 12 touches, while Ben King could only muster a pair of majors as Harris Andrews made life difficult for the man who is set to move to the Hawks in 2027. In contrast, once the Lions got a sniff, they put the foot down. Dayne Zorko was typically composed in directing counterattacking traffic – even drawing a 50-metre free before striking for one of the goals of the match – while Zac Bailey (27 disposals), and Ashcroft brothers carried that momentum downfield. Will Ashcroft won the Marcus Ashcroft Medal, named in honour of his father (left). AFL Photos The forwards were eager to benefit from that work – Logan Morris backing up his seven-goal haul against the Suns earlier this year with another four, while Oscar Allen (two goals) and Eric Hipwood (one) joined him on the scoresheet and offered the strongest glimpse yet into what threat the three talls could present come September.



Levi Ashcroft’s increased involvement in the past two weeks will undoubtedly please Fagan, backing up his 27 touches against Hawthorn with another 26 and a goal against the Suns. Ahead of Lachie Neale’s likely departure at season’s end, the 19-year-old Ashcroft will have every chance to stamp his claim to the two-time Brownlow medallist’s job next year – particularly in the absence of Hugh McCluggage, who Fagan confirmed during the week would not been seen on field until the finals, rather than be rushed back from a calf concern against Collingwood next week. World.title: Walsh suffers World Cup blow in Broncos’ demolition. It wasn’t the most heartbreaking scene
World.content:
Brisbane 6 New Zealand 40 SportNRLNRL 2026 Walsh suffers World Cup blow in Broncos’ demolition. It wasn’t the most heartbreaking scene Nick Wright August 15, 2026 — 9:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Reece Walsh’s hopes of retaining his Kangaroos’ jumper for the Rugby League World Cup have been dealt a savage blow, after falling victim to a hip drop tackle in the Broncos’ 40-6 capitulation against the Warriors. The Brisbane fullback was caught awkwardly in a tackle by fullback Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad as he sought to attack the line, leading to the latter being sent to the sin bin. Reece Walsh lies injured during the round 24 match between the Broncos and the Warriors. Getty Images While Walsh made to hobble off after the incident inside the opening 20 minutes, by which time New Zealand had already scored with Jacob Laban and Chanel Harris-Tavita, he attempted to make one final play with his under-siege outfit on the hunt. It proved a costly decision, as the mercurial No.1 threw an intercept pass for Alofiana Khan-Pereira to streak the length of the field at score, before Walsh eventually made his way up the tunnel to receive treatment on a high ankle sprain.



Walsh had surged into Australian colours for last year’s Ashes tour in England on the back of his remarkable finals campaign en route to the Broncos’ drought-breaking premiership. Despite Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters suggesting the 24-year-old was his preferred custodian, his inconsistent form in a Brisbane side languishing in second-last already had him facing an uphill battle to feature in the World Cup on home soil. Loading Now, he may get no chance to push his case – or even take the field – if scans confirm something sinister has occurred. The longer Walsh’s absence went on, the more glaring it became his presence was missed, with the Warriors scoring twice after Brisbane failed to defuse attacking bombs – Nicoll-Klokstad and Dallin Watene-Zelezniak both beneficiaries of the Broncos’ indecisiveness.



Broncos coach Michael Maguire was unable to provide further information post-game whether Walsh would be ruled out for a period of time. Metcalf agony The sight was heartbreaking to witness. As Luke Metcalf struck his conversion attempt of Khan-Pereira’s try, he admittedly reached for his hamstring and cut a distraught figure. Loading The Warriors’ halfback has endured a gut-wrenching career on the injury-front. This had been just his fourth appearance of the year after tearing his hamstring in April, which came just two games into his comeback from a ruptured ACL suffered in 2025.



At the time of the latter incident, the soon-to-be Dragons recruit was on a collision course for a shock Dally M Medal. Metcalf came into the Warriors’ side last week after Te Maire Martin suffered his own hamstring issue at training, and even he had only taken the No.7 jumper after Tanah Boyd’s season was brought to an end to undergo a knee reconstruction. Metcalf’s two-try heroics against the Panthers was poised to create a massive headache for coach Andrew Webster when Martin was ready to make his return – expected to be in round 26. He looked strong early on Saturday night, laying on quick hands to give Harris-Tavita the chance to produce some classy footwork to score. Now, to keep the Warriors hopes of a top two finish alive, Webster needs an answer. “I’m sure he’s hurting, but he’s a good teammate – at halftime he joined the team. He’s never done a hamstring kicking goals, and he hasn’t done that hamstring for a long time,” Webster said.



“I don’t think Te Maire will be ready next week, but we’ll wait and see – he might be. We’ll worry about that next week.” Will Reynolds get his swan song? Broncos captain Adam Reynolds is in a race against the clock to get an NRL swan song before he sails into retirement. But given the way his side’s attack failed to fire in his absence, there will be a growing argument that the man who looms as his successor should be given the rest of the campaign to find his feet. Brisbane confirmed this week Reynolds, who missed last week’s clash with the Dolphins after suffering a concussion against the Knights, had sustained a calf injury at training, and would be monitored on a week-to-week basis before determining a comeback timeline.



Related Article Parramatta 32 North Queensland 30

NRL 2026 Late drama as Eels pip Cowboys to keep rivals’ finals hopes alive Until then, Tom Duffy has been given the reins alongside Ezra Mam, but the pair – aside from an early onslaught against the Dolphins, only for the Broncos to cough up a 24-0 lead – have largely failed to fire and will take time to blossom as a partnership. The Broncos were tackled 41 times inside the Warriors’ 20-metre zone, yet could only muster a try through Xavier Willison at close range. In contrast, New Zealand only needed 20 tackles in Brisbane’s red zone to cross six times – with only Khan-Pereira’s try from long range, as centres Ali Leiataua and Leka Halasima crossed late. Reynolds delivered this club a first premiership in 19 years, and deserves to go out on his terms. But with their season well and truly over, perhaps the new-look halves pairing should be given time to gel, ahead of Jonah Pezet’s arrival to add another contender to the mix. Bumper Barnett



He won’t be arriving at Red Hill for several months yet, but Mitchell Barnett has given Broncos fans a glimpse at what he can bring to the struggling glamour club once he begins his three-year deal from 2027. The 32-year-old has been brought to Brisbane to replace his outgoing NSW State of Origin teammate Payne Haas, and he won the match-up battle between the pair at Suncorp Stadium. While Haas, who will leave for South Sydney at season’s end, was well-contained – as he largely has been in the past month, Barnett embodied the toughness Maguire is determined to inject back into his flailing squad. He played out the entire first half – finishing with 88 running metres and 22 tackles for just the one miss – while Haas was limited to just 49 metres from six carries. World.title: Why the Hawks and Pies both won out of their historic draw
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Why the Hawks and Pies both won out of their historic draw Andrew Wu August 16, 2026 — 2:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

This was the draw where there were two winners. On a night the same two clubs played in their second draw in the same season for the first time in VFL/AFL history, both Collingwood and Hawthorn had reason to celebrate – even though they could not sing the song. The Hawks salvaged two precious points, which keeps them in control of their fate, though they did much wrong. For the second time this season, Dylan Moore had a shot after the siren against the Magpies. AFL Photos Even if Dylan Moore’s shot on the siren was not heroically cleared on the line by Sam Swadling, it would not have changed the equation for the Hawks. They still need to beat West Coast next week to remain in the top four.



There is a silver lining to the two points “lost” and the slide to fourth. A qualifying final against Fremantle in Perth, as seems likely, would spare them a preliminary final in the west when they would not have the safety net of a second chance. They will need to improve significantly in the next three weeks to challenge Fremantle, Sydney or any of the other leading flag fancies. In a mid-August encounter that had the feel of a final, the Hawks fell short everywhere but the scoreboard. Moore after his shot on goal after the siren was spoiled on the line by Sam Swadling - reducing the Hawks and Pies to a draw for the second time this season. Fox Footy Jarman Impey papered over many cracks. Their midfield had individual highlights – like Josh Ward’s two quick goals to start the last quarter – but was beaten, losing clearance by 12 and giving up big scores from their losses at stoppage. It remains a weakness, as it was on preliminary final night last year.



Hawks pair Jai Newcombe and Josh Ward. Getty Images Tom Barrass, 30, is playing like a defender who has aged four years in four months. He is not inspiring confidence in the air, and is out of the game once the ball hits the deck. He made Tim Membrey look like an Olympic sprinter in one ground-ball contest. Barrass, who has strained a hamstring this year, is not carrying an injury, Mitchell said, but his coach concedes he is in a trough. “If you’re full-back, [and] you make a couple of mistakes, they usually cost goals, and he had a couple of those tonight,” Mitchell said. “He’s not physically carrying anything, but he’s he’s just not been quite as consistent as he’d like to be. I don’t think everyone plays well every week. It’s just the difference is when you’re the full-back, everyone notices because your errors cost goals.”



This was both one of the games of the season, and its most bizarre. In April, scores were locked at 93 apiece. This time it was 92 each. The final 70 seconds after Roan Steele’s levelling point was full of drama and what ifs. Lloyd Meek had his back to Harry Morrison, who was streaming up the MCC wing, then coughed up a lasso free kick with his handball. Ed Allan, superb for much of the night, will wonder why he bombed the ball long to several Hawks, instead of handballing to Nick Daicos on the run. Jack Gunston had the chance to send the ball to the goal square for his teammates to rush a behind when Collingwood’s defence was not organised. Pinpointing Dylan Moore, albeit in a difficult spot, was still a satisfactory result. Sam Mitchell and the Hawks have plenty to work out before the finals. AFL Photos



Moore was the saviour in April when he kicked a goal after the siren to draw the game for the Hawks. Here, his shot from 45 metres out on the boundary went across the face of goal and was touched on the line. If he had his time again, he may have erred to miss on the near side, as Gunston had done minutes earlier, the precious metres saved being the difference between a score or a spoil. Such was the drama, even Mitchell could not compute what was happening. “Do we want a draw, or do we need to win this game?” Mitchell said. “It was quite an odd moment. When you’ve been in the game a long time, you sort of feel like you’ve seen most things, but [I] certainly haven’t seen that.” Rarely has a coach celebrated a draw with as much gusto as Craig McRae, who was fist pumping the crowd moments after Swadling’s game-saving heroics.



Craig McRae pumped his fist after the Magpies came away with a draw. Getty Images There was good reason for McRae to respond in such a manner, even if the result officially consigned the Pies to the long route to the premiership cup. Despite a 23 including nine players who have played fewer than 50 games, the Pies served it up to one of the leading flag contenders. Missing premiership heroes Brayden Maynard, Jeremy Howe, Steele Sidebottom and skipper Darcy Moore just to name a few, the Pies rescued a game that appeared gone three times in the second half. The most stunning act was saved for after the final siren when Swadling, in just his seventh game, out-jumped Hawthorn triple towers Mitch Lewis, Mabior Chol and Lloyd Meek to prevent a match-winning point.



This may be one of the youngest sides the Pies have fielded under McRae, but they still have the muscle memory to do the right thing at the right time. As Moore took his kick with seconds left, Jack Crisp was one of the senior players organising teammates so they would be in position to spoil a short kick. The attention to detail was so meticulous they made sure players were coming from the correct angle so that any spoil would send the ball away from goal. View post on X “I think everyone got the gist of what we had to do,” Crisp said. “The big boys on their fellas, just making sure were coming from the fence side.



“As you saw, our celebration at the end, our fight to get back in it after we were up, and then we just got Hawthorn back in it. They had some serious momentum. To fight back to get back in front again and give ourselves a chance, it’s good – it’s a great group.” McRae gave the Magpies’ reserves players a stern talking to in June, warning them time was running out for several to make their mark. A young Collingwood side lost no fans on Saturday night. Getty Images Within two months, youngsters such as Swadling, Allan, Harvey Harrison, Will Hayes and Charlie West have taken big leaps. It’s not quite an overnight rebuild, but the future is looking brighter for the Pies’ list than it appeared mid-season. The Pies have now won seven of nine since the King’s Birthday long weekend. Winning five knockout finals in a row to win the flag is improbable, but they are a team no rival will want to face in September.



“There’s a spirit in the whole squad right now,” McRae said. “Winning creates an energy.” Related Article AFL 2026 Why ‘one of the nicest blokes you’ll meet in footy’ is set to face MRO heat With an MCG wildcard final guaranteed, and no prospect of breaking into the top six, the Pies now have the luxury of managing their team in the final home-and-away round when they host Brisbane off a six-day break on Friday night. McRae said Maynard, Patrick Lipinski, Howe and Harry Perryman are all in contention to return from injury. Veteran Scott Pendlebury is likely to be one who will be rested after playing off six days coming back from Perth. “I was pretty deliberate with [high-performance boss] Jarrod Wade that we’ll manage them if they need to be managed, not just for the sake of it,” McRae said.



“If they’re really sore, and they can’t perform well, they won’t play next week. But right now, there’s an energy everyone wants to play, so that’ll be interesting how that plays out.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Watch: Socceroos star announces new club in epic Michael Jackson-themed video
World.content:
SportSoccerSocceroos Watch: Socceroos star announces new club in epic Michael Jackson-themed video Roy Ward August 16, 2026 — 12:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Socceroos star Nestory Irankunda and Sporting Lisbon have lent into his love of Michael Jackson in a spectacular video posted to social media announcing his official move to the club. The Portuguese giants released the video late on Saturday evening (AEST) showing dancers performing to Michael Jackson’s Bad in a parking garage before Irankunda emerges from a car wearing a glittering Jackson glove. He then dances with the group before the lights flicker, and he emerges in Sporting’s famous green-and-white home jersey. Irankunda made headlines at AAMI Park earlier this year when he scored in a friendly against Curacao and, in a pre-arranged move, a photographer handed him a glittering glove and he performed a Jackson-style dance move.



He also brought out the dance moves during a photoshoot for Good Weekend in the lead-up to the World Cup. Big clubs will often produce videos for their major signings, but most involve a player sitting on a couch or perhaps performing some tricks with a ball. To have the 20-year-old Irankunda dancing is an eye-catching way to introduce the Adelaide United product. Nestory Irankunda throws on a silver glove and performs a Michael Jackson dance after scoring against Curacao. Getty Images The video also confirms Irankunda has signed with Sporting for five years, while reports in Europe suggest his transfer from English Championship club Watford was for €16 million ($26 million) plus add-ons that could take it to €18 million ($29.5 million). The Socceroos forward was greeted by droves of fans and media when he arrived in Lisbon last week to do his physical and finalise the move.



Irankunda has had a mercurial off-season, scoring against Turkey in the Socceroos’ 2-0 win at the FIFA World Cup, and performing strongly in the other matches as the team went out in a heart-breaking penalty shootout loss to Egypt in the round of 32. Editor's pick A-League Men The 12-year sacrifice behind Socceroo’s life-changing decision Mentor and Socceroos teammate Awer Mabil praised Irankunda’s move to Lisbon and urged his dear friend to continue to be himself, advice he must have taken in agreeing to the MJ video. At Sporting, Irankunda will have the chance to play in the UEFA Champions League, and in high-profile league matches against Portugal’s other leading sides, Porto and Benfica. “It’s a very good move for him,” Mabil said after his own move home to Melbourne City.



“It’s a perfect club also for him to take that next step, and then from there on he will make a bigger step for sure. “You are playing a game very three days, so you have to manage your body well and secondly, you might have one or two bad games, but that doesn’t mean you should change who you are. “You just keep working hard. He will learn these things. There is much more attention now but my advice is not to change, keep being himself as that is what has got him there.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: How our region cracked the secret to the ultimate luxury stay
World.content:
InspirationTravel tips How our region cracked the secret to the ultimate luxury stay Jane Richards August 16, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Flat whites, the pavlova, Crowded House and even the much-loved late Sam Neill: Australia and New Zealand have a long history of inventing, claiming and adopting each other’s inventions and heroes. History, character, and adventure … Holme Station Homestead. Guests can dine alone or together. But when it comes to luxury lodges, New Zealand may win the origin contest thanks to its long history of creating spectacular getaways such as the iconic Huka Lodge in Taupo on the North Island, established – albeit on a more rustic scale – in 1925, and Blanket Bay Lodge in Glenorchy on the South Island. Of course, Australia has well and truly joined the party with groups like Beckons (formerly Baillie Lodges), which has built a reputation for standout properties like Southern Ocean Lodge, Longitude 131 at Uluru, and Capella Lodge on Lord Howe Island – (plus they’ve now also hooked Huka). The truth is both countries excel at providing this type of world-class exclusive getaway that is increasingly difficult to replicate, mainly because luxury like this is not simple, no matter how much money and expertise you throw at it.



Tom Gibson, an Australian who recently moved to Queenstown on New Zealand’s South Island – a gateway to some of the world’s finest luxury lodges – has been involved in luxury stays across the world, including Huka, Silky Oaks Lodge in the Daintree and Clayoquot Wilderness Lodge on Vancouver Island. 



Guests also expect the culinary and service standards of the world’s best hotels, delivered in a much more intimate, tailored way, plus real access to world-class or unique local experiences. “This could be fly-fishing, wine, golf, hiking, or cultural experiences nearby.” And another clincher? They must also be able to connect guests to something special beyond their boundaries. History meets luxury at Holme Station. Suite success … Holme Station Homestead is a new addition to New Zealand’s acclaimed luxury-lodge catalogue. One newly opened New Zealand property that has cemented a place in this true luxury realm is Holme Station Homestead, a beautifully restored 1912 South Canterbury sheep station set on more than six hectares of private gardens and surrounded by farmland just two and a half hours from Christchurch. As well as providing all the must-haves such as luxurious suites, an onsite chef, expansive views and privacy, it is carving a place in lodge luxury by also offering unique adventures in the alpine landscapes of the Mackenzie and Waitaki districts, home to Aoraki/Mount Cook, turquoise glacial lakes, and the Alps 2 Ocean Cycle Trail.



Guests can arrive at Holme Station by chopper if they choose and visit the Southern Alps’ highest altitude whisky hut – with optional hot tub. They can also enjoy a round of eco golf, teeing off at almost 2000 metres; ski on private fields, or try fly-fishing in glacier-fed river systems. On the walk to view ancient rock drawings. But one of Holme Station’s most amazing exclusive guest outings is a guided hike to see charcoal drawings of the extinct Giant Eagle (or Haast’s eagle), located on private land. Guests can also hike to the nearby Valley of Moa to view 700 to 1000-year-old drawings of the moa. Both sets of drawings offer rare and moving glimpses into Aotearoa’s earliest stories, and are depicted on rock walls which once sheltered the artists, the Waitaha people.
