With Spider-Man: Brand New Day behind us, and its reveal of Sadie Sink as Jean Grey, Marvel is finally ready to officially welcome the X-Men into the MCU. At the D23 event in Anaheim yesterday, the company revealed the cast for its upcoming, untitled X-Men film, which is scheduled to hit theaters on May 5th of 2028. Though, seeing as that’s quite far into the future, we wouldn’t be surprised if that date shifted slightly before then.

In addition to Sink, the film will star Kit Connor as Scott Summers (Cyclops), Christopher Abbott as Charles Xavier (Professor X), Samara Weaving as Emma Frost, Maya Boyd as Storm, and Inde Navarrette as Rogue. Navarrette is fresh off a potentially star-making turn in the surprise critical and commercial hit Obsession. The team will be facing off against Nathaniel Milbury, AKA Mister Sinister, played by Adam Driver.

The addition of the X-Men to the MCU has been highly anticipated and teased several times over the years, but it was only in the latest Spider-Man that the Marvel mutants were finally brought into the fold.

Tech.title: Xteink’s tiny e-readers are getting access to free books through Libby
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

One of the big tradeoffs with Xteink’s pocket-friendly e-readers is a lack of easy access to ebooks. On a Kindle or Kobo you can download tens of thousands of titles through each device’s respective online bookstores, but with Xteink’s devices you have to source DRM-free ebooks on your own. That’s about to change, as the developers of CrossPoint Reader, a free alternative firmware for the X3, X4, and X4 Pro, are introducing support for third-party plug-ins that will expand the e-readers’ capabilities. One of the first from the community will give the devices access to DRM-protected ebooks borrowed through OverDrive’s Libby library app, or purchased through bookstores like Kobo’s.

The new functionality is still in beta, but while the team behind CrossPoint Reader provided me with custom firmware I’ve been testing on the X4 Pro for the past few days, it’s now available to anyone who wants to try it. Getting ebooks from Libby onto the tiny e-readers isn’t as streamlined as using its mobile app or as simple as Kobo’s native OverDrive support, but it’s much easier than I expected. If you’re already comfortable with wirelessly transferring files to your tiny e-reader, loading ebooks from Libby isn’t much harder.

Until now, you had to source DRM-free ebooks to load and read on Xteink’s e-readers.

The first step is saying good riddance to the frustrating stock firmware on Xteink’s devices and installing the free CrossPoint Reader alternative. The easiest approach is to connect your e-reader to your computer with its USB-C cable, power it on, and then flash the new firmware directly through a browser using the CrossPoint Reader website that lets you select your specific device and which version of the firmware you want.

You then need to download and install CrossPoint Reader’s new Plugin Store, which is available here. Installation is as simple as unzipping a few files onto your e-reader’s microSD card, which will put a new Plugins section on the e-reader’s homescreen. It’s currently populated with a few different tools you can download, but the important one to install is the “Protected Content” plug-in. It runs through CrossPoint Reader’s built-in web server (which is probably much easier to use than you think) and allows Xteink’s devices to access ebooks protected by the Adobe Digital Editions DRM.

To get it all working you’ll need a free ByteBooks account (or you can convert an older Adobe Digital Editions account you haven’t touched in years) so you can login and authorize your e-reader to open DRM-protected ebooks. You’ll also need access to Libby itself on another device, which requires a library card to sign in. For several reasons, including the fact that Xteink’s devices use low-power ESP-32 processors, you’re not able to search or download ebooks from Libby directly on the e-readers themselves.

You can use CrossPoint Reader’s built-in web server to wirelessly copy ebooks to your e-reader. But its new “Protected Content” plug-in now allows you to load DRM-protected ebooks, too.

Once you borrow a book the Libby apps will let you download it as a protected EPUB file. What you’re actually downloading first is a tiny ACSM file that an authorized reading app uses to access the DRM-protected ebook file. The new “Protected Content” plug-in running through the CrossPoint Reader web server processes an ACSM file moved to the microSD card, downloads a copy of the book, and copies the EPUB file to your e-reader, where you can read it for as long as the loan allows.

The process is similar for ebooks purchased from stores like Kobo’s that use the EPUB format with ADE. (Amazon doesn’t.) When logged into Kobo’s website (not the desktop app) you can download an ACSM file for a book you’ve purchased, copy it to your Xteink device, and then process it with the plug-in to access the ebook you can actually read.

Common Stacks is a free mobile and desktop app that streamlines the process of borrowing library books through Libby and getting them onto Xteink’s e-readers.

If you want to simplify the Libby process, you can instead download and install an app called Common Stacks (available for Android, Windows, and macOS, with iOS support coming soon) that’s designed to provide access to multiple free ebook libraries, including ones you host yourself. The app includes full access to Libby and can both download and send ebook files directly to Xteink’s e-readers with just a couple of clicks. Common Stacks also relies on CrossPoint Reader’s web server functionality running in the back end, but getting borrowed books onto the X4 Pro was as easy as borrowing library books on my Kobo is.

While Libby and Common Stacks is one of the best ways to get free ebooks onto Xteink’s devices, you’ll want to be mindful that selection will vary from library to library, and you may occasionally have to wait to download a popular title depending on how many digital copies are available or are already loaned out. However, now that Xteink’s tiny e-readers finally have access to DRM-protected ebooks — whether borrowed or bought — they’re an even more tempting alternative to Kindles and Kobos.

Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

Tech.title: We’re reaching peak camera with the Sony A7R VI
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

It wasn’t long ago that shooting with a super high-resolution camera meant making serious sacrifices for the sake of all those megapixels. Enter the A7R VI.

Sony’s latest flagship high-res camera is a 66.8-megapixel spec monster. In addition to its modest bump in resolution from the last-gen A7R V, it uses a new sensor and processor that unlock nearly any kind of shooting — from sports and action to usable 8K video. It’s a huge departure from years ago, when high-resolution cameras were slower, noisier, and more specialized as a result of all those megapixels.

The A7R VI’s fully stacked sensor and new Bionz XR2 processor allow it to shoot full-resolution bursts at up to 30 frames per second without any viewfinder blackout. And that faster sensor means there’s little downside to using the electronic shutter full time, meaning you get truly silent shooting for any moment you want to be stealthy. The A7R VI also has 8.5 stops of in-body image stabilization, dual USB-C ports (because why not), and Sony’s new AI-based autofocus system.

The A7R V was pretty quick, shooting 60-megapixel images at up to 10 frames per second with its mechanical shutter, but the A7R VI pumps out its 9984 x 6656 resolution RAW files lightning-fast. And these files are huge. They average about 60 megabytes in lossless compressed RAW format, so that one-second burst of 30 shots can soak up 1.8GB. Wild.

I already use a pretty high-res Sony camera that shoots fast: the original A1. I pair it with the even faster but much lower-res A9 III for my wedding photo gigs. But even though I’m used to Sony’s speedy shooters, the A7R VI’s over-the-top resolution and flexibility really impressed me. In the past, super high-res cameras were reserved for studio work, but the A7R VI blows away any reservations over using a camera with 60-plus megapixels of resolution on just about anything: landscapes, sports, action, photojournalism, street photography, portraits, etc. It. Does. Everything.

Previous Next





















1 / 12 All these features, and of course the body is still weather sealed and rugged as well.

I got to spend some time testing an A7R VI, and in that time I used it for casual snapshots, family weekend trips (including a mini safari), Verge product images, and a freelance wedding shoot (as the second photographer). I quickly realized that despite its new battery and ever-so-slightly revised grip around it, the A7R VI feels just like the A7R V — and therefore a whole lot like nearly any other A7 camera. The higher-end A1 II and A9 III still have slightly better ergonomics, but as I’ve said before, any of Sony’s cameras can still cramp my hands after long use.

The upside of the A7R VI’s sameness is that it should easily slot into a pro’s existing Sony system — it feels the same, it shoots the same, and the files process with the same predictable looks. The only real point of friction is dealing with the new NP-SA100 battery if you already own a bunch of the old NP-FZ100 ones (as I do). It’s a shame Sony’s new SA battery doesn’t boost the camera’s life beyond the CIPA-rated 600+ shots, but its added capacity allows the new processor to tap more power while maintaining parity with previous models.

Previous Next









































1 / 22 Here are various sample images I shot using the A7R VI, with some extreme crops to show how much resolution there is to use in these huge files. For reference, our full-image files in these galleries are 2040 x 1360 (our usual web size of about 2.8 megapixels). The crops were done off the original 66.8-megapixel files.

Pretty much all current Sony Alpha cameras have exceptional autofocusing systems. They’re the best in the market, even if recent models from Canon and Nikon are mostly caught up. When I started shooting Sony cameras about five years ago, it drastically changed the way I use autofocus. I keep my cameras on continuous tracking mode nearly 100 percent of the time now, relying on subject and eye detection to make shooting much easier, especially in high-stress situations like a wedding. The A7R VI’s revised autofocus system is Sony’s latest and greatest, but to me it just felt a touch more “sticky” to a subject’s eye than what I’ve got on my last-gen cameras — nothing monumentally better.

The real draw for me was getting these huge 66.8-megapixel files and being able to shoot them as fast as I wanted, as quietly as I needed. The speedy, stacked sensor minimizes any rolling shutter anomalies to the point they’re not really noticeable, so I shot with the electronic shutter almost the entire time. I love this freedom, because I can shoot as much as I want during a wedding ceremony or a speech and not disturb the peace. And even when shooting product images for The Verge, having no mechanical shutter slapping up and down in the camera reduces vibrations just that extra bit more — so I can use even slower handheld shutter speeds. This is particularly helpful when photographing products in difficult lighting.

Previous Next













1 / 8 Here are some before and after edits to show a little of pushing the dynamic range.

And if I want to be extra fast (or sometimes just lazy) all that resolution means I can crop horizontal files to vertical ones without sacrificing print quality — definitely no worry with web quality. Or while under pressure at a busy tech event, I can take one picture of a product and make multiple crops from it to show close-up details I didn’t get to capture further. (Yes, I have done this before. And no, I don’t prefer it.) I’ve already done these kinds of things with my Sony A1, but having more megapixels gives me even more leeway. And this is in a $4,500 camera, compared to the newer version of my camera, which currently costs $7,000.

This is the first of Sony’s R cameras I’ve looked at and thought, “Yeah, this could be my one camera for everything.” (If I wanted that and if I only needed one camera, of course.) It does much of what I need from my A1 and A9 III at a higher resolution and a lower price. There are of course still reasons to go with the A9 III or the A1 II — niche features of a global shutter or a higher flash sync speed — but when it comes to generalist “do anything” cameras, this is it. This is the grail.

A Sony doesn’t have the impeccable handling of a Canon or a Nikon, or the romance of a Fujifilm or a Leica, but what makes the A7R VI captivating are the stone-cold results it delivers. Camera tech is constantly improving, but it will probably be a while before any camera — from Sony or anyone else — is superior enough to justify an upgrade from here.

Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge
